events.enhanced_description: In 1228, Emperor Robert I of the Latin Empire passed away after a seven-year reign in Morea, leading to the ascension of his young brother Baldwin II. The transition of power was overseen by John of Brienne, highlighting the instability of the Latin Empire during this period.
events.name: Emperor Robert I dies in Morea

events.enhanced_description: In 1228, King James I of Aragon initiated a significant military campaign against the Almohads in Majorca, marking a pivotal moment in the Reconquista. This offensive coincided with political shifts in the region as local leaders began to assert independence from Almohad rule.
events.name: James I launches offensive against Almohads

events.enhanced_description: In 1228, the Battle of Bolnisi saw Khwarazmian forces led by Sultan Jalal al-Din Mangburni defeat a coalition of various groups, including Georgians and Kipchaks. This battle was significant in the context of regional power struggles during the early 13th century.
events.name: Battle of Bolnisi

events.enhanced_description: In 1228, King Sukaphaa founded the Ahom Dynasty in Assam, marking the beginning of a significant political and cultural era in the region. His reign would last until 1268, establishing a legacy that would shape the history of Assam.
events.name: King Sukaphaa establishes the Ahom Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The town of Reghin in Transylvania was first mentioned in a charter issued by King Andrew II in 1228, marking its historical significance in the region. This documentation reflects the administrative practices of the time and the growth of settlements in medieval Hungary.
events.name: Reghin first mentioned in charter

events.enhanced_description: In 1228, the city of Tournai issued its first recorded life annuity, a financial instrument that indicated a growing trend in public debt management. This development was part of a broader economic evolution in medieval Europe.
events.name: Tournai issues first recorded life annuity

events.enhanced_description: In 1228, evidence emerged of the Knights Templar acting as cashiers for King Henry III of England, facilitating the transfer of significant funds across Europe. This practice demonstrated the Templars' crucial role in the financial systems of the medieval period.
events.name: Knights Templar used as cashiers by Henry III

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1228, Isabella II, the young Holy Roman Empress and wife of Frederick II, died shortly after giving birth to her second child, Conrad IV. This event had significant political implications, as it left Frederick as regent for the newly born king.
events.name: Isabella II dies after childbirth

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1228, Emperor Frederick II embarked on a Crusade, sailing from Brindisi with a well-equipped army to Acre in the Holy Land. His journey was marked by political tensions, including his excommunication by Pope Gregory IX for proceeding without papal absolution.
events.name: Frederick II sails from Brindisi to Acre

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1228, Pope Gregory IX canonized Saint Francis of Assisi, recognizing his contributions to the Catholic Church and his role in the spiritual revival of the time. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the Franciscan Order.
events.name: Saint Francis of Assisi canonized

events.enhanced_description: In autumn 1228, Frederick II met with an embassy from Sultan Al-Kamil at the Hospitaller camp near Acre. This meeting was crucial as it occurred during a time when Al-Kamil was engaged in military actions in Syria, and it highlighted the complex diplomatic landscape of the Crusades.
events.name: Frederick II receives an embassy from Sultan Al-Kamil

events.enhanced_description: In November 1228, Frederick II showcased his military strength by marching his Crusader army to Jaffa, where he fortified the city. This display was intended to pressure Sultan Al-Kamil into negotiations, which had been interrupted due to hostilities.
events.name: Frederick II pressures negotiations with military display

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1228, Stephen of Anagni was commissioned to collect a special tax across England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales to fund Pope Gregory X's War of the Keys against Frederick II. This tax highlighted the financial strains of the papacy in its conflicts with the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Stephen of Anagni collects special tax for War of the Keys

events.enhanced_description: In 1229, Abu Zakariya Yahya expanded his influence by conquering the cities of Constantine and Béjaïa, establishing himself as the founder and first ruler of the Hafsid Dynasty in Ifriqiya. This expansion marked a significant shift in power dynamics in North Africa.
events.name: Abu Zakariya Yahya expands his influence by conquering the cities of Constantine and Béjaïa (modern Algeria)

events.enhanced_description: In 1229, the Catholic Church permanently established the Inquisition, placing it under the charge of the Dominican Order in Rome. This institution aimed to combat heresy and enforce religious orthodoxy within Christendom.
events.name: The Catholic Church permanently establishes the Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: In 1229, the University of Toulouse was founded in France, with Raymond VII being compelled to finance the teaching of theology. This institution became a significant center of learning in medieval Europe.
events.name: The University of Toulouse is founded in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1229, the episcopal seat was relocated from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near modern-day Turku, with the approval of Pope Gregory IX. This event is often regarded as the founding moment of Turku, which would become an important religious and cultural center.
events.name: Episcopal seat moved to Koroinen

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1229, Emperor Frederick II signed the Treaty of Jaffa, establishing a 10-year truce with Sultan Al-Kamil. This treaty allowed Frederick to regain significant territories in the Holy Land through diplomacy rather than military conflict.
events.name: Treaty of Jaffa signed

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1229, students at the University of Paris rioted over a dispute with a tavern owner, prompting Queen Blanche of Castile to intervene. This incident reflected the growing tensions between the student population and authorities in medieval Paris.
events.name: University of Paris strike

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1229, Frederick II entered Jerusalem, receiving the keys from the Muslim governor in a formal surrender. This event symbolized a significant achievement in Frederick's Crusade, despite the ongoing tensions with the local Muslim population.
events.name: Frederick II enters Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1229, Frederick II crowned himself King of Jerusalem in an impromptu ceremony at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This act underscored his authority and ambitions in the region, as he sought to consolidate power following the Treaty of Jaffa.
events.name: Frederick II crowns himself King of Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1229, Count Raymond VII was compelled to sign the Treaty of Paris, effectively ending the Albigensian Crusade. This treaty allowed Raymond to retain some feudal rights while swearing allegiance to King Louis IX, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in southern France.
events.name: Treaty of Paris signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1229, Frederick II departed from Acre amidst public unrest, where he was met with hostility from the local populace. This departure highlighted the challenges he faced in maintaining control and support in the Holy Land.
events.name: Frederick II departs from Acre

events.enhanced_description: In May 1229, Frederick II attended the wedding proxy of the young King Henry I of Cyprus and Alice of Montferrat, strengthening political ties through marriage. This event was part of Frederick's broader strategy to consolidate power in the region.
events.name: Frederick II attends wedding proxy in Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: In June 1229, Emir Al-Ashraf Musa successfully captured Damascus, subsequently acknowledging the supremacy of his elder brother, Al-Kamil. This strategic move also involved compensating their brother, An-Nasir Dawud, with the lordship of Al-Karak in the Transjordan region.
events.name: Emir Al-Ashraf Musa captures Damascus and acknowledges the supremacy of his elder brother Al-Kamil

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1229, King James I of Aragon launched a major expedition to conquer Majorca, departing from Tarragona with a formidable fleet. This military campaign was part of the broader Reconquista efforts against Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: James I embarks on expedition to Majorca

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1229, Ögedei Khan, the third son of Genghis Khan, was proclaimed 'Great Khan' of the Mongol Empire during a Kurultai council. His ascension marked a pivotal moment in the consolidation of Mongol power and the continuation of Genghis Khan's legacy.
events.name: Ögedei Khan is proclaimed 'Great Khan' of the Mongol Empire

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1229, Frederick II successfully regained lost territories in Italy while navigating the complex political landscape of the Papal States. His efforts to stabilize his rule were met with various challenges, including local unrest.
events.name: Frederick II recovers lost Italian territories

events.enhanced_description: In October 1229, King Henry III of England called for an army to assemble at Portsmouth to reclaim lost territories in Normandy from the French. The expedition faced logistical issues, leading to tensions between Henry and his chief minister, Hubert de Burgh, marking the beginning of a significant rift between them.
events.name: King Henry III calls for an army to be assembled at Portsmouth to be transported to Normandy to regain lost territories from the French

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1229, the Battle of Olustra resulted in the defeat and deposition of King Eric XI of Sweden by Canute II. This battle marked a significant shift in the Swedish monarchy and the power struggle within the region.
events.name: Battle of Olustra

events.enhanced_description: In 1230, King Alfonso IX of León achieved a significant victory over Ibn Hud al-Yamani, known as Almogàver by Christians. This victory opened the path for Leonese troops towards Badajoz, furthering the Reconquista efforts.
events.name: King Alfonso IX defeats Ibn Hud al-Yamani

events.enhanced_description: In 1230, Frederick II granted the Teutonic Order special privileges for the conquest of Prussia, including Chełmno Land, under papal sovereignty. This act facilitated the forced conversion of the Prussians to Christianity and expanded the Order's influence.
events.name: Frederick II bestows on the Teutonic Order a special privilege for the conquest of Prussia

events.enhanced_description: In 1230, Norman forces under Richard Mór de Burgh invaded Connacht and besieged Galway. Despite the initial assault, the siege ended inconclusively after a week, forcing the Normans to retreat.
events.name: Siege of Galway

events.enhanced_description: In 1230, the Battle of Yassıçemen occurred, where a Seljuk-Ayyubid coalition of approximately 40,000 men defeated the Khwarazmians led by Sultan Jalal al-Din Mangburni at Erzincan on the Upper Euphrates. This battle was significant in the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Yassıçemen

events.enhanced_description: Around 1230, the Carmina Burana, a collection of medieval poetry and songs, was created. This work reflects the social and cultural life of the time, showcasing themes of love, fate, and the joys and sorrows of life.
events.name: Creation of the Carmina Burana poetry and song collection

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1230, the Battle of Klokotnitsa took place, where Byzantine forces led by Theodore Komnenos invaded Bulgaria, breaking a peace treaty with Tsar Ivan Asen II. The battle ended in a decisive Bulgarian victory, leading to significant territorial gains for Bulgaria.
events.name: Battle of Klokotnitsa

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1230, King Henry III embarked from Portsmouth with a large expeditionary force, landing at Guernsey before proceeding to Saint-Malo. His forces marched through the County of Anjou, capturing strategic locations, including the castle of Mirebeau.
events.name: King Henry III embarks from Portsmouth with a large expeditionary force

events.enhanced_description: In August 1230, Emperor Frederick II returned from the Sixth Crusade and signed the Treaty of Ceprano with Pope Gregory IX. This peace agreement included concessions regarding territories held by the Papal States and marked a significant moment in the relationship between the Empire and the Papacy.
events.name: Treaty of Ceprano

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1230, Alfonso IX of León died after a 42-year reign, and his son Ferdinand III succeeded him. Ferdinand's ascension marked a continuation of the efforts to consolidate and expand the Kingdom of León.
events.name: Alfonso IX dies and is succeeded by Ferdinand III

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1230, King Henry III signed a truce with King Louis IX of France, marking a temporary cessation of hostilities. This agreement allowed Henry to leave a small force in Brittany and Normandy while returning to England.
events.name: Henry III signs a truce with King Louis IX

events.enhanced_description: In 1231, Emperor Frederick II promulgated the Constitutions of Melfi, a comprehensive collection of laws for Sicily, alongside the Edict of Salerno, which regulated medical practices. This legislation was significant in establishing legal frameworks and advancing medical education in the region.
events.name: Emperor Frederick II promulgates the Constitutions of Melfi

events.enhanced_description: In 1231, during the Reconquista, Castillian forces led by King Ferdinand III successfully re-conquered the city of Quesada. This victory was part of the broader efforts to reclaim territories from Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Reconquista: Castillian forces under King Ferdinand III re-conquer the city of Quesada

events.enhanced_description: In 1231, Peter des Roches, Bishop of Winchester, played a crucial role in negotiating a three-year truce between England and France. This agreement aimed to stabilize relations and reduce hostilities between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Peter des Roches negotiates a 3-year truce between England and France

events.enhanced_description: In 1231, the University of Cambridge received formal recognition from King Henry III through a writ of authority over its townspeople. This recognition marked an important step in the establishment of Cambridge as a leading center of learning in medieval England.
events.name: The University of Cambridge is recognised by Henry III

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the Lombards in 1231, Richard Filangieri successfully sailed to Beirut, where the town was surrendered to him. He subsequently occupied Sidon and Tyre, while also convening a meeting of the High Court in Acre, asserting his authority with letters from Frederick II.
events.name: War of the Lombards: Richard Filangieri sails for Beirut, where the town is handed over to him

events.enhanced_description: In 1231, Mongol forces besieged the city of Kuju, employing siege towers and ladders to assault the defenses. Despite being heavily outnumbered, the Goryeo garrison displayed remarkable resilience and refused to surrender.
events.name: Siege of Kuju: Mongol forces besiege the city of Kuju

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1231, Hubert de Burgh emerged as a powerful lord in the Welsh Marches, controlling key castles at Cardigan and Carmarthen. His growing influence prompted a campaign by Llywelyn the Great to challenge Norman lordship in Wales.
events.name: Spring – Hubert de Burgh becomes a powerful lord in the Welsh Marches

events.enhanced_description: In April 1231, a devastating fire erupted in the southeastern district of Hangzhou during the Song dynasty, consuming approximately 10,000 houses. The limited visibility at night hampered firefighting efforts, leading to significant destruction.
events.name: A huge fire breaks out at night in the southeast of Hangzhou during the Song dynasty

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1231, Pope Gregory IX issued the papal bull Parens scientiarum, which guaranteed the independence and self-governance of the University of Paris. This decree marked a significant moment in the history of academic freedom and institutional autonomy.
events.name: Pope Gregory IX issues Parens scientiarum

events.enhanced_description: In August 1231, Ögedei Khan commanded the Mongol invasion of Korea, initiating a military campaign that began with the crossing of the Yalu River. The Mongol forces quickly secured the surrender of Uiju, aided by Goryeo general Hong Pok-wŏn and his contingent.
events.name: August – Ögedei Khan orders the invasion of Korea

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1231, King Henry III ordered the sheriffs of Hampshire, Dorsetshire, and Wiltshire to grant Simon de Montfort the lands of his father, Simon de Montfort the elder. This act solidified Simon's position and influence within the English nobility.
events.name: King Henry III orders the sheriffs to give Simon de Montfort possession of his father's lands

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1231, Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II appointed Marshal Richard Filangieri as his imperial legate, dispatching a significant expeditionary force primarily composed of Lombard knights and infantry to bolster the defense of Jerusalem. This military campaign aimed to reinforce Christian presence in the Holy Land amid ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Autumn – Frederick II appoints Marshal Richard Filangieri as his imperial legate, and sends an expeditionary army of mostly Lombards for the defense of Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In December 1231, King Henry III concluded his Welsh campaign by negotiating peace with Llywelyn the Great. This agreement marked a temporary respite in the ongoing conflicts between the English crown and Welsh leaders.
events.name: Henry III ends his Welsh campaign and makes peace with Llywelyn the Great

events.enhanced_description: In 1232, Peter de Rivaux was appointed as Lord Treasurer of King Henry III's household, a position that granted him substantial influence over the king's financial affairs. This appointment was part of a broader strategy by Henry to consolidate power within his administration.
events.name: Peter de Rivaux is made Lord Treasurer of Henry III's household

events.enhanced_description: In 1232, King Henry III established the Domus Conversorum, or 'House of the Converts,' in London, which served as an institution for Jewish converts to Christianity. This initiative reflected the complex religious dynamics of medieval England.
events.name: The Domus Conversorum is established by Henry III

events.enhanced_description: In 1232, the Almohad army laid siege to the city of Ceuta, where Abu Musa, the rebellious brother of Caliph Idris al-Ma'mun, sought refuge. The siege highlighted the internal strife within the Almohad Caliphate and the shifting power dynamics in North Africa.
events.name: The Almohad army besieges the city of Ceuta

events.enhanced_description: During the Second Mongol invasion of Korea in 1232, the original set of woodblocks used to print the Tripitaka Koreana was tragically destroyed by fire. This loss represented a significant cultural and religious setback for the Korean Buddhist community.
events.name: The original set of woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana is destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: In 1232, the northern French city of Troyes issued its first recorded life annuities, a financial instrument that confirmed the trend of consolidating local public debts. This development reflected the evolving financial practices in medieval Europe.
events.name: The northern French city of Troyes issues its first recorded life annuities

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1232, the Mongol army, led by General Subutai, decisively defeated the Jin forces near Yuzhou in the Battle of Sanfengshan. This victory marked a significant step towards the Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty, as the Jin army was left demoralized and disorganized.
events.name: Battle of Sanfengshan: The Mongol army defeats the Chinese Jin forces near Yuzhou

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1232, during the Mongol–Jin War, Ögedei Khan and his brother Tolui initiated the siege of Kaifeng, the capital of the Jin dynasty. The siege was marked by political intrigue and a devastating plague that further weakened the city's defenses.
events.name: Mongol–Jin War: The Mongol army begins the siege of Kaifeng

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1232, Anthony of Padua was canonized by Pope Gregory IX in Spoleto, less than a year after his death. His canonization underscored his significant impact on the Catholic Church, and he became recognized as the patron saint of lost items.
events.name: Anthony of Padua is canonized by Pope Gregory IX

events.enhanced_description: In June 1232, amid the Mongol invasion of Korea, military dictator Choe Woo ordered the relocation of the royal court to Ganghwa Island, defying the wishes of King Gojong and other officials. This strategic move aimed to fortify defenses against the advancing Mongol forces.
events.name: Mongol invasion of Korea: Choe Woo orders the royal court to be moved to Ganghwa Island

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1232, the Cypriot army, led by King Henry I, achieved a decisive victory against the Lombard forces of Emperor Frederick II at the Battle of Agridi. This battle was pivotal in the ongoing conflicts over control of Cyprus.
events.name: Battle of Agridi: The Cypriot army under King Henry I defeats the Lombard forces of Emperor Frederick II

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1232, Muhammad I was elected as the ruler of the Taifa of Arjona, marking the beginning of the Nasrid dynasty. His election was a significant political shift as he revolted against Ibn Hud, the independent ruler of Al-Andalus.
events.name: Muhammad I is elected as ruler of the Taifa of Arjona

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1232, King Henry III of England dismissed his justiciar Hubert de Burgh, replacing him with Frenchmen Peter des Roches and Peter de Rivaux. This decision caused significant discontent among the English barons, highlighting the tensions between the monarchy and the nobility.
events.name: King Henry III dismisses his justiciar Hubert de Burgh

events.enhanced_description: In August 1232, Pope Gregory IX found himself confined to his summer residence at Anagni due to pressures from Lombard forces in Rome. This situation highlighted the political tensions between the papacy and local powers during this period.
events.name: Gregory IX is forced to remain in his summer residence at Anagni

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1232, Pope Gregory IX proclaimed the Stedinger Crusade in northern Germany, targeting the Stedinger peasants who had resisted the authority of the Church. This crusade reflected the ongoing conflicts between ecclesiastical and secular powers in medieval Europe.
events.name: Gregory IX orders the Stedinger Crusade to be proclaimed in northern Germany

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1232, Emperor Go-Horikawa abdicated the throne in favor of his one-year-old son, Shijō, after an 11-year reign. Due to Shijō's young age, real power was largely held by his relatives, leading to a period of political maneuvering.
events.name: Emperor Go-Horikawa abdicates in favor of his son Shijō

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1232, Korean forces achieved a significant victory against a Mongol attack at Cheoin, modern-day Yongin. This battle marked a turning point in the Mongol invasion of Korea, leading to a peace treaty and the withdrawal of Mongol troops.
events.name: Battle of Cheoin: Korean forces defeat a Mongol attack

events.enhanced_description: In 1233, after a protracted 10-month siege, Lombard forces at Kyrenia surrendered to John of Beirut. The terms allowed the defenders to leave with their possessions, and the event marked the restoration of Cyprus under the rule of King Henry I.
events.name: War of the Lombards: Lombard forces at Kyrenia surrender to John of Beirut

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 1233, King Ferdinand III of Castile, known as 'the Saint,' successfully conquered the cities of Trujillo and Úbeda as part of the ongoing Reconquista. His military campaigns significantly advanced Christian control in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Winter – Reconquista: King Ferdinand III of Castile conquers Trujillo and Úbeda

events.enhanced_description: In 1233, Gendt was granted city rights by Otto II, count of Guelders, marking an important milestone in its development and governance. This recognition facilitated Gendt's growth as a significant urban center in the region.
events.name: Gendt receives city rights

events.enhanced_description: In 1233, Pope Gregory IX established the Papal Inquisition, a significant move aimed at standardizing the Church's approach to heresy. This institution would play a crucial role in the Church's efforts to maintain doctrinal purity throughout Europe.
events.name: Establishment of the Papal Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1233, during the Mongol–Jin War, Ögedei Khan's forces successfully captured Kaifeng, the capital of the Jin dynasty, after a grueling 13-month siege. The fall of the city marked a significant victory for the Mongols, leading to widespread plunder and the flight of Emperor Aizong.
events.name: Mongol army captures Kaifeng

events.enhanced_description: In August 1233, Richard Marshal, 3rd Earl of Pembroke, forged a significant alliance with Llywelyn the Great, aiming to challenge the authority of King Henry III. This collaboration marked a pivotal moment in the Welsh struggle for independence, as they sought to unite their forces against the English crown.
events.name: Richard Marshal signs an alliance with Llywelyn the Great

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1233, King Andrew II of Hungary took the Oath of Bereg, pledging to the Holy See that he would not employ Jews and Muslims in the administration of royal revenues. This vow led to significant diplomatic complaints and ecclesiastical censure.
events.name: Oath of Bereg: King Andrew II of Hungary vows to the Holy See

events.enhanced_description: In November 1233, Henry III's forces stationed at Grosmont Castle were ambushed by a coalition of Welsh and English rebels. The surprise attack resulted in the capture of several of the king's supporters and the temporary loss of the castle to the insurgents, highlighting the growing unrest in the region.
events.name: Attack on Henry III's army at Grosmont Castle

events.enhanced_description: In December 1233, the Mongol forces under Ögedei Khan laid siege to Caizhou, aligning with the Song dynasty to eliminate the Jin dynasty. This strategic partnership was crucial in the Mongol conquest of northern China.
events.name: Siege of Caizhou

events.enhanced_description: In 1234, King Canute II of Sweden, known as 'the Tall', passed away after a brief five-year reign. His death led to the return of his rival, Eric XI, who may have reclaimed the throne following a civil conflict.
events.name: Death of King Canute II of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1234, King Andrew II of Hungary declared his son, Coloman of Galicia, as the ruler of Bosnia. This controversial decision led to a power struggle, as Coloman's authority was contested by Matej Ninoslav, the legitimate ruler.
events.name: Proclamation of Coloman of Galicia as ruler of Bosnia

events.enhanced_description: In 1234, during the Reconquista, King Sancho II of Portugal successfully captured the cities of Aljustrel and Mértola from Moorish control. This victory was part of the broader Christian efforts to reclaim the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Sancho II of Portugal conquers cities from the Moors

events.enhanced_description: In 1234, the Manden region initiated a revolt against the Kaniaga Kingdom, setting in motion a series of events that would eventually lead to the establishment of the Mali Empire. This uprising was a crucial step in the region's political transformation.
events.name: Manden region rises against Kaniaga Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 1234, Lund Cathedral in Sweden suffered extensive damage due to a catastrophic fire. The incident prompted significant donations for its reconstruction, highlighting the community's commitment to restoring this important religious site.
events.name: Fire damages Lund Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1234, the Mongol army led by Ögedei Khan captured Caizhou, marking the end of the Jin dynasty. The fall of the city followed a two-month siege and resulted in the abdication and subsequent suicide of Emperor Aizong to avoid capture.
events.name: Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In November 1234, Pope Gregory IX declared war on the city of Rome following a revolt that forced him into exile. He issued a papal bull calling for a new crusade, reflecting the intense political and religious turmoil of the period.
events.name: Pope Gregory IX proclaims war on Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 1235, the Hiberno-Norman lord Richard Mór de Burgh successfully conquered Connacht, expelling Felim Ua Conchobair from power. This event marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Ireland during the period.
events.name: Conquest of Connacht by Richard Mór de Burgh

events.enhanced_description: In 1235, a general inquisition was initiated in France, reflecting the Church's growing efforts to root out heresy and enforce orthodoxy. This marked a significant development in the relationship between the Church and the French populace.
events.name: General inquisition begins in France

events.enhanced_description: In 1235, Elizabeth of Hungary was canonized by Pope Gregory IX, recognizing her contributions to the Church and her charitable works. Her canonization reflected the growing veneration of saints in medieval Europe.
events.name: Canonization of Elizabeth of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: A Chinese text from 1235 documents the vibrant social life in Hangzhou, the capital of the Song dynasty, highlighting various clubs such as the West Lake Poetry Club and the Buddhist Tea Society. This reflects the cultural richness and communal activities of the time.
events.name: Social clubs in Hangzhou City

events.enhanced_description: Around 1235, Lancaster Royal Grammar School was founded in northern England, contributing to the educational landscape of the region. This establishment marked an important step in the development of formal education in medieval England.
events.name: Foundation of Lancaster Royal Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: Around 1235, the Battle of Kirina took place, where Mandinka prince Sundiata Keita defeated Sosso king Soumaoro Kanté. This victory is traditionally viewed as the founding moment of the Mali Empire, leading to significant political and cultural developments in West Africa.
events.name: Battle of Kirina

events.enhanced_description: In early 1236, a tournament at Tickhill escalated into a conflict between northern and southern factions, but was ultimately resolved by papal legate Otto of Tonengo. This event highlighted the tensions within English nobility during this period.
events.name: Tournament at Tickhill

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, the Mongols led by Batu Khan began a sweeping campaign across Central Asia, establishing dominance in the Russian steppe and imposing tribute on neighboring states, significantly disrupting the Kievan Rus' and its relations with the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Mongol Expansion under Batu Khan

events.enhanced_description: During the Mongol-Song War in 1236, the Mongols, led by Ögedei Khan, penetrated deep into Southern Song territory, capturing the strategic city of Xiangyang. This victory was crucial for the Mongols as they sought to expand their influence in China.
events.name: Mongol-Song War

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, King Kalinga Magha, known as 'the Tyrant', was expelled from Polonnaruwa to Jaffna, marking a significant shift in power within the region of modern Sri Lanka. This event was pivotal in the political landscape of the island.
events.name: Expulsion of King Kalinga Magha

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, the Kouroukan Fouga, the constitution of the Mali Empire, was established by an assembly of nobles from the Mandinka clan. This constitution laid the groundwork for governance and social structure in one of West Africa's most powerful empires.
events.name: Kouroukan Fouga Constitution

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, the Goryeo court in Korea initiated the preparation of new woodblocks for printing the Buddhist Tripiṭaka, aimed at both spiritual protection against Mongol invasions and replacing a previously destroyed set. This effort underscored the importance of Buddhist texts in Korean culture.
events.name: Preparation of Buddhist Tripiṭaka Woodblocks

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, Pope Gregory IX issued a condemnation of the connections between the Knights Templar and Knights Hospitaller with the Assassin fighters in the Middle East. This papal bull aimed to sever these ties and prevent further collaboration.
events.name: Papal Condemnation of Knights' Links to Assassins

events.enhanced_description: In 1236, Ibn al-Nafis moved to Egypt with some colleagues at the request of the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil. He was appointed chief physician at al-Naseri hospital.

image.caption: Opening page of a medical work by Ibn al-Nafis, in an illuminated manuscript.

events.name: Ibn al-Nafis moved to Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1236, King Henry III of England married Eleanor of Provence at Canterbury Cathedral, with Simon de Montfort overseeing the banquet. This union strengthened political ties and Eleanor was subsequently crowned queen at Westminster Abbey.
events.name: Marriage of King Henry III and Eleanor of Provence

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1236, a fleet from the republics of Venice, Genoa, and Pisa, led by Geoffrey II of Villehardouin, arrived at Constantinople. Their intervention successfully broke the blockade of the city, showcasing the strategic naval power of these republics.
events.name: Arrival of ships at Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1236, Roger of Wendover, an English Benedictine monk and chronicler, died at St Albans Abbey. His historical writings were continued by Matthew Paris, contributing significantly to the chronicling of English history.
events.name: Death of Roger of Wendover

events.enhanced_description: In June 1236, the Novgorodians elected the 16-year-old Alexander Nevsky as their prince, entrusting him with military leadership during a time of external threats. His election marked the beginning of a significant political career that would shape the future of Novgorod.
events.name: Election of Alexander Nevsky as prince of Novgorod

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1236, the Treaty of Kremmen was signed, where Duke Wartislaw III acknowledged the seignory of Henry Borwin III following a successful military campaign. This treaty aimed to ease tensions in the region and stabilize the political landscape.
events.name: Treaty of Kremmen

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1236, Castilian forces under King Ferdinand III captured the Muslim city of Córdoba from Emir Ibn Hud during the Reconquista. This victory was a crucial step in the Christian reclamation of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Siege of Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: In July 1236, at a diet in Piacenza, Emperor Frederick II expressed his ambitions to reclaim all of Italy for the Holy Roman Empire. This proclamation underscored the ongoing power struggles in Italy and the emperor's aspirations for greater control.
events.name: Diet in Piacenza

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Saule, fought on September 22, 1236, marked a significant victory for the Lithuanians and Semigallians against the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. This battle was pivotal in halting the expansion of the Christian military orders in the Baltic region.
events.name: Battle of Saule

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1236, the Mongols under Batu Khan successfully besieged and captured the capital city of Bilär after 45 days. This victory contributed to the Mongol conquest of the Volga Bulgars and further solidified their power in the region.
events.name: Siege of Bilär

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1236, Razia Sultana became the first female Muslim ruler of the Indian subcontinent after deposing her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz. Her reign marked a significant moment in the history of female leadership in Islamic governance.
events.name: Razia Sultana's Ascension

events.enhanced_description: At the behest of King Louis IX of France, Thomas II married Joanna, widow of Ferdinand of Flanders, in 1237. This marriage solidified Thomas's claim to the countship of Flanders, enhancing his political stature.
events.name: Marriage of Thomas II and Joanna

events.enhanced_description: In 1237, the Livonian Brothers of the Sword were absorbed into the Teutonic Order, forming the autonomous Livonian Order. This marked a significant consolidation of military and religious power in the Baltic region, coinciding with an Estonian rebellion.
events.name: Livonian Crusade

events.enhanced_description: In 1237, Grand Prince Yuri II of Vladimir gathered forces to confront the Mongols at the Voronezh River. Despite their efforts, the Rus' forces were overwhelmed, leading to a retreat and further Mongol advances into Russian territories.
events.name: Battle of Voronezh River

events.enhanced_description: In 1237, Cölln was founded on Fischerinsel, becoming a vital trade center linked to Magdeburg and Frankfurt an der Oder. This establishment laid the groundwork for the later development of Berlin.
events.name: Foundation of Cölln

events.enhanced_description: In 1237, the Teutonic Order, led by Grand Master Hermann von Balk, established the fortified settlement of Elbląg along the Elbląg River. This strategic stronghold played a significant role in the Order's expansion into the region, influencing trade and military operations in medieval Poland.
events.name: Elbląg is founded by the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Hermann von Balk

events.enhanced_description: In spring 1237, Al-Ashraf Musa, the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, rallied his allies to support Kayqubad I of the Sultanate of Rum amidst rising tensions. This political maneuvering set the stage for potential civil conflict within the Seljuk realm.
events.name: Al-Ashraf Musa's Support for Kayqubad I

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1237, Emperor Frederick II assembled a force of approximately 15,000 men to confront the rebellious Lombard League. His campaign included crossing the Alps to Verona, where he allied with local lords, intensifying the conflict in Northern Italy.
events.name: Emperor Frederick II's Expedition against the Lombard League

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1237, the Battle of the Puig saw Aragonese forces under Bernat Guillem de Montpeller decisively defeat the Almohad army of Zayyan ibn Mardanish. This victory forced Zayyan into exile and marked a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Puig

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1237, Al-Ashraf Musa died after an eight-year reign, leading to his brother As-Salih Ismail's succession. This transition heightened tensions as Ismail fortified Damascus against his brother Al-Kamil's forces from Egypt.
events.name: Death of Al-Ashraf Musa

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1237, King Henry III of England and Alexander II of Scotland signed the Treaty of York, establishing Henry's sovereignty over Scotland and marking the end of Scottish territorial claims in Northern England.
events.name: Treaty of York

events.enhanced_description: In 1239, the Mongols under Batu Khan continued their invasion of Kievan Rus', devastating the region and sacking key cities such as Pereyaslavl. This campaign further solidified Mongol dominance in Eastern Europe and contributed to the fragmentation of Rus' principalities.
events.name: Mongol Invasion of Kievan Rus'

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1237, Frederick II achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Cortenuova against the forces of the Lombard League, capturing around 5,000 Lombards. His triumphal entry into Cremona symbolized his dominance in Northern Italy.
events.name: Battle of Cortenuova

events.enhanced_description: In December 1237, Rus' forces led by Yuri II of Vladimir faced annihilation at Kolomna during a siege by the Mongols. The swift capture of Kolomna led to the fall of Vladimir, marking a critical point in the Mongol invasion of Rus'.
events.name: Siege of Kolomna

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1237, the Mongols under Batu Khan laid siege to Ryazan, breaching the city walls after five days of fierce fighting. The siege culminated in the city's plunder and the death of its prince, Yuri Igorevich.
events.name: Siege of Ryazan

events.enhanced_description: After the Mongols devastated Ryazan in 1237, Kievan knight Evpaty Kolovrat rallied 1,700 survivors to pursue Batu Khan's forces. His audacious attack on the Mongol rearguard resulted in significant casualties for the invaders, although Kolovrat ultimately fell in battle.
events.name: Evpaty Kolovrat's Revenge

events.enhanced_description: In January 1238, Simon de Montfort secretly married Eleanor, sister of King Henry III, despite her previous vow of chastity. This controversial union, performed without the approval of the barons, drew condemnation from Archbishop Edmund of Abingdon.
events.name: Simon de Montfort marries Eleanor

events.enhanced_description: In 1238, the Nizari Imam Muhammad III and Abbasid caliph Al-Mustansir attempted to forge a Muslim-Christian alliance against the Mongols by sending a diplomatic mission to European kings Louis IX of France and Henry III of England. Unfortunately, this initiative proved unsuccessful.
events.name: Nizari Imam and Abbasid caliph's diplomatic mission

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1238, the Mongol forces under Batu Khan and Subutai besieged Moscow, a fortified village crucial for trade and military strategy. After five days of relentless assault, the Mongols captured the settlement, marking a significant point in their campaign against the Kievan Rus'.
events.name: Siege of Moscow

events.enhanced_description: In early 1238, the 12-year-old Prince Vasily of Chernigov led a valiant defense against the Mongol siege of Kozelsk, managing to hold out for nearly two months. Despite his courageous efforts and successful sorties, the city eventually fell, resulting in tragedy for its defenders.
events.name: Siege of Kozelsk

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1238, the Mongol army decisively defeated the Kievan Rus' forces led by Grand Prince Yuri II at the Sit River. This battle not only resulted in Yuri's death but also shattered hopes for a united resistance against the Mongol invasion in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Sit River

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1238, Al-Kamil, the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt, died in Damascus, leading to a power struggle as his son Al-Adil II ascended the throne. The ensuing civil war would reshape the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Death of Al-Kamil

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1238, the Teutonic Knights and King Valdemar II of Denmark finalized the Treaty of Stensby, mediated by papal diplomat William of Modena. This agreement resolved disputes and integrated the Livonian Brothers of the Sword into the Teutonic Order.
events.name: Treaty of Stensby

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on July 11, 1238, Emperor Frederick II laid siege to Brescia, rejecting negotiations with the Lombard League. His aggressive tactics and refusal to compromise ultimately led to a failed siege, as the city's defenders mounted a successful counterattack.
events.name: Siege of Brescia

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1238, the Battle of Örlygsstaðir saw Sighvatr Sturluson and his son defeated by Kolbeinn ungi Arnórsson and Gissur Þorvaldsson, marking a significant conflict during the Age of the Sturlungs in Iceland. This battle was pivotal in the struggle for control over the island.
events.name: Battle of Örlygsstaðir

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1238, King James I of Aragon successfully captured Valencia from the Moors, who retreated to Granada. This victory was significant in the Christian Reconquista, although it came at the cost of James' cousin, Bernat Guillem de Montpeller.
events.name: King James I of Aragon captures Valencia

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1238, Batu Khan ordered the withdrawal of Mongol forces from the ravaged northern territories of Rus'. This retreat followed a campaign marked by widespread destruction and the subjugation of local populations.
events.name: Mongol Withdrawal from Northern Rus'

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1238, Muhammad I, the Almohad ruler of the Emirate of Granada, began the construction of the Alhambra Complex, a stunning architectural feat that would become a symbol of Islamic art and culture in Spain. This project was built on the site of a pre-Islamic fortress, blending history with new artistic vision.
events.name: Construction of the Alhambra Complex

events.enhanced_description: In 1239, King Louis IX of France convened a parlement, or court of law, in Paris, marking a significant development in the legal and political framework of Ancien Régime France. This event underscored the growing importance of royal authority and judicial processes in governance.
events.name: King Louis IX holds a parlement in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1239, Pope Gregory IX renewed the excommunication of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, while he was at his court in Padua. In retaliation, Frederick expelled the Franciscans and Dominicans from Lombardy, escalating tensions between the papacy and the imperial authority.
events.name: Renewal of Excommunication of Frederick II

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1239, Edward I of England, known as Longshanks, was born at the Palace of Westminster. His birth was significant not only for the royal lineage but also because he was named after Edward the Confessor and had Simon de Montfort as his godfather, linking him to the influential baronial class.
events.name: Birth of Edward I of England

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1239, Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, launched an invasion of Romagna and Tuscany, aiming to capture Rome. He appointed his son Enzo as vicar general for Northern Italy, while also reorganizing the Holy Roman Empire's administration to support his military ambitions.
events.name: Frederick II's invasion of Romagna and Tuscany

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1239, a Crusader force led by King Theobald I of Navarre arrived at Acre, where they convened with local barons to strategize against the Ayyubids in Egypt. This marked a renewed effort in the Crusades, highlighting the ongoing conflict between Christian and Muslim powers in the region.
events.name: Barons' Crusade arrives at Acre

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1239, King Béla IV of Hungary permitted approximately 40,000 Cumans, fleeing the Mongol invasion, to settle in Hungary. This decision was contingent upon their leader Kötens' promise to convert to Christianity, reflecting the complex interplay of politics and religion during this turbulent period.
events.name: Cumans settle in Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In October 1239, the Mongols led by Batu Khan launched a brutal attack on Chernigov, where the local garrison attempted to defend the city. Despite the arrival of Prince Mstislav III Glebovich with reinforcements, the Mongols' superior tactics and weaponry led to a devastating defeat, resulting in the pillaging of the city and surrounding areas.
events.name: Sack of Chernigov

events.enhanced_description: In November 1239, Pope Gregory IX officially granted Crusade status to King Ferdinand III of Castile, empowering him to lead a campaign against the Almohads in Murcia. This endorsement was part of the broader Christian Reconquista efforts in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Pope Gregory IX grants Crusade status to Ferdinand III

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1239, an expeditionary force of around 4,000 knights under Theobald I departed Acre for the Egyptian frontier, accompanied by local barons and military orders. This campaign aimed to re-establish Crusader presence in the region and confront the Ayyubid forces.
events.name: Theobald I's expedition to the Egyptian frontier

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1239, Sultan as-Salih Ayyub dispatched an Ayyubid army to Gaza to secure the Egyptian border against Crusader advances. This strategic move was part of the ongoing military engagements between the Ayyubids and the Crusaders in the region.
events.name: Ayyubid army sent to Gaza

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 2007, the Hamas militant wing achieved a decisive victory in the Battle of Gaza, effectively gaining control over the Gaza Strip. This conflict marked a significant escalation in the Fatah-Hamas rivalry and had lasting implications for Palestinian governance.

locations.name: Gaza City, Gaza Strip, State of Palestine

events.name: Battle of Gaza

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1239, Ayyubid forces under An-Nasir Dawud marched into largely undefended Jerusalem, leading to the city's surrender. The fall of Jerusalem marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict, as the Ayyubids dismantled the city's fortifications.
events.name: Ayyubid forces capture Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 1240, Alexander Nevsky faced conflict with the Kievan nobles and merchants of Novgorod over trade issues, leading to his banishment along with his family. This event marked a significant shift in his political career, as he relocated to the region around Moscow.
events.name: Alexander Nevsky's Quarrel with Novgorod Nobles

events.enhanced_description: During the Reconquista, King Sancho II of Portugal successfully conquered the city of Ayamonte from the Almoravids, further securing Portuguese influence in Al-Andalus in 1240. This victory was part of the broader Christian efforts to reclaim territories from Muslim rule.
events.name: Reconquista: Conquest of Ayamonte

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 1240, the Mongols under Batu Khan besieged Kiev, leading to a catastrophic assault on the city. The siege culminated in brutal street fighting, resulting in the massacre of nearly the entire population, with only about 2,000 survivors.
events.name: Siege of Kiev by the Mongols

events.enhanced_description: In 1240, Pope Gregory IX authorized a Crusade against Novgorod, anticipating that the Kievan Rus' would be too engaged with the Mongol threat to mount a defense. This strategic move aimed to expand papal influence in the region amidst the chaos of the Mongol invasions.
events.name: Pope Gregory IX Authorizes Crusade Against Novgorod

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1240, Duke Skule Bårdsson, a claimant to the Norwegian throne, was defeated by King Haakon IV. Seeking refuge in Elgeseter Priory, Skule met a tragic end as the monastery was burned down, solidifying Haakon's rule and ending a prolonged civil war in Norway.
events.name: Defeat of Duke Skule Bårdsson

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1240, the Disputation of Paris commenced at the court of King Louis IX, where four rabbis defended the Talmud against accusations of blasphemy made by Nicholas Donin. This event highlighted the tensions between Jewish and Christian communities in medieval Europe.
events.name: Disputation of Paris

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1240, As-Salih Ayyub ascended to the throne of Egypt after deposing his half-brother Al-Adil II. His reign was marked by internal conspiracies and the establishment of a Mamluk military force, which would play a crucial role in the region's future.
events.name: As-Salih Ayyub Becomes Ruler of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1240, the Battle of the Neva saw a Swedish army led by Bishop Thomas confront the forces of Prince Alexander Nevsky near Novgorod. Alexander's decisive victory not only thwarted the Swedish invasion but also earned him the title 'Nevsky' at the young age of 19.
events.name: Battle of the Neva

events.enhanced_description: In August 1240, Frederick II laid siege to the town of Faenza during the ongoing conflict between the Guelphs and Ghibellines. This military action was part of Frederick's broader strategy to consolidate power against the Papal States, aided by an alliance with Pisa.
events.name: Siege of Faenza

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1240, Richard of Cornwall arrived in Acre for a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, sanctioned by Emperor Frederick II. His visit included negotiations that led to the release of prisoners and support for the construction of a citadel in Ascalon.
events.name: Richard of Cornwall's Pilgrimage

events.enhanced_description: In 1241, Emperor Lizong of the Song Dynasty embraced the Neo-Confucian teachings of Zhu Xi, including his commentary on the Four Books. This acceptance significantly influenced philosophical thought in China and its neighboring countries, including Korea and Japan.
events.name: Emperor Lizong Accepts Neo-Confucian Teachings

events.enhanced_description: In 1241, during the Livonian Crusade, the Livonian Order suppressed the Estonian rebellion that had begun in 1237 on Saaremaa Island. This military action was part of the broader efforts to convert and control the pagan populations of the Baltic region.
events.name: Livonian Crusade: Suppression of Estonian Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 1241, the University of Valladolid was founded in Spain, marking a significant development in the educational landscape of medieval Europe. This institution would become a center of learning and scholarship, influencing the region for centuries.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Valladolid

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1241, the Mongols overwhelmed the Polish armies at the Battle of Chmielnik, leading to the plunder of the abandoned city of Kraków. This battle was part of the larger Mongol invasion of Poland, showcasing their military dominance.
events.name: Battle of Chmielnik

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1760, Frederick the Great executed a series of brilliant maneuvers to defeat the Austrian army led by Marshal Laudon at the Battle of Legnica. This victory was crucial in maintaining Prussian dominance in the ongoing conflicts of the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Legnica

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1241, the Battle of Mohi marked a significant defeat for Béla IV of Hungary at the hands of Batu Khan and Subutai. This battle represented the last major event in the Mongol invasion of Europe, leading to a period of Mongol dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Mohi

events.enhanced_description: In May 1241, an Imperial fleet achieved a notable victory over a Genoan fleet in the Tyrrhenian Sea. This battle was part of the ongoing naval conflicts that characterized the power struggles in the Mediterranean during this period.
events.name: Battle of Giglio

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1241, the Milesian Irish septs, including the Ó Dónaills and Ó Néills, defeated the last Tuatha Dé Danann sept, the Meic Lochlainn, at the Battle of Cameirge in Ulster. This victory solidified the dominance of the Ó Néill dynasty in the region.
events.name: Battle of Cameirge

events.enhanced_description: In the early northern summer of 1241, a succession crisis led to the Mongols withdrawing from their conquests in Europe, retreating behind their river barriers. This withdrawal allowed Poland and Hungary to begin their recovery and reorganization after the devastation of the Mongol invasions.
events.name: Mongol Withdrawal from Europe

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1241, the Treaty of Gwerneigron was signed between Henry III of England and Dafydd ap Llywelyn, following Henry's invasion of Wales. This treaty curtailed Dafydd's authority and denied him royal title, reflecting the ongoing tensions between England and Wales.
events.name: Treaty of Gwerneigron

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1241, Snorri Sturluson, the renowned Icelandic saga writer, was murdered by Gissur Þorvaldsson, an emissary of King Haakon IV of Norway. This event marked a significant moment in Icelandic history, reflecting the political tensions of the time.
events.name: Murder of Snorri Sturluson

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1241, Pope Celestine IV succeeded Pope Gregory IX, becoming the 179th pope. His papacy came during a tumultuous period marked by ongoing conflicts and challenges to papal authority.
events.name: Papal Succession: Celestine IV

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, Siegfried III, the archbishop of Mainz, led a campaign to conquer Wiesbaden, a free imperial city, and ordered its destruction during the conflict between Emperor Frederick II and the Papal States. This event underscored the power struggles within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Siegfried III, archbishop of Mainz, conquers Wiesbaden

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, King Sancho II of Portugal continued his Reconquista efforts by conquering the cities of Tavira, Alvor, and Paderne from Muslim control. This expansion was part of the broader Christian campaign to reclaim territory in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: King Sancho II conquers cities in the Reconquista

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Grobnik Field in 1242 saw Croatian forces under King Béla IV successfully halt the Mongol invasion into Hungary and Croatia. This victory was crucial for the defense of the region and led to the rebuilding of fortifications across Béla's kingdom.
events.name: Battle of Grobnik Field

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, Mongol forces led by Subutai besieged and captured the city of Sernya. The siege was marked by the tragic death of Queen Narchat, who was killed while attempting to flee the city.
events.name: Siege of Sernya

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, Batu Khan established the Golden Horde at Sarai, marking a significant development in Mongol governance in the region. This establishment followed the news of the death of Great Khan Ögedei, leading to a strategic withdrawal of Mongol forces.
events.name: Batu Khan establishes the Golden Horde at Sarai

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir died, leading to the succession of al-Musta'sim to the Caliphal throne. This transition marked a significant moment in the history of the Abbasid Caliphate during a period of decline.
events.name: Death of Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, William of Modena, an Italian bishop and papal diplomat, established four dioceses in Poland, including the Archdiocese of Warmia. His efforts were part of the broader Christianization of Eastern Europe.
events.name: William of Modena sets up dioceses in Poland

events.enhanced_description: In 1242, Ibn al-Nafis, an Arab polymath, made significant contributions to medical science by suggesting that the right and left ventricles of the heart are separate and describing the lesser circulation of blood. His work laid the groundwork for future advancements in cardiovascular physiology.
events.name: Ibn al-Nafis describes blood circulation

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1242, the young Emperor Shijō of Japan died unexpectedly, leading to a succession dispute. Ultimately, Go-Saga, the son of former Emperor Tsuchimikado, ascended to the throne amidst the political turmoil.
events.name: – The 10-year-old Emperor Shijō of Japan dies

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1242, Prince Alexander Nevsky was joined by his brother Andrey II in Novgorod, bolstered by their elite druzhina. Their united front allowed Alexander to retake the city with minimal resistance, thwarting the Crusader threat from Izborsk.
events.name: Alexander Nevsky Joins Forces with Andrey II

events.enhanced_description: In April 1242, Alexander Nevsky led a Russian force across the frontier into Livonian territory, aiming to raid Catholic Estonia. His campaign was met with resistance from local Crusader forces, culminating in a defeat at Mooste bridge, which forced him to retreat.
events.name: April – A Russian force led by Alexander Nevsky crosses the frontier between Novgorod and Livonian Crusader territory, to raid into Catholic Estonia

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1242, the Mongols under Batu Khan besieged the city of Esztergom, causing significant destruction. This siege was part of the Mongol invasions that threatened much of Eastern Europe during this period.
events.name: Spring – Siege of Esztergom

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1242, the Templar Knights conducted a raid on the city of Hebron, amidst rising tensions in the region. An-Nasir Dawud, the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, responded by sending forces to cut off access to Jerusalem.
events.name: Spring – The Templar Knights raid Hebron

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1242, the Battle of Lake Peipus, also known as the Battle on the Ice, took place where Alexander Nevsky's Russian forces successfully repelled an invading Crusader army of Teutonic Knights. The battle was notable for its challenging icy conditions, which contributed to the defeat of the outnumbered Crusaders.
events.name: – Battle of Lake Peipus (or Battle on the Ice)

events.enhanced_description: In May 1242, Isabella of Angoulême, mother of King Henry III of England, successfully persuaded him to mount an expedition to retake Poitou. This military campaign was marked by Henry's arrival at Royan, where he joined forces with rebelling French nobles.
events.name: May – Isabella of Angoulême persuades Henry III

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1242, the Avignonet massacre occurred when a group of Cathars, allegedly with the support of Count Raymond VII of Toulouse, murdered inquisitor William Arnaud and eleven companions. This event highlighted the ongoing tensions between the Catholic Church and the Cathar heretics in the region.
events.name: – Avignonet massacre

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1242, Alexander Nevsky preemptively sent envoys to Batu Khan, acknowledging Mongol rule over Novgorod before the Mongols had even reached the city. This strategic capitulation aimed to secure peace and stability for his territory amid the looming threat of Mongol invasion.
events.name: Summer – Alexander Nevsky sends envoys to Batu Khan

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1242, Hafsid forces under Sultan Abu Zakariya Yahya conquered the city of Tlemcen, establishing it as a vassal state. This victory was part of the Hafsid expansion against the Almohad Caliphate in the Maghreb region.
events.name: Summer – Hafsid forces conquer Tlemcen

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1242, the Battle of Taillebourg saw French forces under King Louis IX decisively defeat King Henry III of England at the Charente River. Following the battle, Louis IX pursued the retreating English troops, capturing many prisoners and solidifying French dominance in the region.
events.name: 22 – Battle of Taillebourg

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1242, King Béla IV of Hungary issued the Golden Bull, granting the inhabitants of Gradec (modern-day Zagreb) and Samobor the status of a royal free city. This decree was part of Béla's efforts to strengthen his rule and promote urban development in his kingdom.
events.name: – King Béla IV issues the Golden Bull

events.enhanced_description: In 1243, Emperor Frederick II besieged the city of Viterbo at the request of the rebel citizens. The siege was marked by fierce resistance, and after a peace treaty was signed, Frederick withdrew his forces.
events.name: Siege of Viterbo

events.enhanced_description: In March 1243, King Ferdinand III of Castile transformed the independent Taifa of Murcia into a protectorate, initiating a process of colonization and Christianization. This marked a significant step in the Reconquista, as Ferdinand sought to consolidate Christian rule in the region.
events.name: March – King Ferdinand III turns Taifa of Murcia into a protectorate

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1243, King Henry III granted Simon de Montfort the custody of Kenilworth Castle, adding to Simon's control over Odiham Castle. This consolidation of power marked a significant moment in the political landscape of England.
events.name: Spring – Henry III bestows custody of Kenilworth Castle to Simon de Montfort

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1243, the Treaty of Bordeaux was signed, establishing a truce between King Louis IX of France and King Henry III of England, effectively ending the Saintonge War. Despite the treaty, tensions and skirmishes continued between the two kingdoms.
events.name: – Treaty of Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: In May 1243, Castillan troops were garrisoned in Murcia to support the Hudid Dynasty, reflecting the ongoing military and political complexities of the region during the Reconquista.
events.name: – Castillan troops garrisoned in Murcia

events.enhanced_description: In June 1243, Pope Innocent IV was elected as the 180th pope of the Catholic Church, succeeding Celestine IV after a sede vacante that lasted seven months. His papacy would later be marked by significant political and religious challenges, including conflicts with the Holy Roman Emperor.
events.name: Pope Innocent IV succeeds Celestine IV

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243 saw the Mongol forces under Baiju Noyan decisively defeat the Seljuk Turks of the Sultanate of Rum and their Byzantine allies. This defeat resulted in the Seljuks and the Empire of Trebizond becoming vassals of the Mongols, significantly altering the power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Battle of Köse Dağ

events.enhanced_description: In 1243, a Crusader force led by Balian III of Beirut successfully captured the city of Tyre after a prolonged siege, marking a significant military victory in the context of the Crusades. The siege was bolstered by the arrival of reinforcements from Alice, queen of Cyprus, effectively ending the War of the Lombards.
events.name: Crusader force under Balian III captures Tyre

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Montségur in 1244 culminated in the capture and destruction of the Château de Montségur by French forces after a nine-month siege. This event marked the tragic end of the Cathar resistance in the region, with many adherents burned at the stake, leading to the scattering of the remaining followers.
events.name: Siege of Montségur

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Almizra, signed in March 1244, was an agreement between King James I of Aragon and King Ferdinand III of Castile regarding the distribution of Muslim territories yet to be conquered in the Iberian Peninsula. This treaty effectively curtailed further Aragonese expansion southward.
events.name: Treaty of Almizra

events.enhanced_description: In June 1244, Khwarazmian forces invaded Syrian territory, inflicting devastation on the land and burning villages. Unable to besiege the fortified city of Damascus, they captured Galilee and advanced toward Jerusalem, showcasing the ongoing instability in the region.
events.name: Khwarazmian invasion of Syrian territory

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1244, Pope Innocent IV was forced to flee Rome due to the imperial forces of Emperor Frederick II. Disguised, he traveled to Sutri, where Genoese galleys awaited to transport him to safety.
events.name: Pope Innocent IV driven from Rome

events.enhanced_description: In April, the Rashidun army, led by Amr ibn al-As, conquered Jerusalem after a protracted six-month siege. The surrender of the Byzantine garrison to Caliph Umar I marked a significant moment in Islamic history, as Umar declined to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre to preserve its status.
events.name: Siege of Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1244, the Tower of David surrendered to Khwarazmian forces, resulting in the exodus of approximately 6,000 Christians from Jerusalem. Tragically, many were massacred upon their return, highlighting the brutal consequences of the siege.
events.name: Surrender of the Tower of David

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1244, Crusaders gathered a force of around 7,000 men outside Acre in response to the news of Jerusalem's sacking by Khwarazmian forces. They were joined by Ayyubid forces, indicating a significant coalition against the invaders.
events.name: Crusaders assemble outside Acre

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1244, Pope Innocent IV fled to France, arriving in Lyon where he sought protection from King Louis IX. Despite Lyon's nominal allegiance to the Holy Roman Empire, Innocent found refuge and support in France.
events.name: Innocent IV flees to France

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of La Forbie on October 17, 1244, resulted in a catastrophic defeat for a Crusader army of approximately 10,000 men, led by Walter IV of Brienne, against Egyptian and Khwarazmian forces. The battle saw around 7,500 Crusaders killed, and many leaders captured, marking a severe blow to Crusader hopes in the region.
events.name: Battle of La Forbie

events.enhanced_description: In December 1244, King Louis IX of France fell gravely ill due to a severe malarial infection. Near death, he vowed to embark on a crusade if he recovered, which he did, leading to his preparations for the Seventh Crusade.
events.name: King Louis IX falls ill

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1244, Pope Innocent IV convened a general council in Lyon, which would later be recognized as the First Council of Lyon. This council was significant in addressing various church matters and reaffirming papal authority.
events.name: Innocent IV summons a general council

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 1245, Castilian forces under King Ferdinand III besieged the Moorish-held city of Jaén. Despite attempts to breach the city gates, the siege faced challenges, including counterattacks from Moorish knights.
events.name: Siege of Jaén

events.enhanced_description: In 1245, the region of Segovia in the Kingdom of Castile was reported to be depopulated and sterile, reflecting the devastating impact of ongoing warfare and fiscal pressures on the local population.
events.name: Segovia described as depopulated

events.enhanced_description: In 1245, King Henry III initiated the rebuilding of Westminster Abbey as a tribute to Edward the Confessor. This project would lead to the creation of one of England's most iconic religious structures.
events.name: Rebuilding of Westminster Abbey

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1245, Thomas, the bishop of Turku, was granted resignation by Pope Innocent IV after admitting to serious misconduct, including torture and forgery. This incident highlighted the challenges of ecclesiastical authority during this period.
events.name: Thomas, bishop of Turku resigns

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1245, Pope Innocent IV dispatched Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and Stephen of Bohemia to the Mongol court at Karakorum, urging the Mongols to consider converting to Christianity. This mission marked one of the earliest diplomatic efforts between the papacy and the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Innocent IV sends envoys to the Mongols

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1245, during the First Council of Lyon, Pope Innocent IV declared Emperor Frederick II excommunicated and deposed, while also proclaiming the Seventh Crusade. This council was pivotal in addressing the conflicts between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: First Council of Lyon

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, Frederick II of the Holy Roman Empire quelled a revolt in Sicily, a region rife with political tension. Following the suppression, he ordered the deportation of the remaining Muslim inhabitants of Lucera, a significant act that reflected the broader conflicts of the era.
events.name: Frederick II suppresses a Sicilian revolt and deports the remaining Muslim inhabitants of Lucera

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, Alice of Champagne, the queen and regent of Jerusalem, passed away after a brief reign of three years. Her death led to the ascension of her son, Henry I of Cyprus, who appointed Balian III of Beirut as his bailli, indicating a shift in the political landscape of the Crusader states.
events.name: Alice of Champagne dies after a 3-year reign

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, after a protracted siege lasting four months, Damascus fell to the Ayyubid vizier Mu'in al-Din Hasan ibn al-Shaykh. This event marked a significant shift in control within the region and underscored the ongoing conflicts between the Ayyubids and their adversaries.
events.name: Damascus falls to the Ayyubid vizier Mu'in al-Din Hasan ibn al-Shaykh

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, Robert Grosseteste completed his translation of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics from Greek into Latin, a pivotal moment that initiated the broader rediscovery of Aristotelian philosophy in Medieval Europe. This translation played a crucial role in the intellectual revival of the time.
events.name: Robert Grosseteste translates Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, a notable astronomical event occurred when the perihelion of the Earth's orbit coincided with the December solstice. This phenomenon is significant in the study of celestial mechanics and Earth's seasonal cycles.
events.name: The perihelion of the Earth's orbit coincides with the December solstice

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, Beaulieu Abbey in England was dedicated in the presence of King Henry III, Queen Eleanor, and their young son, Prince Edward. This event underscored the importance of monastic institutions in medieval society and royal patronage.
events.name: Beaulieu Abbey is dedicated

events.enhanced_description: In 1246, Katedralskolan was established beside Uppsala Cathedral, serving as a seminary for clergy. This institution played a significant role in the education and training of religious leaders in Sweden.
events.name: Katedralskolan in Uppsala is established

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1246, Emperor Go-Saga of Japan abdicated the throne in favor of his young son, Go-Fukakusa, who became the 89th Emperor of Japan. This transition marked a significant moment in the Japanese imperial lineage and governance.
events.name: Emperor Go-Saga abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1246, Castilian forces led by King Ferdinand III successfully captured the city of Jaén from the Andalucians. The surrender of Sultan Muhammad I marked a significant victory for Castile and established the Emirate of Granada as a vassal state.
events.name: Siege of Jaén successful

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1246, Henry Raspe was elected as an anti-king in Germany, opposing Conrad IV and his father, the excommunicated Emperor Frederick II. This election highlighted the ongoing political strife within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Henry Raspe elected anti-king

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1246, the Battle of the Leitha River saw Hungarian forces under King Béla IV defeat Duke Frederick II (the Quarrelsome). The battle resulted in Frederick's death and the dissolution of the House of Babenberg, significantly impacting the political landscape of Austria.
events.name: Battle of the Leitha River

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1246, Güyük Khan was enthroned as the 3rd Great Khan of the Mongol Empire in Karakorum, a ceremony attended by a papal mission led by Giovanni da Pian del Carpine. His ascension marked a pivotal moment in Mongol politics, as he sought to reverse his mother's edicts and expand Mongol influence into the Middle East.
events.name: Güyük Khan is enthroned as the 3rd Great Khan of the Mongol Empire

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1246, Yaroslav II, the father of Alexander Nevsky, was poisoned by Töregene Khatun after being summoned to Karakorum by Güyük Khan. This political assassination highlighted the intense power struggles within the Mongol Empire during this period.
events.name: Yaroslav II is poisoned by Töregene Khatun

events.enhanced_description: In November 1246, Michael II Asen ascended to the throne of the Bulgarian Empire, succeeding his brother Kaliman I, who may have been poisoned. His reign was marked by efforts to reclaim Bulgarian territories from the Byzantine Empire under John III Doukas Vatatzes.
events.name: Michael II Asen succeeds Kaliman I

events.enhanced_description: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi proposed the Tusi couple in 1247 as a solution for the latitudinal motion of the inferior planets. The mechanism converts circular motions into linear oscillation.

image.caption: Animated diagram of the Tusi couple showing circles, ellipses, and hypotrochoid paths.
image.date_qualification: Modern animation illustrating the mathematical mechanism proposed in 1247; the saved image date is 2017-04-11.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Al-Tusi proposes the Tusi couple

events.enhanced_description: In 1248, Pope Innocent IV grants the Croatians of southern Dalmatia permission to use their own language and script in the Roman Rite liturgy. This decision reflects the growing recognition of local languages in religious practices.
events.name: Pope Innocent IV grants permission for Croatian language use in liturgy

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1248, the Battle of Parma sees Imperial forces led by Emperor Frederick II defeated by the Lombard League. This loss not only results in significant treasure loss for Frederick but also marks a pivotal moment in the struggle for power in Italy.
events.name: Battle of Parma
