events.name: Marco Polo’s Asian journey begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1271, Mamluk forces under Baibars successfully capture the strategically vital Krak des Chevaliers from the Knights Hospitaller. The defenders receive a letter urging them to surrender, and they retreat under safe-conduct to Tripoli.
events.name: Siege of Krak des Chevaliers

events.enhanced_description: In May and June of 1271, Baibars attempts an unsuccessful siege of Tripoli and a naval invasion of Cyprus. His Egyptian fleet faces disastrous weather, resulting in the loss of ships and crews to the Cypriots.
events.name: Baibars' unsuccessful siege of Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1271, Lord Edward of England and King Charles I of Anjou arrive in Acre with a fleet of 30 galleys, marking the start of Edward's crusade against Baibars. Despite their efforts, they fail to capture any territory, leading to a swift peace negotiation.
events.name: Lord Edward's crusade begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1271, Kings Ottokar II of Bohemia and Stephen V of Hungary sign the Peace of Pressburg, resolving territorial disputes following Ottokar's failed invasion of Hungary. The treaty ensures stability in the region by preventing Stephen from supporting Ottokar's rivals in Carinthia.
events.name: Peace of Pressburg

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Alphonse, Count of Poitiers, on August 21, 1271, the counties of Poitou and Toulouse are integrated into the French crown's territories. This consolidation reflects the growing power of the French monarchy during this period.
events.name: Absorption of Poitou and Toulouse into French domains

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1271, Pope Gregory X is elected as the 184th pope of the Catholic Church, following a prolonged three-year conclave. His election represents a compromise between French and Italian cardinals.
events.name: Pope Gregory X succeeds Clement IV

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1271, the Japanese Buddhist priest Nichiren is arrested by soldiers and nearly executed. This incident, known as Hosshaku Kenpon, marks a pivotal moment in the development of Nichiren Buddhism.
events.name: Nichiren's arrest

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1271, Kublai Khan officially renames his empire to 'Great Yuan', marking the formal establishment of the Yuan dynasty in China. This change signifies the consolidation of Mongol rule over China.
events.name: Kublai Khan renames his empire

events.enhanced_description: In February 1272, Charles I of Anjou occupies the city of Durrës, establishing the Angevin Kingdom of Albania. This move is part of his broader ambitions in the region, supported by local Albanian nobles.
events.name: Charles I occupies Durrës

events.enhanced_description: In June 1272, Marinid forces invade Spain, causing widespread destruction and chaos. Their attacks prompt King Alfonso X of Castile to abandon diplomatic efforts and declare war against Granada.
events.name: Marinid forces land in Spain

events.enhanced_description: In November 1272, Charles I of Anjou orders the capture of all Genoese within his territories, sparing only the Guelphs. This aggressive policy leads to the occupation of Ajaccio by the Sicilian fleet and condemnation from Pope Gregory X.
events.name: Charles I orders Genoese prisoners

events.enhanced_description: During the Reconquista, King Afonso III of Portugal successfully eliminates the last Moorish community in Faro, completing the reconquest of the western Iberian Peninsula around 1272. This victory marks a significant milestone in the Christian reclamation of the region.
events.name: Reconquista - Elimination of Moorish community

events.enhanced_description: In 1272, the Worshipful Company of Cordwainers and Curriers is granted the rights to regulate the leather trade in the City of London, marking an important development in the organization of trade guilds. This year also sees the Fishmongers Company receiving its first Royal Charter.
events.name: Regulation of leather trade in London

events.enhanced_description: The Alfonsine tables, a set of astronomical tables compiled during the reign of King Alfonso X of Castile, were completed in 1272. These tables were significant for their accuracy and were used for centuries in navigation and astronomy.
events.name: In astronomy, the recording of the Alfonsine tables is completed

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1272, Charles I signs a treaty proclaiming himself King of Albania, pledging to protect the local nobility and honor their privileges from the Byzantine Empire. This treaty solidifies the union between Albania and Sicily under his rule.
events.name: Charles I signs treaty in Albania

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1272, King Hugh III of Cyprus signs a peace treaty with Sultan Baibars of the Mamluks at Caesarea. This agreement secures the Kingdom of Jerusalem's lands and the right to safe passage for pilgrims for a decade.
events.name: Peace signed between Hugh III and Baibars

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1272, an assassination attempt is made on Lord Edward, heir to the English throne, while he is in Acre. A Syrian Nizari assassin infiltrates his chamber and stabs him with a poisoned dagger, but Edward survives, albeit seriously ill for months.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Lord Edward

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1272, King Stephen V of Hungary falls ill and is taken to Csepel Island, where he dies. His death leads to the ascension of his young son Ladislaus IV, with Queen Elizabeth serving as regent during his minority.
events.name: King Stephen V falls ill

events.enhanced_description: In 1272, Nubian forces launched a significant raid on the Egyptian Red Sea outpost of Aydhab and the city of Aswan, prompting a military response from Baibars, the Sultan of Egypt, who invaded the kingdom of Makuria in retaliation. This event highlights the ongoing conflicts and territorial disputes in the region during the medieval period.
events.name: Nubian forces sack the Egyptian Red Sea outpost of Aydhab and raid the southern frontier city of Aswan

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1272, Floris V, Count of Holland, leads an unsuccessful military campaign against Frisia to recover his father's remains. This battle reflects the ongoing tensions and conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Heiloo

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1272, King Henry III of England dies at the Palace of Westminster after a lengthy reign of 56 years. His death leads to the ascension of his son Edward I, who is returning from the Holy Land.
events.name: Death of King Henry III of England

events.enhanced_description: The Congregatio Regni totius Sclavonie Generalis, the oldest surviving document of the Croatian parliament (Sabor), was established in 1273. This document reflects the early development of parliamentary governance in Croatia and the region's political history.
events.name: The Congregatio Regni totius Sclavonie Generalis is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1273, the Sambyeolcho Rebellion against the Goryeo dynasty, a vassal state of the Yuan dynasty, came to an end with the defeat of the rebel forces. This rebellion was significant as it reflected the struggles of local powers against foreign domination.
events.name: Sambyeolcho Rebellion ends in Korea

events.enhanced_description: In 1273, the Holy Redeemer khachkar, a remarkable example of Armenian stone-carving art, was created in Haghpat. This khachkar symbolizes the rich cultural heritage and artistic traditions of medieval Armenia.
events.name: Holy Redeemer khachkar carved in Haghpat

events.enhanced_description: In 1273, King Alfonso X of Castile established the Mesta, granting privileges to promote the wool industry and protect livestock owners. This move was crucial for the economic development of Castile and reflected the importance of agriculture in medieval Spain.
events.name: Alfonso X creates privileges for the Mesta

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1273, Sultan Muhammad I of Granada suffered fatal injuries from a fall during a military expedition near Granada. His death led to his son, Muhammad II, succeeding him and engaging in negotiations with King Alfonso X of Castile, which reflected the complex political dynamics of the Iberian Peninsula during this period.
events.name: Sultan Muhammad I suffers fatal injuries after falling from his horse near Granada

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1273, the Battle of Xiangyang concluded with the surrender of Chinese forces to Kublai Khan's general Aju after a grueling six-year siege. This battle was notable for being one of the first instances where firearms were used in combat, marking a significant development in military technology.
events.name: Battle of Xiangyang

events.enhanced_description: In July 1273, Mamluk forces under Baibars successfully captured Al-Kahf Castle, the last stronghold of the Order of Assassins. This event marked a significant victory for the Mamluks and the decline of the Assassin sect's influence in the region.
events.name: Mamluk forces capture Al-Kahf Castle

events.enhanced_description: In August 1273, Mongol forces surrounded the castle of Al-Bira, leading to a strategic maneuver by Baibars, who managed to launch a counterattack that routed the Mongols. This encounter illustrates the ongoing military conflicts between the Mamluks and the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Mongol forces surround the castle of Al-Bira

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1273, Sultan Muhammad II of Granada sent an embassy to King Alfonso X in Seville, where it was received with honor. This diplomatic move resulted in a significant agreement that established tribute payments and a temporary truce with the Banu rebels, showcasing the intricate political maneuvering of the time.
events.name: Sultan Muhammad II of Granada sends an embassy to Alfonso X in Seville

events.enhanced_description: In October 1273, Rudolf I was elected King of Germany, marking the end of the Great Interregnum. His election was contested by Ottokar II of Bohemia, leading to a significant power struggle that would culminate in war, illustrating the political fragmentation of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Rudolf I is elected King of Germany

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1273, Thomas Aquinas, the influential Italian priest and theologian, began writing his seminal work, Summa Theologica. This text would become a cornerstone of Catholic theology, although he left it unfinished after a profound mystical experience during mass.
events.name: Thomas Aquinas writes Summa Theologica

events.enhanced_description: In December 1273, followers of the Persian poet and mystic Rumi established the Mevlevi Order, also known as the Whirling Dervishes, in Konya. This order became known for its unique spiritual practices and contributions to Sufi mysticism and Turkish culture.
events.name: Establishment of the Mevlevi Order in Konya

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, the first main survey of the Hundred Rolls, an English census aimed at assessing landholdings and rights, was initiated. This survey served as a follow-up to the Domesday Book and was crucial for understanding land ownership and governance in medieval England.
events.name: Hundred Rolls survey begins in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq, the Marinid ruler, peacefully entered Ceuta, effectively ending the city's independence that had lasted for approximately 40 years. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq enters Ceuta

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, the Japanese priest and philosopher Nichiren entered exile on Mount Minobu, where he continued to lead a significant movement through his prolific letter-writing. His teachings and writings would later have a profound impact on Japanese Buddhism.
events.name: Nichiren enters exile on Mount Minobu

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, Italian poet Bonvesin da la Riva authored the didactic-allegoric poem Liber di Tre Scricciur, one of the first major literary works in Italy. This poem, written in the Western Lombard language, explores themes of Hell, the Passion of Jesus, and Paradise, foreshadowing later works like Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy.
events.name: Bonvesin da la Riva writes Liber di Tre Scricciur

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, Pope Gregory X instituted reforms for papal elections, mandating the use of conclaves to expedite the process that had previously taken over three years. This reform aimed to enhance the efficiency and integrity of the election of future popes.
events.name: Pope Gregory X reforms papal elections

events.enhanced_description: In 1274, Pope Gregory X secured the region of Romagna from Rudolf I, solidifying the Papal States' status as a major power in Italy, second only to the Kingdom of Sicily. This exchange marked a significant political maneuver in the complex landscape of Italian city-states and papal influence.
events.name: Gregory X obtains the region of Romagna from Rudolf I, in exchange for acknowledging him as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: In May 1274, the 9-year-old Dante first encountered the 8-year-old Beatrice in Florence, marking the beginning of a profound and lifelong inspiration for the poet. Beatrice would later become a central figure in Dante's works, symbolizing divine love and guidance.
events.name: Dante first sees Beatrice in Florence

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1274, Pope Gregory X convened the Second Council of Lyon, following assurances from Byzantine Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos regarding the Orthodox Church's willingness to reunite with Rome. The council aimed to address key theological disputes but ultimately failed to achieve lasting reconciliation.
events.name: Second Council of Lyon convened by Pope Gregory X

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1274, Edward I of England was crowned king at Westminster Abbey, marking his return from the Holy Land two years after the death of his father, King Henry III. This event was significant in establishing Edward's rule and influence in medieval England.
events.name: Edward I of England crowned king

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1274, Walter de Merton, the English chancellor and regent, retired from royal service, paving the way for Robert Burnell to become a key ally of the Edwardian regime. This transition was significant for the political landscape of England during Edward I's reign.
events.name: Walter de Merton retires from royal service

events.enhanced_description: In November 1274, the Imperial Diet at Nuremberg ordered the restoration of all crown estates seized since the death of Emperor Frederick II to King Rudolf I. This decision was largely supported by European rulers, except for Ottokar II of Bohemia, who had gained significantly from these lands.
events.name: Imperial Diet at Nuremberg orders restoration of crown estates

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1274, the Battle of Bun'ei occurred when Mongol forces, led by Kublai Khan, invaded Japan. Despite initial successes, the invasion was ultimately repelled, aided by a typhoon that destroyed much of the Mongol fleet, marking a pivotal moment in Japanese history.
events.name: Battle of Bun'ei: Mongol forces invade Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, the Byzantine Empire launched a military campaign led by Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos against the Latin principalities in Thessaly. Despite initial successes, the Byzantine forces faced unexpected resistance and ultimately retreated after a surprise attack from a smaller Latin force, showcasing the volatility of medieval warfare.
events.name: Battle of Neopatras

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Demetrias in 1275 saw a fierce naval confrontation between the Byzantine fleet and a joint Latin fleet. The Byzantines initially struggled but were ultimately saved by timely reinforcements, leading to a significant victory that highlighted the strategic importance of naval power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Demetrias

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, the first main survey of the Hundred Rolls, an English census initiated as a follow-up to the Domesday Book, was completed. This survey provided valuable insights into land ownership and rights in medieval England.
events.name: Completion of the Hundred Rolls survey

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, Marinid forces successfully captured the city of Algiers, which was independent at the time. This event marked a significant expansion of Marinid influence in North Africa.
events.name: Marinid forces take the city of Algiers

events.enhanced_description: In March 1275, Mongol forces led by Bayan of the Baarin defeated a Chinese army commanded by Chancellor Jia Sidao on the Yangtze River. This battle was pivotal in the Mongol conquest of the Southern Song dynasty.
events.name: Mongol forces defeat Chinese army on the Yangtze River

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, 17-year-old Marco Polo, along with his father and uncle, arrived at Kublai Khan's summer palace in Shangdu after a four-year journey. Their visit marked the beginning of a significant relationship between the Polos and the Mongol court, influencing European perceptions of Asia.
events.name: Marco Polo arrives at Kublai Khan's palace

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, a Nizari force under Shams al-Din Muhammad temporarily recaptured the mountain fortress of Alamut Castle from Mongol control. This event highlighted the ongoing resistance of the Nizari Ismailis against Mongol domination.
events.name: Recapture of Alamut Castle

events.enhanced_description: In April 1275, the Japanese era of Bun'ei concluded, giving way to the Kenji era during the reign of the young Emperor Go-Uda. This transition marked a significant period in Japanese history, reflecting changes in governance and culture.
events.name: End of the Bun'ei era and beginning of the Kenji era in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, Jean de Meun completed the French allegorical poem Roman de la Rose, building upon the earlier work by Guillaume de Lorris. This literary achievement became one of the most influential texts of medieval literature, exploring themes of love and philosophy.
events.name: Completion of Roman de la Rose

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, Ghent recorded the first instance of a town in the Low Countries issuing life annuities, marking a significant development in public finance. This practice reflected broader trends in the consolidation of local public debt in medieval Europe.
events.name: Emission of life annuities in Ghent

events.enhanced_description: Around 1275, the verge escapement, an essential mechanism in clockmaking, was invented. This innovation played a crucial role in the development of mechanical clocks, significantly impacting timekeeping technology.
events.name: Invention of the verge escapement

events.enhanced_description: In August 1275, Pope Gregory X successfully persuaded King Alfonso X of Castile to relinquish his claim to the title of 'King of the Romans.' This diplomatic achievement strengthened the papacy's influence in northern Italy and solidified alliances with German nobility.
events.name: Gregory X persuades Alfonso X to give up his claim to the title of King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: In 1275, Ramon Llull, a prominent Spanish scholar and theologian, founded a school in Majorca to teach Arabic to preachers. This initiative aimed to facilitate the proselytization efforts among the Moors, reflecting the intersection of education and religious outreach during this period.
events.name: Ramon Llull establishes a school in Majorca

events.enhanced_description: Rabban Bar Sauma, a Chinese Nestorian monk, undertakes a significant pilgrimage from China to Jerusalem, traversing key locations such as Hotan, Kashgar, and Khorasan. His journey reflects the cultural and religious exchanges along the Silk Road during the late 13th century.
events.name: Rabban Bar Sauma, Chinese Nestorian monk, embarks on a pilgrimage from China to Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: The conclusion of the tosafot era marks the end of a significant period of Jewish scholarly commentary on the Talmud, which began around 1100. This transition reflects changes in Jewish intellectual life in medieval Europe.
events.name: The era of the tosafot (medieval commentators on the Talmud) ends (it began in 1100)

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1275, King Edward I of England demanded a meeting with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the prince of Wales, to pay homage. Llywelyn's refusal and subsequent attempts to secure a political marriage highlighted the tensions between England and Wales during this period.
events.name: King Edward I demands homage from Llywelyn ap Gruffudd

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1275, the first Statute of Westminster was established, defining legal privileges for landowners in England. This legislation was a significant development in the evolution of English law and governance.
events.name: First Statute of Westminster

events.enhanced_description: In May 1275, Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq of the Marinids responded to a call from Muhammad II of Granada, landing in Spain with a force of 5,000 men. This military action aimed to bolster Muslim power in the region, demonstrating the ongoing conflict between Christian and Muslim states in the Iberian Peninsula.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Marinid forces led by Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq land in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1275, the Battle of Hova took place in the forest of Tiveden, where King Valdemar of Sweden was defeated by his brother Magnus III. This conflict was pivotal in the struggle for the Swedish throne, leading to significant shifts in power within the kingdom.
events.name: Battle of Hova

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1275, Magnus III was elected king of Sweden at the Stones of Mora, following the deposition of his brother Valdemar Birgersson. This event marked a significant transition in Swedish monarchy and governance.
events.name: Magnus III deposes Valdemar Birgersson

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1275, a Castilian army led by Nuño González de Lara faced defeat against Marinid forces in the Battle of Écija. This battle underscored the ongoing military tensions between Christian and Muslim forces in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Battle of Écija

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1275, a significant earthquake struck southern England, with its epicenter possibly located near Portsmouth or in Glamorgan, Wales. This natural disaster had lasting impacts on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: 1275 British earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1275, Scottish forces under John de Vesci decisively defeated the Manx people at the Battle of Ronaldsway, establishing firm Scottish control over the Isle of Man. This battle was crucial in the context of Scottish expansion and influence in the region.
events.name: Battle of Ronaldsway

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1275, a Castilian army under Sancho of Aragon was defeated by Moorish forces at Martos. This battle illustrated the persistent conflict in southern Spain during the Reconquista.
events.name: Battle of Martos

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1275, Floris V, Count of Holland, granted the city of Amsterdam freedom from taxes, a significant act that contributed to the city's growth and autonomy in the region. This decision marked an important moment in the development of municipal rights in medieval Europe.
events.name: Floris V grants Amsterdam freedom from taxes

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1275, Ghibelline forces achieved victory over a Neapolitan army at the Battle of Roccavione in Piedmont. This battle was part of the larger conflict between Guelphs and Ghibellines in Italy.
events.name: Battle of Roccavione

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dongola in 1276 sees Mamluk forces under Sultan Baibars decisively defeat the Kingdom of Makuria, capturing its capital and forcing King David to flee. This victory expands Mamluk control in the region and marks a significant moment in the history of Nubia.
events.name: Battle of Dongola: Mamluk forces led by Sultan Baibars gain a decisive victory against the Kingdom of Makuria

events.enhanced_description: In 1276, the Mongols successfully capture Alamut Castle from the Nizari forces led by Shams al-Din Muhammad, marking a pivotal moment in the Mongol campaign against the Nizari Ismailis. This event underscores the Mongols' relentless expansion and the fall of significant strongholds.
events.name: The mountain fortress Alamut Castle ("Eagle's Nest") is again captured by the Mongols from a Nizari force under Shams al-Din Muhammad

events.enhanced_description: In 1276, a severe drought begins to impact the Grand Canyon area, leading to significant changes in the lifestyle of the agriculture-dependent Puebloans. This environmental shift forces many to migrate, marking a critical transition in the region's cultural landscape.
events.name: A severe 23-year drought begins to affect the Grand Canyon area, eventually forcing the agriculture-dependent Puebloans (or Anasazi) to migrate out of the region

events.enhanced_description: In 1276, Merton College, Oxford, is first documented as possessing a collection of books, establishing its library as the oldest in continuous daily use in the world. This milestone highlights the importance of academic institutions in preserving knowledge during the medieval period.
events.name: Merton College, Oxford, is first recorded as having a collection of books, making its Library the world's oldest in continuous daily use

events.enhanced_description: In 1276, Henry of Ghent emerges as the last prominent theologian to publicly debate the nature of annuities as a form of usury. His considerations contribute to the evolving discourse on finance and morality in medieval Europe.
events.name: Henry of Ghent (or Henricus) becomes the last major theologian openly to consider annuities as a usurious contract

events.enhanced_description: In 1276, Ottokar II lays the foundation stone for the Minoritenkirche in Vienna, a significant architectural project that reflects the cultural and religious aspirations of the time. This church would become an important landmark in the city.
events.name: The foundation stone of the Minoritenkirche in Vienna is laid by Ottokar II

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1276, Pope Gregory X passes away in Arezzo after a four-year pontificate, leaving a significant legacy in the Catholic Church. He is succeeded by Innocent V, marking a transition in papal leadership during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Pope Gregory X dies after a 4-year pontificate at Arezzo

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1276, Augsburg is officially granted the status of a Free Imperial City, allowing it greater autonomy and self-governance within the Holy Roman Empire. This status enhances its political significance and economic power in the region.
events.name: Augsburg is granted the status of an Free imperial city

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1276, Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq and Muhammad II of Granada negotiate a two-year truce with King Alfonso X of Castile, reflecting the complex political dynamics of the Reconquista. This truce aims to stabilize relations amidst ongoing conflicts in Al-Andalus.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq and Muhammad II, ruler of Granada, agree to a truce with King Alfonso X of Castile ("the Wise") for two years

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1276, the Southern Song dynasty's court and a vast number of citizens flee from Hangzhou to Fujian and Guangdong to evade the advancing Mongol forces led by Kublai Khan. This mass migration signifies the dire straits faced by the Song dynasty during the Mongol conquest.
events.name: Spring – The court of the Southern Song dynasty of China and hundreds of thousands of its citizens flee from Hangzhou to Fujian, and then Guangdong, in an effort to escape a Mongol invasion under Kublai Khan

events.enhanced_description: In June 1276, King Rudolf I of Germany declares war on Ottokar II of Bohemia, leading to a six-month campaign that results in Ottokar's surrender of significant territories. This conflict marks the rise of the Habsburgs as a dominant force in Central Europe.
events.name: King Rudolf I of Germany declares war on his rival Ottokar II of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1276, the remnants of the Southern Song court in Fuzhou crown Prince Zhao Shi as Emperor Duanzong, symbolizing the continuation of the Song dynasty's legacy despite the Mongol invasion. This event marks a significant moment in the struggle for Chinese sovereignty.
events.name: Remnants of the Chinese Song court in Fuzhou province conduct the coronation ceremony for Prince Zhao Shi to become Emperor Duanzong (until 1278)

events.enhanced_description: Pope Innocent V dies on June 22, 1276, after a brief five-month reign, marking another transition in the papacy. His short tenure reflects the instability and challenges faced by the Church during this era.
events.name: Innocent V dies after a 5-month reign at Rome

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1276, Pope Adrian V dies after a mere two-month reign in Viterbo, further contributing to the rapid succession of papacies during this period. His death necessitates yet another election for the papacy.
events.name: Adrian V (Hadrian) dies after a 2-month reign at Viterbo

events.enhanced_description: In August, Sultan Abu Yusuf led Marinid forces across the Strait of Gibraltar, launching a devastating campaign that ravaged the districts of Jerez de la Frontera, Seville, and Córdoba. This military action highlighted the ongoing conflicts in the Iberian Peninsula during the period.
events.name: Marinid forces cross the Strait of Gibraltar

events.enhanced_description: In a notable incident reflecting the tensions between science and religious doctrine, Roger Bacon, a Franciscan friar and lecturer at the University of Oxford, was arrested for promoting views that contradicted the Church's teachings, particularly regarding the Greek philosopher Galen. This event underscores the challenges faced by early scientists in a predominantly religious society.
events.name: Roger Bacon's arrest

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, the Burmese army, numbering around 80,000 and led by King Narathihapate, invaded Mongol territory in Yunnan. Despite their size, the Burmese forces were repelled by the Mongols, who counterattacked and advanced into northern Myanmar, contributing to the eventual disintegration of the Pagan Empire.
events.name: Battle of Ngasaunggyan

events.enhanced_description: In a significant demographic shift, approximately 50,000 citizens of the Southern Song dynasty migrated to Macau, becoming its first recorded inhabitants as they fled from the advancing Yuan dynasty armies. This migration marked the beginning of a new chapter in the region's history.
events.name: Migration of the Southern Song dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In response to the Mongol invasion attempts, a 20-kilometer stone wall was completed along the coast of Hakata Bay in Fukuoka, Japan. This fortification was a crucial defensive measure that reflected the heightened state of alert and preparation against further invasions.
events.name: Completion of stone wall in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In April, Pope John XXI dispatched a papal embassy to Constantinople, urging Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos and his son Andronikos to reaffirm their allegiance to the Union of Lyon. The refusal of Michael to accept this religious union underscored the ongoing tensions between the Eastern Orthodox Church and the Roman Catholic Church.
events.name: Papal embassy to Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1277, the Battle of Desio occurs, where Lombard forces led by Archbishop Ottone Visconti defeat the Della Torre family, solidifying Visconti's control over Milan. This victory marks a significant shift in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Battle of Desio: Lombard forces under Archbishop Ottone Visconti defeat the Della Torre family troops for the rule of Milan

events.enhanced_description: In February 1277, Duke Henry IV Probus of Wrocław is kidnapped from his estates by Bolesław II the Bald, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the region. This event underscores the power struggles among local nobility during this period.
events.name: The Duke of Wrocław Henry IV Probus is kidnapped from his estates in Jelcz

events.enhanced_description: In March 1277, Siger of Brabant, a Dutch philosopher, faces condemnation by the French Inquisition for advocating the Averroist doctrine, which posits that reason is separate from faith. This condemnation highlights the tensions between emerging philosophical ideas and established religious doctrines.
events.name: Siger of Brabant, Dutch teacher and philosopher, is condemned by the French Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, Pope John XXI directed Bishop Étienne Tempier to investigate and address complaints regarding certain philosophical and theological doctrines at the University of Paris. This led to the prohibition of 219 propositions, including those associated with Averroism, reflecting the Church's efforts to maintain doctrinal control.
events.name: Condemnation of 1277

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1277, Charles I of Sicily purchases the title to the Kingdom of Jerusalem from Maria of Antioch, marking a significant transaction in the political landscape of the Crusader states. This acquisition reflects the ongoing interest of European monarchs in the Holy Land.
events.name: Charles I, king of Sicily, buys the title to the Kingdom of Jerusalem from Maria of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1277, Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos finalizes a treaty with the Republic of Venice, establishing a two-year truce and renewing commercial privileges. This agreement aims to strengthen Byzantine defenses against external threats while maintaining economic ties.
events.name: Byzantine–Venetian Treaty: Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos concludes an agreement with the Republic of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, the Battle of Elbistan saw a Mamluk army led by Sultan Baibars decisively defeat a Mongol occupation force in the Sultanate of Rum. Following this victory, Baibars advanced triumphantly to Kayseri, marking a significant moment in the struggle against Mongol dominance in Anatolia.
events.name: Battle of Elbistan

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political move, Mehmet I of Karaman, the Seljuk vizier, issued a firman that mandated the use of the Turkish language in government offices, replacing Arabic and Persian. This decree marked an important step in the promotion of Turkish identity and governance during a period of cultural transition.
events.name: Mehmet I of Karaman issues a firman

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, Pope John XXI passed away after a brief pontificate lasting only eight months. His death marked a significant transition in the papacy, paving the way for Nicholas III to assume leadership of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Death of Pope John XXI

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1277, the Uprising of Ivaylo erupts in northeastern Bulgaria, driven by discontent with Emperor Konstantin Tih's inability to fend off Mongol invasions. Ivaylo leads a successful campaign to drive out the Mongols, ultimately challenging the emperor's authority.
events.name: Uprising of Ivaylo: An uprising under Ivaylo breaks out in northeastern Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, the Treaty of Aberconwy was signed between Prince Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and King Edward I of England, resulting in Llywelyn retaining only the western part of Gwynedd. This treaty was a pivotal moment in the struggle for Welsh independence and territorial integrity.
events.name: Treaty of Aberconwy

events.enhanced_description: In late 1277, Michael VIII Palaiologos dispatches an expeditionary force under John Synadenos to invade Thessaly, but the Byzantines are ambushed and defeated by local Greek forces. This battle highlights the ongoing struggles of the Byzantine Empire to maintain its territorial integrity.
events.name: Battle of Pharsalus: Michael VIII sends a Byzantine expeditionary army under John Synadenos to invade Thessaly

events.enhanced_description: The second survey of the Hundred Rolls, a comprehensive census aimed at assessing landholdings and rights in England, began in 1279 as a follow-up to the Domesday Book. This survey was crucial for understanding feudal obligations and taxation in medieval England.
events.name: The second of two main surveys of the Hundred Rolls is begun

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, the Royal Mint was relocated to the Tower of London, centralizing the production of currency in England. This move was part of a broader effort to enhance control over coinage and reduce the number of mints operating outside the capital.
events.name: The Royal Mint is moved into the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, Abu Ishaq, the uncle of Hafsid caliph Abu Ishaq Ibrahim I, allied with Almohad rebels from Béjaïa to seize control of Tunis. This event marked a significant power shift within the region and highlighted the ongoing conflicts among various factions in North Africa.
events.name: Abu Ishaq takes Tunis

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, a Mongol Yuan embassy sent by Kublai Khan to Japan was killed on the orders of Hōjō Tokimune, escalating tensions that would lead to a second invasion attempt. This incident exemplified the fraught relations between the Mongol Empire and Japan during this period.
events.name: Mongol Yuan embassy killed in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, Ram Khamhaeng ascended to the throne as the third king of the Phra Ruang dynasty, ruling over the Sukhothai Kingdom, which is considered a precursor to modern Thailand. His reign is noted for significant cultural and political developments, including the promotion of the Thai script.
events.name: Ram Khamhaeng becomes king of the Sukhothai Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, the Chola dynasty of South India faced its decline due to aggressive incursions from the Hoysala Empire and the Pandya kingdom. This marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Southern India, leading to the rise of new regional powers.
events.name: The Chola dynasty falls

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, the town of Haapsalu in Estonia was founded, which would later become the center of the Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek. This establishment played a crucial role in the region's ecclesiastical and cultural development.
events.name: Haapsalu is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1279, the medical writings of Abu Bakr al-Razi, also known as Rhazes, were translated into Latin by Faraj ben Salim, marking a significant moment in the transmission of medical knowledge from the Islamic world to Europe. This translation helped to influence the development of medicine in the West.
events.name: Al-Razi's medical writings translated into Latin

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1279, the Battle of Yamen took place, where Kublai Khan's Mongol Yuan fleet engaged the Chinese Song fleet under Admiral Zhang Shijie. This decisive battle led to the fall of the Song dynasty, marking the Mongol Empire's dominance in China and the end of a significant era in Chinese history.
events.name: Battle of Yamen

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1279, Mamluk forces led by the young Sultan Al-Said Barakah and Qalawun invaded Cilician Armenia. The campaign was marred by a revolt in Egypt that forced Barakah to abdicate, leading to Qalawun's rise to power and significant shifts in Mamluk authority in the region.
events.name: Spring – Mamluk forces invade Cilician Armenia

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1279, Thawun Gyi established himself at Taungoo, becoming the first ruler of the Toungoo dynasty, which would play a crucial role in the history of Myanmar until 1317. His reign marked the beginning of a significant political entity in the region.
events.name: Thawun Gyi settles at Taungoo

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1279, the Dai-Gohonzon, the supreme object of veneration in Nichiren Shōshū Buddhism, is said to have been inscribed by the founder Nichiren. This event is pivotal in the history of Nichiren Buddhism, symbolizing the core teachings and practices of the faith.
events.name: Dai-Gohonzon inscribed by Nichiren

events.enhanced_description: In November 1279, King Alfonso X of Castile, known as 'the Wise', granted the cities of Medina-Sidonia and Alcalá de los Gazules to the Order of Saint Mary of Spain, thereby strengthening the influence of the military orders in the region. This act was part of his broader efforts to consolidate power and manage territorial disputes during his reign.
events.name: November – Alfonso X ("the Wise") grants the cities of Medina-Sidonia and Alcalá de los Gazules to the Order of Saint Mary of Spain

events.enhanced_description: In November 1279, during the reign of King Edward I of England, the first of the Statutes of Mortmain was enacted, which aimed to prevent land from being transferred into the possession of the Church. This legislation reflected the tension between the monarchy and ecclesiastical authorities over land ownership and taxation.
events.name: November – The first of the Statutes of Mortmain are passed during the reign of King Edward I ("Longshanks")

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, Tsar Ivan Asen III of Bulgaria fled from Tarnovo, effectively ending the Asen dynasty in Bulgaria. This event marked a significant political shift and the decline of the dynasty that had ruled Bulgaria for several generations.
events.name: Tsar Ivan Asen III flees from Tarnovo

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, Syria attempted to secede from the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, but was met with military resistance from Al Mansur Qalawun, who successfully defeated the rebels. This event underscored the challenges faced by the Mamluks in maintaining control over their territories.
events.name: Syria attempts to secede from the Mamluk Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, Thomas III of Savoy conquered Turin, establishing it as the capital of the House of Savoy. This conquest was pivotal in solidifying the power of the Savoy dynasty in Northern Italy.
events.name: Turin conquered by Thomas III of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, construction began on the northern section of the Grand Canal of China, a monumental engineering project that would enhance trade and transportation across the country. This canal would later become one of the longest and most significant waterways in the world.
events.name: Construction on the northern section of the Grand Canal of China is begun

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, the final expansion of Lincoln Cathedral in England was completed, marking a significant achievement in Gothic architecture. This cathedral became one of the most important religious structures in England, renowned for its stunning design and historical significance.
events.name: Final expansion of Lincoln Cathedral completed

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, the second survey of the Hundred Rolls, which began in 1279, was completed. This census provided vital information about landholdings and feudal obligations, continuing the legacy of the earlier Domesday Book.
events.name: The second of two main surveys of the Hundred Rolls is finished

events.enhanced_description: Around 1280, the ancestors of the Māori people from eastern Polynesia are believed to have become the first human settlers of New Zealand. This migration marked the beginning of a rich cultural history that would shape the future of the islands.
events.name: Approximate date – The ancestors of the Māori people become the first human settlers of New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: In 1280, the Wolf minimum, a period of low solar activity, began. This phenomenon has been studied for its potential impacts on climate and agricultural productivity during the late medieval period.
events.name: The Wolf minimum of solar activity begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1280, during the Reconquista, the Battle of Moclín saw the troops of the Emirate of Granada defeat those of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of León. This battle was part of the ongoing struggle for control over the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Battle of Moclín

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1280, King Magnus III of Sweden enacted a law that established a Swedish nobility by allowing contributions of cavalry members as a substitute for ordinary tax payments. This legislation marked a significant development in the feudal structure of Sweden.
events.name: King Magnus III of Sweden founds a Swedish nobility

events.enhanced_description: In 1281, Osman I ascended to the leadership of the Söğüt tribe following the death of his father, Ertuğrul Ghazi. His rise to power was marked by internal conflict within the clan, particularly against his uncle Dündar Bey, setting the stage for the eventual establishment of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Osman I Becomes Bey

events.enhanced_description: In 1281, Kublai Khan ordered the burning of sacred Taoist texts, drastically reducing the volumes of the Daozang from 4,565 to 1,120. This act reflected the tensions between different cultural and religious practices within the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Kublai Khan Orders Burning of Taoist Texts

events.enhanced_description: In 1281, the Mon Kingdom of Hariphunchai fell as its capital, Lamphun, was captured by King Mangrai of the Lannathai Kingdom. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, contributing to the rise of the Lannathai Kingdom.
events.name: Fall of Hariphunchai

events.enhanced_description: In 1281, Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, granted licenses to the first Lombard merchants to establish a changing business in his realm. This decision facilitated increased trade and economic interaction between Flanders and Italy.
events.name: Lombard Merchants Licensed in Flanders

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1281, Simon de Brion was elected as Pope Martin IV, becoming the 189th pope of the Catholic Church. His papacy would be marked by significant political and religious conflicts, particularly involving the Byzantine Empire and the Sicilian crown.
events.name: Election of Pope Martin IV

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1281, a Byzantine relief force led by Michael Tarchaneiotes arrived at the citadel of Berat, strategically important for its control over the region. Tarchaneiotes employed ambush tactics against the Angevin forces, leading to the capture of their commander, Hugh of Sully, which incited panic among the Angevin troops and resulted in a chaotic retreat.
events.name: Spring – Siege of Berat

events.enhanced_description: In June 1281, King Alfonso X of Castile led an invasion into the lowlands of Granada, accompanied by his sons. Despite initial success in defeating the Moorish forces led by Sultan Muhammad II, the Castilian forces ultimately retreated after failed negotiations, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflict in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Invasion of Granada by Castilian Forces

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1281, the Treaty of Orvieto was signed in the Papal Palace, where Charles I, Giovanni Dandolo, and Philip I agreed on a plan to recover the Latin Empire. This treaty reflected the complex political alliances and ambitions in the wake of the Fourth Crusade.
events.name: Treaty of Orvieto

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1281, the second Mongol invasion of Japan was thwarted by a devastating typhoon, known as kamikaze or 'divine wind,' which destroyed a significant portion of the Mongol fleet. This event solidified Japan's reputation for resilience against foreign invasions during this period.
events.name: Battle of Kōan

events.enhanced_description: In September 1281, two Mongol armies, totaling around 50,000 men, advanced into Syria, with one led by Abaqa Khan targeting Mamluk fortresses and the other, commanded by Möngke Temür, coordinating with Leo III of Cilician Armenia. This military campaign was part of the broader Mongol expansion into the Middle East.
events.name: Mongol Advance into Syria

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1281, Pope Martin IV excommunicated Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, authorizing Charles I of Sicily to launch a Crusade against him. This act escalated tensions between the Byzantine Empire and the Sicilian crown, leading to military preparations that would significantly impact the region.
events.name: Excommunication of Emperor Michael VIII

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1281, the Mamluk forces, numbering around 30,000 and led by Sultan Qalawun, decisively defeated the Mongol army at the Battle of Homs. The battle resulted in significant losses for the Mongols and marked a critical moment in the ongoing conflict between the Mamluks and the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Battle of Homs

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vronen saw Dutch forces, led by Floris V, count of Holland, successfully defeat the West Frisians. This victory was notable not only for its military significance but also for the retrieval of the body of Floris V's father, William II, after 26 years.
events.name: Battle of Vronen

events.enhanced_description: King Stefan Dragutin of Serbia abdicated the throne following a hunting accident that left him injured and ill. His abdication led to the ascension of his younger brother, Stefan Milutin, who would rule Serbia until 1321.
events.name: King Stefan Dragutin's Abdication

events.enhanced_description: Peter III of Aragon secured the support of Nasrid Granada in preparation for the Aragonese Crusade, which was led by Philip the Fair of France. This alliance was crucial in bolstering military efforts against common enemies during the period.
events.name: Support from Nasrid Granada

events.enhanced_description: Daniel of Moscow, the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, was recognized as an independent prince of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. This marked a significant step in the evolution of Moscow as a political entity, eventually leading to the rise of the Tsardom of Russia.
events.name: Daniel of Moscow's Independence

events.enhanced_description: Hertford College was founded at the University of Oxford, contributing to the rich educational tradition of one of the world's oldest universities. The establishment of this college marked an important development in the academic landscape of medieval England.
events.name: Foundation of Hertford College

events.enhanced_description: The Trial of the Pyx was established as a formal process to ensure that newly minted coins conformed to required standards. This practice played a vital role in maintaining the integrity of currency and financial systems in medieval England.
events.name: Trial of the Pyx Established

events.enhanced_description: Evidence of consolidated public debt was discovered in Bruges, marking a significant advancement in the use of annuities to fund government expenditures in the Low Countries. This development highlighted the growing complexity of medieval financial systems.
events.name: Consolidated Public Debt in Bruges

events.enhanced_description: The most recent eruption of Larderello was observed at Boracifero crater lake in southern Tuscany, showcasing the geological activity in the region. This event is part of the historical record of volcanic activity in Italy.
events.name: Eruption of Larderello

events.enhanced_description: The technology of watermarks was introduced by paper manufacturers in Bologna, Italy, representing a significant innovation in the production of paper. This technique would later become essential for authentication and security in documents.
events.name: Introduction of Watermarks

events.enhanced_description: John Peckham, the Archbishop of Canterbury, issued orders to close all synagogues in London and prohibited Jewish doctors from practicing on non-Jews. This action reflected the prevailing attitudes towards Jews in medieval England and the intersection of religious authority and civil governance.
events.name: John Peckham's Orders

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Albi Cathedral in Languedoc began, marking a significant architectural endeavor in medieval France. This cathedral would later become a symbol of the region's religious and cultural heritage.
events.name: Construction of Albi Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In March 1282, Welsh forces led by Prince Dafydd ap Gruffydd captured Hawarden Castle, massacring the garrison and taking the constable prisoner. This act of rebellion against English rule was part of a larger struggle for Welsh independence.
events.name: Capture of Hawarden Castle

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on March 30, 1282, the War of the Sicilian Vespers saw Sicilian conspirators rise against King Charles I, resulting in the deaths of thousands of French. This uprising not only forced Charles to abandon his planned Crusade against the Byzantines but also allowed Peter III to seize control of Sicily.
events.name: War of the Sicilian Vespers

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1282, a French expeditionary army under Jean d'Eppe launched an assault on Forlì, breaching the outer wall. However, they were ambushed and ultimately defeated by Guelph and Ghibelline forces, forcing d'Eppe to retreat.
events.name: Battle of Forlì

events.enhanced_description: In June 1282, Prince Sancho, heir to the throne of Castile, initiated a rebellion against his father, King Alfonso X, gathering a coalition of nobles. This rebellion significantly weakened Alfonso's political position, isolating him from much of his support.
events.name: Prince Sancho's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1282, English forces led by Gilbert de Clare were ambushed and defeated by Welsh troops at Llandeilo Fawr. This battle marked a significant setback for English expansion into southern Wales.
events.name: Battle of Llandeilo Fawr

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1282, King Denis I of Portugal married the 11-year-old Elizabeth of Aragon, daughter of Peter III. This union not only strengthened political ties but also enriched the cultural landscape of Portugal during Denis's reign.
events.name: Marriage of King Denis I and Elizabeth of Aragon

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1282, Peter III of Aragon led an expeditionary army to North Africa in support of a rebellion against the Hafsid Sultanate. However, the rebellion was quickly suppressed, and Peter's forces failed to capitalize on the situation, returning to Sicily amid rising tensions.
events.name: Peter III's Expedition to North Africa

events.enhanced_description: In July 1282, Alfonso X allied with Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq of the Marinid Sultanate, establishing a camp at Zahara de la Sierra. This alliance was marked by a significant financial transaction that showcased the complexities of medieval politics in the Iberian Peninsula.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Alfonso X's Alliance with Marinid Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In August 1282, Castilian forces under Sancho laid siege to Badajoz, but they were ultimately forced to retreat when Alfonso X's combined armies arrived to relieve the city. This event underscored the ongoing power struggles within Castile.
events.name: Siege of Badajoz

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1282, Peter III arrived in the Sicilian town of Trapani while on a military expedition against Tunis. His presence was a response to requests from the inhabitants of Palermo for assistance against Charles I, signaling the shifting political landscape in Sicily.
events.name: Peter III's Arrival in Trapani

events.enhanced_description: In September or October 1282, the Battle of Lake Hód saw Hungarian forces led by King Ladislaus IV successfully repel an invading Cuman army. This victory earned Ladislaus the title 'the Cuman,' highlighting his military prowess.
events.name: Battle of Lake Hód

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1282, Peter III was proclaimed King of Sicily, a significant development that forced Charles I to flee to the Kingdom of Naples. This event marked a pivotal moment in the struggle for control over Sicily and the broader Mediterranean region.
events.name: Peter III Proclaimed King of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: In November 1282, Castilian forces under Alfonso X reconquered Córdoba, a significant victory that marked the end of Prince Sancho's rebellion. This event reinforced Alfonso's authority and restored stability to his reign.
events.name: Reconquest of Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Moel-y-don was a significant conflict in which English forces, led by Luke de Tany, were ambushed and decisively defeated by Welsh troops while attempting to cross a floating bridge to Anglesey. This battle exemplified the fierce resistance of the Welsh against English encroachment during the late 13th century.
events.name: Battle of Moel-y-don

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Orewin Bridge, English forces under King Edward I, numbering around 6,000, achieved a crucial victory against the Welsh army, resulting in the death of their leader, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. This battle marked a pivotal moment in the English conquest of Wales, further solidifying English dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Orewin Bridge

events.enhanced_description: King Rudolf I of the Habsburg dynasty invested his sons, Albert I and Rudolf II, as co-rulers of the duchies of Austria and Styria, laying the groundwork for the House of Habsburg's influence in Central Europe. This event marked a significant consolidation of power within the Habsburg family.
events.name: Investment of Albert I and Rudolf II

events.enhanced_description: King Peter III convened the first regulated Catalan Courts for the Principality of Catalonia, establishing one of the earliest forms of parliamentary governance in medieval Europe. This assembly marked a significant step towards limiting royal power and promoting local autonomy.
events.name: First Regulated Catalan Courts

events.enhanced_description: King Philip III of France enacted an edict that expelled Jews from small villages and rural areas, leading to a mass migration of Jewish communities. This decision reflected the growing anti-Semitic sentiments in medieval France and the precarious status of Jews in society.
events.name: Philip III's Edict Against Jews

events.enhanced_description: An earthquake devastated two-thirds of the cave city of Vardzia in Georgia, a significant historical site. This natural disaster had lasting effects on the region's architecture and population.
events.name: Earthquake in Vardzia

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Caernarfon, Conwy, and Harlech Castles by Edward I of England marks a significant military and political strategy aimed at consolidating control over Wales and preventing future uprisings. These fortifications became symbols of English dominance in the region and played a crucial role in the conflicts between the Welsh and the English crown.
events.name: Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd

events.enhanced_description: In 1283, the Hafsid Sultanate faced a significant upheaval as ruler Abu Ishaq Ibrahim I was overthrown by a Bedouin rebellion led by Abd al-Aziz I. This event marked a pivotal moment in the political landscape of North Africa, reflecting the tensions between local tribes and established dynasties.
events.name: Overthrow of Abu Ishaq Ibrahim I

events.enhanced_description: In 1283, the Mongol forces invaded the Khmer Empire, prompting King Jayavarman VIII to opt for tribute over conflict. This decision reflected the strategic choices faced by regional rulers when confronted with the formidable Mongol military machine.
events.name: Mongol Invasion of the Khmer Empire

events.enhanced_description: During his reign around 1283, Ram Khamhaeng, the ruler of the Sukhothai Kingdom, developed the Thai alphabet, which played a crucial role in the cultural and linguistic identity of the Thai people. This innovation laid the foundation for written communication in Thailand and influenced the region's literary traditions.
events.name: Creation of the Thai Alphabet

events.enhanced_description: Around 1283, King Alfonso X of Castile commissioned the Libro de los juegos, an early European treatise on board games that included chess, dice, and backgammon. This work not only reflects the cultural interests of the time but also serves as an important historical document on leisure activities in medieval Europe.
events.name: Commissioning of the Libro de los juegos

events.enhanced_description: In 1283, Ramon Llull, a Spanish theologian, authored Blanquerna, which is considered the first major work of literature written in Catalan and possibly the first European novel. This work marked a significant contribution to the literary heritage of Catalonia and the broader European narrative tradition.
events.name: Ramon Llull Writes Blanquerna

events.enhanced_description: In 1283, the German city of Goslar began efforts to redeem its issued annuities, signaling financial difficulties that may have been indicative of a broader economic crisis in 13th-century Europe. This event reflects the economic challenges faced by cities during this turbulent period.
events.name: Goslar's Financial Difficulties

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic fire swept through Dublin, destroying much of the city, including St. Patrick's Cathedral. This event had profound implications for the city's infrastructure and community.
events.name: Fire in Dublin

events.enhanced_description: King Edward I of England captured Dolwyddelan Castle from the Welsh, further consolidating English control over Wales. This event was part of Edward's broader campaign to subdue Welsh resistance.
events.name: Capture of Dolwyddelan Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1283, a Mongol-led Yuan expeditionary force landed at Thị Nại Bay, launching an assault on the Champa kingdom's capital, Vijaya. Despite initial successes, the Cham forces, under King Indravarman V, resorted to guerrilla tactics to resist the Mongol invaders, showcasing the resilience of local powers against foreign domination.
events.name: Battle of Thị Nại Bay

events.enhanced_description: Cynfrig ap Madog surrendered Castell y Bere, marking the fall of the last independent Welsh stronghold to English forces. This event symbolized the end of significant Welsh resistance against English rule.
events.name: Surrender of Castell y Bere

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Rheinfelden forced the young Rudolf II to relinquish his claims to the duchies of Austria and Styria in favor of his elder brother, Albert I. This treaty was pivotal in shaping the future of the Habsburg dynasty and its territorial ambitions.
events.name: Treaty of Rheinfelden

events.enhanced_description: In June 1283, Qalawun, the Mamluk ruler of Egypt, signed a peace treaty with the Crusader States at Caesarea, ensuring a decade of relative peace in the region. This treaty allowed for Christian pilgrimage to Nazareth while maintaining territorial disputes, highlighting the complex relationships between Muslim and Christian states during the Crusades.
events.name: Peace Treaty at Caesarea

events.enhanced_description: A parliament summoned by Edward I at Shrewsbury Abbey marked a historic moment as it included commoners for the first time. This assembly aimed to decide the fate of the captured Welsh prince, Dafydd ap Gruffydd.
events.name: Parliament of England at Shrewsbury Abbey

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq launched a punitive expedition from Córdoba, marching through challenging terrain to Jaén and Úbeda. This military campaign aimed to assert control over the region and counter threats from the Order of Santiago.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Sultan Abu Yusuf's Expedition

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Malta featured an Aragonese fleet, commanded by Admiral Roger of Lauria, attacking and defeating Angevin ships in the Grand Harbour. This victory was crucial in supporting a rebellion on the island and solidifying Aragonese influence in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Malta

events.enhanced_description: Dafydd ap Gruffydd, the last independent ruler of Wales, was executed in Shrewsbury, becoming the first prominent figure to be hanged, drawn, and quartered for high treason against Edward I of England. His execution marked a brutal end to Welsh independence.
events.name: Execution of Dafydd ap Gruffydd

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, the Aragonese Crusade commenced as French armies under King Philip III and his son Charles of Valois invaded Roussillon, supported by James II of Majorca. The campaign led to significant conflict with local populations, culminating in the occupation and destruction of Elne, illustrating the violent struggles for control in the region.
events.name: Aragonese Crusade

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, King Rudolf I imposed a trade embargo on Norway in response to the pillaging of a German ship, leading to widespread famine as vital supplies were cut off. This action highlights the interconnectedness of trade and politics in medieval Europe and the consequences of maritime conflicts.
events.name: Trade Embargo on Norway

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, the events that inspired the story of the Pied Piper of Hamelin are believed to have taken place in Lower Saxony. This legend has since become a significant part of European folklore, symbolizing themes of betrayal and the consequences of broken promises.
events.name: Pied Piper of Hamelin Legend

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, Edward I organized a Round Table event and tournament in Nefyn, Wales, promising the local populace a Prince of Wales. This event was part of his broader strategy to integrate Welsh nobility into his rule and establish a sense of loyalty among the Welsh.
events.name: Round Table Event in Nefyn

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, Hafsid forces under Abu Hafs Umar I successfully reconquered Tunis, re-establishing the Hafsid Dynasty's dominance in Ifriqiya after the Bedouin rebellion. This event marked a significant restoration of power and stability in the region following a period of turmoil.
events.name: Hafsid Reconquest of Tunis

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, King Peter III of Aragon took advantage of the Hafsid Dynasty's weakened state to raid the island of Djerba, resulting in a massacre of the local population. This brutal campaign exemplified the aggressive territorial ambitions of Aragon during this period.
events.name: King Peter III's Raid on Djerba

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, the construction of Beauvais Cathedral was interrupted by a partial collapse of the choir, causing significant concern among French masons who were pioneering the Gothic style. This incident highlighted the challenges and risks associated with ambitious architectural projects of the time.
events.name: Beauvais Cathedral Construction Collapse

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, Jean de Meun translated Vegetius' 4th-century military treatise De Re Militari from Latin into French, making this important work more accessible to a broader audience. This translation reflects the growing interest in military strategy and history during the medieval period.
events.name: Translation of De Re Militari

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, Peterhouse was established by Bishop Hugh de Balsham as the oldest collegiate foundation of the University of Cambridge. This institution played a crucial role in the development of higher education in England and remains a significant part of the university's legacy.
events.name: Establishment of Peterhouse

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, the Al-Mansuri bimaristan (hospital) was completed in Cairo, representing a significant advancement in medical care and public health in the Islamic world. This institution exemplified the sophisticated understanding of medicine and healthcare during the medieval period.
events.name: Completion of Al-Mansuri Bimaristan

events.enhanced_description: In 1284, the Republic of Venice commenced the minting of the ducat, a gold coin that would become a cornerstone of European commerce for the next six centuries. The ducat's standardization and widespread acceptance facilitated trade across the continent, solidifying Venice's economic power.
events.name: The Republic of Venice begins coining the ducat

events.enhanced_description: Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun’s funerary complex, including its madrasa and mausoleum, was built from 1284 to August 1285. The text reports that construction took 13 months.

image.caption: Mihrab of the Qalawun complex, with Arabic inscription and decorative mosaic.

events.name: Construction of the Qalawun complex

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1284, the Statute of Rhuddlan was enacted by King Edward I, establishing direct English rule over Wales following the Welsh Wars. This legislation introduced English law while allowing some Welsh customs to persist, marking a significant shift in governance and legal structure in the region.
events.name: Statute of Rhuddlan

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1284, King Alfonso X of Castile passed away after a 32-year reign, leaving a contested succession that saw his son Sancho IV ascend the throne amidst challenges from his cousin Alfonso de la Cerda. This transition marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Castile and León.
events.name: Death of King Alfonso X

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1284, King Magnus III granted town privileges to Jönköping in Sweden, marking a significant step in the development of urban centers in the region. This act facilitated local governance and economic growth, reflecting the broader trends of urbanization in medieval Europe.
events.name: Jönköping Granted Town Privileges

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1284, the Battle of the Gulf of Naples saw an Aragonese-Sicilian fleet led by Admiral Roger of Lauria decisively defeat the Neapolitan ships, capturing King Charles II. This battle significantly altered the power dynamics in the Mediterranean, showcasing the naval prowess of Aragonese forces.
events.name: Battle of the Gulf of Naples

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1284, the Battle of Meloria took place in the Ligurian Sea, where a Genoese fleet led by Admiral Oberto D'Oria defeated the Pisan ships. This battle marked a significant decline in Pisa's maritime power and solidified Genoa's dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Meloria

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, during the Aragonese Crusade, French forces led by King Philip III laid siege to the city of Girona. Despite initial successes, the siege ended with the French retreating due to an epidemic, marking a significant setback in their campaign.
events.name: Aragonese Crusade: French forces besiege Girona

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 1285, the Mongol Golden Horde, led by Nogai Khan and Talabuga, launched a second invasion of Hungary. Their campaign resulted in the subjugation of Slovakia and widespread devastation in the region north of the Carpathians.
events.name: Mongol Golden Horde attacks Hungary

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, the Second Statute of Westminster was accepted in the English Parliament, introducing significant legal reforms. Among its provisions was the clause de donis conditionalibus, which became a cornerstone of medieval property law.
events.name: Second Statute of Westminster

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, King Edward I issued the writ Circumspecte Agatis, which delineated the jurisdictions of church and state. This significant legal document restricted the church's judicial authority, reinforcing the power of the monarchy.
events.name: Writ Circumspecte Agatis

events.enhanced_description: Around 1285, the English romantic poem The Lay of Havelok the Dane was composed, reflecting the literary culture of the time. This work is significant for its contribution to the development of English literature and storytelling.
events.name: The Lay of Havelok the Dane

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, Lübeck recorded the first instance of issuing life annuities, marking a significant development in public finance in Germany. This event reflects the growing trend of local public debt consolidation across northwestern Europe.
events.name: Emission of life annuities in Lübeck

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, the County of Champagne was integrated into the kingdom of France, leading to a decline in its economic significance as a trading hub. The Fairs of Troyes, once bustling with foreign merchants, quickly diminished in importance.
events.name: Integration of the County of Champagne into France

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, the Council of Blachernae saw the Eastern Orthodox Church formally repudiate the Union with the Catholic Church established at the Second Council of Lyon. This event highlighted the ongoing schism between the two branches of Christianity.
events.name: Council of Blachernae

events.enhanced_description: In 1285, the Mor Bar Sauma Monastery, a significant site for the Syriac Orthodox Church, was destroyed. Although a monastic community persisted, the patriarchal seat was relocated to Sis, indicating the shifting religious landscape.
events.name: Destruction of Mor Bar Sauma Monastery

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1285, Archbishop Jakub Świnka convened a synod in Łęczyca, mandating that sermons be delivered in Polish rather than German. This decision played a crucial role in fostering a sense of national identity within the Catholic Church in Poland.
events.name: Synod organized by Archbishop Jakub Świnka

events.enhanced_description: Pope Martin IV died on March 25, 1285, after a four-year pontificate in Perugia. His death led to the election of Honorius IV, marking a transition in the papacy during a tumultuous period for the Catholic Church.
events.name: Death of Pope Martin IV

events.enhanced_description: In April 1285, Marinid forces under Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq crossed from Alcácer Seguir to Tarifa, launching a campaign that included the siege of Jerez de la Frontera. Their brutal tactics devastated the surrounding regions, showcasing the intensity of the conflict.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Marinid forces cross to Tarifa

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on April 17, 1285, Mamluk forces under Sultan Qalawun besieged the Crusader fortress of Margat. After a month of failed assaults, the fortress surrendered, marking a significant victory for the Mamluks in their campaign against the Crusader states.
events.name: Siege of Margat

events.enhanced_description: In May 1285, King Sancho IV of Castile gathered his forces at Seville and dispatched a fleet to blockade the Guadalquivir River. This strategic move aimed to counter the Marinid threat, but faced challenges from Marinid cavalry forces.
events.name: King Sancho IV assembles his army

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1285, Marinid forces under Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq intensified their siege of Jerez de la Frontera. The siege was marked by relentless assaults and raids on the surrounding countryside, reflecting the fierce conflict between the Marinids and Castilian forces.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Siege at Jerez de la Frontera

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1285, the Battle of Chương Dương saw joint forces of Champa and Đại Việt defeat the Mongol-led Yuan fleet on the Red River. This victory was pivotal in repelling Mongol advances into Vietnam, allowing the Vietnamese royal court to return to Thang Long.
events.name: Battle of Chương Dương

events.enhanced_description: In August 1285, Castilian forces led by Sancho IV advanced against the besieging Marinids at Jerez de la Frontera. The Marinids, facing dwindling supplies, ultimately lifted the siege, marking a tactical victory for the Castilians.
events.name: Castilian forces march against the Marinids

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1285, the Battle of Les Formigues took place, where an Aragonese-Sicilian fleet under Admiral Roger of Lauria decisively defeated French and Genoese ships. This victory not only showcased naval prowess but also shifted the balance of power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Les Formigues

events.enhanced_description: In October 1285, the Battle of the Col de Panissars saw Aragonese forces under King Peter III ambush a retreating French army. The battle resulted in significant casualties for the French, contributing to the decline of their military ambitions in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Col de Panissars

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1285, Peter III (the Great) passed away after a nine-year reign in Vilafranca del Penedès. His death led to the ascension of his son Alfonso III, marking a pivotal transition in Aragonese leadership.
events.name: Death of Peter III (the Great)

events.enhanced_description: In 1286, Old Prussians resettled in Samland and initiated an uprising against Teutonic rule, supported by the Principality of Rügen. Despite their efforts, the uprising was quashed by the Teutonic Knights, reinforcing their control over the region.
events.name: Old Prussians uprising against Teutonic rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1286, the War of the Donkey erupted in the Aegean Sea between the rival noble families of Ghisi and Sanudo. This conflict underscored the feudal tensions and power struggles that characterized the region during this period.
events.name: War of the Donkey

events.enhanced_description: In 1286, the Guelph Republic of Siena made a significant political decision by allowing exiled Ghibelline rebels to return to the city, marking a shift in the power dynamics within the region. This event reflects the ongoing conflict between the Guelphs and Ghibellines, two factions vying for control in medieval Italian city-states.
events.name: The Guelph Republic of Siena allows exiled Ghibelline rebels back into the city
