events.enhanced_description: In 1286, Abu Hafs Umar I, ruler of the Hafsid Sultanate, seized control of Béjaïa, establishing himself as a rival to the main Hafsid authority based in Tunis. This power struggle reflects the fragmentation and competition among North African states during this period.
events.name: Abu Hafs Umar I takes control of Béjaïa

events.enhanced_description: In 1286, a coup d'état led by Prince Panya Khamphong resulted in the overthrow of his father, King Panya Leng, in the Lao kingdom of Muang Sua. This event is believed to have been supported by the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty, showcasing the influence of external powers in local politics.
events.name: King Panya Leng is overthrown in Muang Sua

events.enhanced_description: In 1286, Kublai Khan made plans for a final Mongol invasion of Japan, a campaign that had been attempted previously with disastrous results. However, he ultimately aborted these preparations due to a lack of necessary resources, reflecting the challenges faced by the Mongol Empire in sustaining its military ambitions.
events.name: Kublai Khan plans a final invasion of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1286, Philip IV (the Fair) was crowned king of France in Reims. His reign marked a period of administrative reform and consolidation of royal power, setting the stage for future conflicts and changes in French governance.
events.name: Coronation of Philip IV (the Fair)

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1286, John of Genoa completed the Catholicon, a significant Latin dictionary that served as an important resource for scholars and clergy. This work contributed to the preservation and dissemination of Latin language and religious texts during the medieval period.
events.name: The Catholicon is completed by John of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1286, King Alexander III of Scotland tragically died after falling from his horse near Kinghorn in Fife. His death left the throne to his three-year-old granddaughter, Margaret, and an unborn child, leading to a power vacuum that would eventually contribute to the First War of Scottish Independence.
events.name: King Alexander III dies in a fall from his horse at Kinghorn in Fife

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1286, Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq died in Algeciras after a 28-year reign. His death led to the ascension of his son, who sought peace with Castile and the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, reshaping the political landscape of the region.
figures: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq
events.name: Death of Sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq

events.enhanced_description: In June 1286, King Edward I of England and Queen Eleanor of Castile traveled to France to pay homage to King Philip IV and address various political matters. Edward's visit included overseeing the rebuilding of fortifications in Gascony, highlighting the ongoing tensions and alliances between England and France.
events.name: King Edward I and Queen Eleanor of Castile travel to France

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1286, the young Henry II sailed from Cyprus, landing in Acre, where he was initially refused entry into the citadel. He remained in the palace for six weeks, negotiating terms to take control of the city from the Angevins, reflecting the complex political landscape of the region.
events.name: Henry II sails from Cyprus and lands in Acre

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1286, Henry II was crowned king of Jerusalem in Tyre, marking a significant moment in the history of the Crusader states. Following the ceremony, he returned to Acre for celebrations before appointing his uncle as regent, indicating the ongoing political maneuvering in the region.
events.name: Henry II is crowned king of Jerusalem at Tyre

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, King Alfonso III of Aragon was compelled to make significant concessions to the nobility following an uprising known as the Union of Aragon. This included granting a Bill of Rights, which ultimately weakened royal authority and contributed to political instability in the kingdom.
events.name: Alfonso III makes concessions to the nobility

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 1287, Mongol forces led by Talabuga Khan and Nogai Khan launched their third invasion of Poland, devastating cities such as Lublin and Sandomierz. Despite besieging Kraków, the Mongols faced heavy casualties, illustrating the ongoing conflict between the Mongols and Polish defenders.
events.name: Mongol invasion of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 1287, two unidentified merchants traveled from Alexandria to Cairo to alert Sultan Qalawun about the economic threats posed by Genoese dominance in the eastern Mediterranean. Their warnings prompted Qalawun to take action, breaking the truce with Tripoli and reshaping trade dynamics in the region.
events.name: Merchants warn Qalawun of Genoese domination

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, an Aragonese fleet conducted a raid on the Kerkennah Islands in the Gulf of Gabès, demonstrating the ongoing maritime conflicts in the Mediterranean. This raid reflects the broader patterns of naval warfare and territorial disputes during this period.
events.name: Aragonese fleet raids Kerkennah Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, Kings Mangrai of the Lanna Kingdom and Ram Khamhaeng of the Sukhothai Kingdom established a peace treaty, creating a 'strong pact of friendship' that would influence regional stability in modern-day Thailand.
events.name: Peace treaty between Mangrai and Ram Khamhaeng

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Altar of St. James in Pistoia Cathedral, Italy, began in 1287. This masterwork of silversmithing, containing nearly a ton of silver, would take nearly 200 years to complete, showcasing the era's artistic ambitions.
events.name: Construction of the Altar of St. James

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, the city of Siena exacted a forced loan from its taxpayers for the first time, marking a significant development in medieval public finance practices and reflecting the economic pressures of the time.
events.name: Siena's forced loan

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Uppsala Cathedral in Sweden began in 1287 and continued until 1435. This monumental project would become a significant landmark in Swedish history and architecture.
events.name: Construction of Uppsala Cathedral begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1287, Aragonese forces led by King Alfonso III successfully conquered the island of Menorca. Following the conquest, Alfonso signed the Treaty of San Agayz, establishing trade policies and alliances that would shape the region's political landscape.
events.name: Aragonese forces conquer Menorca

events.enhanced_description: In February 1287, a severe storm impacted the south coast of England, causing significant flooding in the Cinque Ports, particularly affecting Hastings and New Romney. This disaster led to the destruction of Old Winchelsea and altered the course of the Rother River, reshaping the region's geography and trade routes.
events.name: South England flood

events.enhanced_description: In March 1287, Mamluk forces under Sultan Qalawun successfully captured Latakia, the last remnant of the Principality of Antioch. The fall of this strategic port marked a significant loss for the Crusaders and solidified Mamluk control in the region.
events.name: Mamluk forces capture Latakia

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1287, the Synod of Würzburg was convened by Cardinal Giovanni Boccamazza and King Rudolf I. The council addressed the taxation of clergy to fund Rudolf's expedition to Rome for his imperial coronation.
events.name: Synod of Würzburg

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1287, Arghun Khan, the Mongol ruler of the Ilkhanate, dispatched an embassy led by Rabban Bar Sauma to negotiate a military alliance against the Mamluk Sultanate. This mission underscored the geopolitical dynamics of the time and the Mongols' ambitions in the region.
events.name: Arghun Khan sends an embassy to form an alliance against the Mamluks

events.enhanced_description: Pope Honorius IV died on April 3, 1287, after a brief two-year pontificate. His reign was marked by attempts to restore papal authority in Sicily, which led to conflicts with King Peter III, who supported Sicilian independence.
events.name: Death of Pope Honorius IV

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, Wareru established the Hanthawaddy Kingdom in modern Myanmar after the collapse of the Pagan Kingdom. He was crowned king on April 5 and declared independence from Pagan, marking a significant shift in regional power dynamics.
events.name: Wareru creates the Hanthawaddy Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In June 1287, Rabban Bar Sauma, a Chinese Nestorian monk and diplomat, embarked on a journey from Constantinople to Italy. His travels included witnessing a naval battle in Naples and engaging with cardinals in Rome, highlighting the cultural exchanges and political negotiations of the time.
events.name: Rabban Bar Sauma travels from Constantinople to Italy

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1287, Welsh forces led by Rhys ap Maredudd revolted against King Edward I, fueled by grievances over taxation. The rebellion resulted in the burning of several towns, including Swansea, and marked a significant moment in the ongoing struggle for Welsh autonomy.
events.name: Welsh forces revolt against King Edward I

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1287, the Battle of the Counts took place near Naples, where an Aragonese-Sicilian fleet under Admiral Roger of Lauria defeated a larger Angevin fleet. This decisive victory not only showcased naval tactics but also shifted the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Battle of the Counts

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1287, in response to the Welsh rebellion, King Edward I raised an army at Gloucester, commanded by Edmund of Almain. The English forces besieged Dryslwyn Castle, ultimately capturing it after three weeks, showcasing the military efforts to suppress the uprising.
events.name: Edward I raises an army in response to the Welsh rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 1287, Nayan, a Mongol prince of the Borjigin clan, revolted against Kublai Khan's rule. Kublai led a punitive expedition to Manchuria, where he decisively defeated Nayan's forces on July 16, reinforcing his control over the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Nayan revolts against Kublai Khan

events.enhanced_description: In September 1287, Rabban Bar Sauma arrived in Paris and was received by King Philip IV. His visit included a tour of the Sainte-Chapelle and discussions aimed at forming a military alliance against the Mamluks, illustrating the diplomatic efforts of the time.
events.name: Rabban Bar Sauma arrives in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1287, Bohemond VII, the ruler of Tripoli, died without an heir, leading to a succession crisis. His sister Lucia was proposed as his successor, but the nobles' discontent with this decision highlighted the ongoing power struggles within the region.
events.name: Bohemond VII dies childless

events.enhanced_description: In December 1287, severe flooding affected parts of Norfolk and devastated the port of Dunwich, leading to the destruction of the monastery of Spalding and many churches. This disaster caused significant loss of life and altered the landscape, particularly in the Fens region.
events.name: Flooding in Norfolk and Dunwich

events.enhanced_description: In December 1287, the Battle of Pagan saw Mongol-led Yuan forces, commanded by Temür Khan, defeat King Thihathu of the Pagan Kingdom. This victory led to the disintegration of the Pagan Kingdom and a period of anarchy in the region.
events.name: Battle of Pagan

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1287, a catastrophic storm known as St. Lucia's flood struck the North Sea and English Channel, resulting in widespread devastation in the Netherlands and England. This disaster caused significant loss of life and reshaped the coastline, particularly impacting the development of Amsterdam as a port city.
events.name: St. Lucia's flood

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, a civil war erupted on Gotland between the burghers of Visby and rural farmers, likely triggered by the construction of a large wall around Visby and the imposition of a toll on farmers.
events.name: Civil war in Gotland

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, the Parliament of Scotland enacted a law allowing women to propose marriage to men during leap years, imposing a fine on men who refused such proposals. This progressive legislation reflected evolving social norms regarding marriage.
events.name: Scottish marriage proposal law

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, the oldest surviving bell, which is part of the clocks atop the dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, was built. This bell remains a significant artifact of religious and artistic heritage.
events.name: Bell in St. Peter's Basilica

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, construction began on Mob Quad in Merton College, Oxford, marking an important development in the architectural history of one of the world's oldest universities.
events.name: Construction of Mob Quad in Merton College

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, the city of Ghent sought rights to start redeeming its issued annuities, indicating financial difficulties and possibly foreshadowing the economic crisis of the late 13th century.
events.name: Ghent seeks to redeem annuities

events.enhanced_description: In 1288, the oldest-known bronze handgun was discovered in Acheng District, China. This firearm played a significant role in the suppression of a rebellion led by the Mongol prince Nayan, marking an important development in military technology during the period.
events.name: The oldest-known bronze handgun in the world is dated to this year, a Chinese gun found in Acheng District, that was once used to suppress the rebellion of the Mongol prince Nayan

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1288, English forces recaptured Newcastle Emlyn Castle in West Wales after a ten-day siege, effectively ending Rhys ap Maredudd's revolt and leading to his exile to Ireland.
events.name: Recapture of Newcastle Emlyn Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1288, Nicholas IV was elected as the successor to the late Pope Honorius IV during a conclave in Rome, becoming the 191st pope of the Catholic Church. His election marked a continuation of the papal leadership during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Election of Pope Nicholas IV

events.enhanced_description: In March-April 1288, Rabban Bar Sauma, a Chinese Nestorian monk and diplomat, arrived in Rome and was received by Pope Nicholas IV, who gave him communion on Palm Sunday. This visit highlighted the cultural exchanges between East and West during this period.
events.name: Rabban Bar Sauma arrives in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1288, the city of Genoa ordered Admiral Benedetto Zaccaria to send five galleys to support its suzerainty over Tripoli. This military action was part of broader efforts to maintain control over strategic territories in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Genoa supports Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: In April 1288, the Japanese era Kōan ended, giving way to the Shōō era during the reign of the 22-year-old Emperor Fushimi. This transition marked a new chapter in Japanese history and culture.
events.name: End of the Kōan era in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1288, Vietnamese general Trần Hưng Đạo achieved a significant victory at the Battle of Bạch Đằng, where he ambushed and sank the fleet of a Mongol-led Yuan expeditionary army. This battle effectively thwarted Kublai Khan's ambitions to conquer Vietnam.
events.name: Battle of Bạch Đằng

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1288, during the War of the Limburg Succession, Duke John I of Brabant led his forces to victory against a coalition army from Cologne, Luxembourg, and Nassau at the Battle of Worringen. This battle was pivotal in the struggle for control over the Duchy of Limburg.
events.name: Battle of Worringen

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1288, Petrus, the bishop of Västerås, purchased one-eighth of the Stora Kopparberg copper mine in Falun, Sweden. This acquisition highlighted the growing interest of nobles and merchants in the mining sector during this period.
events.name: Petrus buys part of Stora Kopparberg mine

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1288, Sultan Muhammad II of Granada successfully expelled the rebellious Banu Ashqilula from his territory. Through military action and diplomatic maneuvering, he also turned the Castilian aristocracy against King Sancho IV.
events.name: Sultan Muhammad II expels Banu Ashqilula

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1288, Pope Nicholas IV proclaimed a crusade against King Ladislaus IV of Hungary, who faced criticism for favoring his semi-pagan Cuman subjects and straying from Western social norms. This proclamation marked a significant moment in the intersection of religion and politics in Hungary.
events.name: Pope Nicholas IV proclaims a crusade

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1288, King Edward I of England signed the Treaty of Canfranc with Alfonso III of Aragon, concerning the release of Charles II, who had been captured during the Battle of the Gulf of Naples. This treaty reflected the complex political alliances of the time.
events.name: Treaty of Canfranc

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1289, King Edward I of England proposed a marriage between his infant son, Edward of Caernarfon, and the six-year-old Margaret, Maid of Norway. This political alliance aimed to strengthen ties between England and Norway.
events.name: Marriage Proposal of Edward I

events.enhanced_description: In 1289, the construction of Conwy Castle in Wales was completed under the orders of King Edward I. This castle was part of Edward's campaign to establish English dominance in Wales and served as a symbol of his power.
events.name: Completion of Conwy Castle

events.enhanced_description: In March 1289, King Henry II of England dispatched his younger brother Almalric with knights and galleys to Tripoli, as the Mamluk army began its siege. This military maneuver reflected the ongoing conflicts in the region and the desperate situation faced by the Crusader states.
events.name: King Henry II sends Almalric to Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: In 1289, Pope Nicholas IV formally established the University of Montpellier in France through a papal bull. This institution combined various existing schools, marking a significant development in higher education during the medieval period.
events.name: University of Montpellier established

events.enhanced_description: In 1289, a group of twenty-three partners, including members of the Bonsignori family, re-created the Gran Tavola in Siena, reviving the most successful European bank that had ceased operations after the death of its founder in 1273. This re-establishment reflected the importance of banking in medieval commerce.
events.name: Re-creation of the Gran Tavola in Siena

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1289, Sultan Qalawun of the Mamluk Sultanate marched his army out of Cairo, leaving his son Al-Ashraf Khalil in command of the Citadel. This movement aimed to mobilize forces in Damascus against external threats.
events.name: Sultan Qalawun marches the Mamluk army out of Cairo

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1289, the Mamluk forces under Sultan Qalawun captured Tripoli after a month-long siege, effectively extinguishing the County of Tripoli. The siege resulted in widespread devastation and a massacre of the city's male inhabitants.
events.name: Siege of Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1289, the Battle of Campaldino took place in Tuscany, where the pro-papal Guelph forces of Florence, led by Viscount Aimery IV, defeated the Ghibelline army. This victory solidified Florence's dominance in Central Italy and marked a shift in power dynamics among the merchant guilds.
events.name: Battle of Campaldino

events.enhanced_description: During July and August of 1289, Admiral Benedetto Zaccaria, having escaped from Tripoli, initiated a naval campaign against Mamluk shipping and raided Tinnis in Egypt. This action was part of the ongoing conflict between Crusader forces and the Mamluks.
events.name: Admiral Benedetto Zaccaria's naval campaign

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1807, the British Royal Navy bombarded Copenhagen in a devastating attack aimed at preventing the Dano-Norwegian navy from aligning with Napoleon. The bombardment resulted in significant destruction, with approximately 30% of the city damaged and thousands of civilian casualties.

image.caption: Painting by Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg depicting the Church of Our Lady burning during the bombardment of Copenhagen.
image.credit: Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg — Photo unknown, original at Royal Danish Library
image.date_qualification: The painting depicts the 1807 bombardment; the saved date supports the year 1807, not a more precise creation date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Copenhagen

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 1290, the second Statute of Mortmain was passed under King Edward I, which prohibited land from being transferred into the possession of the Church. This legislation aimed to control land ownership and maintain royal authority.
events.name: Statutes of Mortmain passed

events.enhanced_description: In 1290, the Quia Emptores statute was enacted by King Edward I, ending the practice of subinfeudations and allowing land sales with royal approval. This law was significant in shaping the feudal system and land ownership in England.
events.name: Quia Emptores statute passed

events.enhanced_description: The 'Year without winter' refers to an exceptionally rare climatic phenomenon where there was an uninterrupted transition from autumn to spring across England and Western Europe. This unusual weather pattern had significant implications for agriculture and daily life during that period.
events.name: Year without winter

events.enhanced_description: The Dnyaneshwari, a significant commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, was authored by the Indian saint Dnyaneshwar. This text is revered in Marathi literature and is considered a profound philosophical work that interprets the Gita's teachings for a broader audience.
events.name: Writing of the Dnyaneshwari

events.enhanced_description: The University of Coimbra was founded in Lisbon by King Denis I, also known as 'the Poet King.' This establishment marked a significant development in higher education in Portugal, as it also saw the official adoption of Portuguese as the language of instruction, replacing Latin.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Coimbra

events.enhanced_description: In June 1290, Genoa finalized a new commercial treaty with the Mamluks, while five galleys sent by King James II of Aragon joined the Venetian Crusader fleet on its way to Acre. This treaty was part of the complex diplomatic relations in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Genoa concludes treaty with Mamluks

events.enhanced_description: Beatrice Portinari, the muse of the renowned Italian poet Dante Alighieri, passed away in Florence. Her memory profoundly influenced Dante's literary work, particularly in his epic poem 'Divine Comedy,' where she symbolizes divine love and spiritual guidance.
events.name: Death of Beatrice Portinari

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1290, Shamsuddin Kayumars, the Mamluk ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, was murdered, leading to the rise of Jalal-ud-din Khalji. This event marked the end of Mamluk rule in India and initiated the Khalji Revolution, which transformed the political landscape.
events.name: Murder of Shamsuddin Kayumars

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1290, King Ladislaus IV of Hungary was assassinated at the castle of Körösszeg. His death led to the election of Andrew III as the new ruler, marking a significant shift in Hungarian politics.
events.name: Assassination of King Ladislaus IV of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1290, King Edward I of England issued the Edict of Expulsion, ordering all Jews to leave the country by November 1. This decree, which affected approximately 2,000 Jews, marked a significant moment in English history regarding religious tolerance.
events.name: Edict of Expulsion of Jews from England

events.enhanced_description: In August 1290, Italian Crusaders in Acre perpetrated a massacre against Muslim merchants and peasants, which escalated tensions in the region. The incident, reportedly sparked by personal grievances, highlighted the volatile nature of inter-religious relations during the Crusades.
events.name: Massacre of Muslims in Acre

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1290, survivors of the Acre massacre brought evidence to Sultan Qalawun in Cairo, demanding justice. The refusal of local nobles to surrender the perpetrators led to Qalawun obtaining religious clearance to break the truce with the Crusader states.
events.name: Qalawun demands justice for Acre massacre

events.enhanced_description: In September 1290, Margaret, Maid of Norway, the queen-designate and heir to the Scottish crown, died en route to the British Isles in Orkney. Her death triggered a succession crisis, leading to a power struggle among thirteen claimants for the Scottish throne.
events.name: Death of Margaret, Maid of Norway

events.enhanced_description: The 6.8 Ms Zhili earthquake struck the province of Zhili in China, causing widespread devastation and resulting in a death toll estimated between 7,270 and 100,000 people. This earthquake is notable for its high Mercalli intensity of IX, indicating violent shaking and significant destruction.
events.name: The 6.8 Ms Zhili earthquake

events.enhanced_description: In October 1290, Sultan Qalawun ordered a general mobilization of Mamluk forces in response to the events in Acre. This decision was part of a broader strategy to reassert Mamluk power in the region and prepare for potential conflict.
events.name: Mobilization of Mamluk forces

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1290, Sultan Qalawun passed away as the Mamluk army prepared to set out for Acre. His death marked a significant transition in leadership, with his son Al-Ashraf Khalil succeeding him and inheriting the challenges of the Mamluk Sultanate.
events.name: Death of Sultan Qalawun

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1290, Eleanor of Castile, the wife of King Edward I, died while traveling in the North. Her death deeply affected Edward, who later commissioned the construction of the Eleanor crosses in her memory.
events.name: Death of Eleanor of Castile

events.enhanced_description: In December 1290, King Edward I traveled with the body of his deceased wife, Queen Eleanor, from Lincoln to London. Along the route, he erected a series of crosses, known as the Eleanor crosses, to commemorate her life and legacy.
events.name: Edward I travels with Eleanor's body

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1290, King Magnus III of Sweden died after a 15-year reign, leading to the ascension of his 10-year-old son Birger. Despite Sweden's elective monarchy, Birger had been appointed heir in 1284, ensuring a smooth transition of power.
events.name: Death of King Magnus III of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Pope Nicholas IV issued a papal bull confirming the independence of San Marino, a significant acknowledgment that solidified its status as a sovereign entity. This act is a testament to the unique historical and political landscape of the region.
events.name: Papal confirmation of San Marino's independence

events.enhanced_description: Klenová Castle was constructed in southern Bohemia near Klatovy as part of a defensive system. This castle played a crucial role in the region's military architecture and defense strategies during its time.
events.name: Construction of Klenová Castle

events.enhanced_description: King Andrew III of Hungary granted royal town privileges to Bratislava, the modern capital of Slovakia. This act was significant in enhancing the town's status and autonomy within the kingdom.
events.name: Royal town privileges granted to Bratislava

events.enhanced_description: The temple of Nanzen-ji was established in Kyoto by Emperor Kameyama, becoming a pivotal center for the Rinzai sect of Zen Buddhism. This temple played a crucial role in the development of Zen practices and education in Japan.
events.name: Establishment of Nanzen-ji temple

events.enhanced_description: Chinese engineer and astronomer Guo Shoujing constructed the artificial Kunming Lake in Khanbaliq, which served as a reservoir and summer garden for the Mongol capital. This project exemplified advanced engineering and urban planning during the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Construction of Kunming Lake

events.enhanced_description: In 1291, four towns in the County of Holland and two in the County of Zeeland collectively secured a loan from Count Floris V. This agreement provided important financial securities and facilitated lower interest rates for the towns, reflecting the growing economic power of urban centers.
events.name: Loan agreement in Holland and Zeeland

events.enhanced_description: In 1291, the Venetian glass manufacturing industry was centralized on the island of Murano to mitigate the risk of fires in Venice. This move not only protected the city but also established Murano as a renowned center for glassmaking, influencing art and commerce for centuries.
events.name: Concentration of Venetian glass manufacture

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1291, several nobles, including John Balliol and Robert de Brus, made unsuccessful claims to the Scottish throne, a situation known as the 'Great Cause.' The Guardians of Scotland sought the arbitration of King Edward I of England to prevent civil war, leading to increased English influence over Scotland.
events.name: Claimants for the Scottish throne

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1291, Italian explorers Vandino and Ugolino Vivaldi set sail from Genoa with the aim of reaching India and establishing a trade route. Their journey along the Moroccan coast marked an early attempt at expanding trade networks, although they ultimately disappeared at sea.
events.name: Exploration by the Vivaldi brothers

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1291, Edward I met with the claimants for the Scottish crown at Norham Castle, asserting his role as the overlord of Scotland. His demands for the surrender of royal castles highlighted the tension between English and Scottish sovereignty.
events.name: Edward I's meeting with claimants

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Acre culminated on May 18, 1291, when Mamluk forces under Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil captured the city after fierce fighting. This event marked the end of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, as many defenders perished or were enslaved, and it signaled a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Siege of Acre

events.enhanced_description: In June 1291, Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil entered Damascus in triumph, showcasing captured Crusaders and their standards as symbols of victory. This event followed the fall of Acre and marked the Mamluks' consolidation of power over the remaining Crusader territories.
events.name: Al-Ashraf Khalil's triumph in Damascus

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1291, the Guardians of Scotland and the Scottish nobles acknowledged Edward I as the overlord of Scotland, agreeing to hand over control until a rightful heir was determined. This agreement marked a significant shift in Scottish autonomy and foreshadowed future conflicts.
events.name: Guardians recognize Edward I as overlord

events.enhanced_description: In July 1291, Thibaud Gaudin arrived in Sidon with surviving knights and the treasure of the Knights Templar, following the siege of Acre. Elected as Grand Master, he faced immediate threats from Mamluk forces, leading to the evacuation of Sidon shortly after his arrival.
events.name: Thibaud Gaudin's arrival in Sidon

events.enhanced_description: The Federal Charter of 1291 marked the formation of a defensive alliance among the three forest cantons of Switzerland: Schwyz, Uri, and Unterwalden. This alliance was a foundational moment for the Old Swiss Confederacy, aimed at protecting against the encroaching House of Habsburg.
events.name: Federal Charter of 1291

events.enhanced_description: A combined fleet of Genoese and Sevillian forces, led by Admiral Benedetto Zaccaria, achieved a decisive victory over a Marinid fleet at Alcácer Seguir. This battle not only showcased naval prowess but also had significant implications for maritime control in the region.
events.name: Victory at Alcácer Seguir

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1291, Mamluk forces captured the Templar fortress of Atlit, marking the end of Crusader presence in Syria. This victory solidified Al-Ashraf Khalil's reputation as a formidable leader against the Crusader states and concluded a significant chapter in the Crusades.
events.name: Mamluk conquest of Atlit

events.enhanced_description: In late September, Abu Yaqub Yusuf an-Nasr crossed the Strait of Gibraltar from Alcácer Seguir to Tarifa, leading Marinid forces in a campaign that included besieging Vejer de la Frontera. This marked a period of aggressive military action against the Christian territories in the region.
events.name: Abu Yaqub Yusuf an-Nasr's crossing

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move against the Marinids, Kings Sancho IV of Castile and James II of Aragon concluded a treaty of friendship in late 1291. This agreement solidified their alliance and coordinated efforts to reclaim territories from the Marinid forces.
events.name: Treaty of friendship between Castile and Aragon

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of Shanghai County marked a significant administrative development in the region. This event laid the groundwork for Shanghai's eventual growth into a major city and economic hub in China.
events.name: Establishment of Shanghai County

events.enhanced_description: In 1292, Kublai Khan, the Mongol emperor, dispatched a massive expeditionary force of approximately 20,000 troops to Java, aiming to expand Mongol influence in Southeast Asia. The fleet, consisting of 500 to 1,000 ships, successfully captured the capital of Kediri but was ultimately unable to maintain control over the territory.
events.name: Kublai Khan sends a Mongol expeditionary force (some 20,000 men) to Java

events.enhanced_description: In 1292, King Mangrai the Great of Ngoenyang successfully conquered the Mon kingdom of Hariphunchai, leading to the establishment of the Lan Na Kingdom. This political union marked a significant expansion of Mangrai's influence in the region.
events.name: King Mangrai the Great of Ngoenyang conquers and annexes the Mon kingdom of Hariphunchai

events.enhanced_description: In 1292, the Vaghela dynasty, ruling over Gujarat, faced subjugation by the Deccan Seuna (Yadava) dynasty based in Daulatabad. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in western India.
events.name: The Vaghela dynasty in Gujarat is subjugated by the Deccan Seuna dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 1292, Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil, accompanied by his vizier Ibn al-Sal'us, arrived in Damascus to besiege the castle of Rumkale. The Mamluks employed over 30 catapults and successfully captured the castle after a month-long siege.
events.name: Mamluk forces under Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil arrive in Damascus

events.enhanced_description: After consolidating his power in Damascus, Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil prepared an army to assault Sis, the capital of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. An Armenian embassy negotiated peace, resulting in territorial concessions to the Mamluks.
events.name: Al-Ashraf Khalil returns to Damascus and assembles an army to attack Sis

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1292, the Taxatio Ecclesiastica, a comprehensive valuation of ecclesiastical properties for taxation purposes, was completed under the orders of Pope Nicholas IV. This document served as a crucial resource for church finances in England, Wales, and Ireland.
events.name: The Taxatio Ecclesiastica is completed under Pope Nicholas IV

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1292, Pope Nicholas IV passed away after a four-year pontificate. His death prompted the cardinals to convene in Perugia for the papal election of 1292-1294, marking a significant transition in the Catholic Church's leadership.
events.name: Nicholas IV dies after a 4-year pontificate in Rome

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1292, the College of Electors chose Adolf, count of Nassau, as the new King of the Romans, succeeding Rudolf I of Habsburg. Adolf's election required him to make significant concessions to the Electors, reflecting the complex political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: The College of Electors select Adolf, count of Nassau, as the new King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: In June 1292, King Sancho IV of Castile initiated the siege of Tarifa, employing advanced siege engines to bombard the city. The siege lasted four months, culminating in the capture of Tarifa on October 13, significantly impacting the power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Castilian forces led by King Sancho IV begin the siege of Tarifa

events.enhanced_description: In November 1292, Michael II was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox patriarch of Antioch, a position he would hold until 1312. His leadership played a significant role in the religious landscape of the region during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Michael II becomes Syriac Orthodox patriarch of Antioch

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1292, John Balliol was chosen by King Edward I of England as the ruler of Scotland at Berwick, amidst a competition involving thirteen candidates. Edward's subsequent treatment of Balliol as a puppet ruler ignited the Wars of Scottish Independence, beginning in 1296.
events.name: John Balliol is selected by King Edward I of England as ruler of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In December 1292, John Balliol was summoned by Edward I to Westminster to address an appeal from Macduff of Fife regarding a judgment by the Scottish Parliament. Balliol's refusal to comply without consulting his subjects further strained relations with Edward and foreshadowed future conflicts.
events.name: John Balliol is summoned by Edward I to Westminster

events.enhanced_description: In December 1292, Muhammad II of Granada sent ambassadors to negotiate the surrender of Tarifa from King Sancho IV. Sancho's refusal to yield led to a shift in alliances, with Muhammad seeking support from the Marinids against Castile.
events.name: Muhammad II sends ambassadors to the Castilian court

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, the Japanese era of Shōō concluded, giving way to the Einin era. This transition reflects the historical and cultural shifts occurring in Japan during this period.
events.name: The Japanese era Shōō ends, and the Einin era begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, Kublai Khan launched a fleet towards the islands of Southeast Asia, including Java, as part of his broader strategy to extend Mongol influence. This expedition was marked by significant military engagements and political maneuvers.
events.name: Kublai Khan sends a fleet to the islands of Southeast Asia, including Java

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, Kertarajasa established the Hindu Majapahit Empire in Java, capitalizing on internal conflicts and the Mongol invasion. This empire would become one of the most powerful and influential in Southeast Asia, known for its cultural and political achievements.
events.name: The Hindu Majapahit Empire is founded by Kertarajasa in Java

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, Torkel Knutsson spearheaded the Third Swedish Crusade against the unchristianized Finnish Karelia. This military campaign was accompanied by the construction of Vyborg Castle, reflecting Sweden's expansionist ambitions in the region.
events.name: Torkel Knutsson leads Sweden in beginning the Third Swedish Crusade

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, the Ordinances of Justice were enacted in the Commune of Florence, marking a significant reform in the city's governance. These ordinances aimed to curb corruption and enhance the rights of the lower classes, shaping the political landscape of Florence.
events.name: The Ordinances of Justice are enacted in the Commune of Florence

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, Isabella de Forz, Countess of Devon, sold the Isle of Wight to King Edward I of England for 6,000 marks. This transaction reflected the shifting allegiances and economic strategies of the English monarchy during this period.
events.name: The Isle of Wight is sold to King Edward I of England

events.enhanced_description: In 1293, Dante Alighieri completed his seminal work, La Vita Nuova, a collection of poems and prose that explores themes of love and spirituality. This work is considered a cornerstone of Italian literature and a precursor to his later masterpiece, The Divine Comedy.
events.name: Dante Alighieri completes the book of verse La Vita Nuova

events.enhanced_description: In January 1293, Ignatius bar Wahib was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Mardin. His leadership would influence the religious community in the region during a period of significant change.
events.name: Ignatius bar Wahib becomes Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Mardin

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1293, King Sancho IV of Castile established the Studium General, which would later evolve into the Complutense University of Madrid. This institution marked a significant advancement in higher education in Spain, promoting scholarship and learning.
events.name: King Sancho IV of Castile creates the Studium General

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1293, a devastating earthquake struck Kamakura, Japan, resulting in the deaths of approximately 23,000 people. This disaster had profound social and political implications for the region, affecting the Kamakura shogunate's stability.
events.name: An earthquake in Kamakura, Japan kills an estimated 23,000

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1293, Raden Wijaya's forces achieved a significant victory against the Mongol invaders in Java, which is often regarded as the founding date of the city of Surabaya. This victory not only marked a turning point in the Mongol campaign but also laid the groundwork for the establishment of the Majapahit Empire.
events.name: The forces of Raden Wijaya win a major victory in the Mongol invasion of Java

events.enhanced_description: In December 1293, Mamluk Sultan Khalil was assassinated by his regent Baydara, who briefly claimed the sultanate before being killed by a rival faction. This power struggle highlighted the instability within the Mamluk leadership during this period.
events.name: Mamluk sultan Khalil is assassinated by his regent Baydara

events.enhanced_description: In 1294, King John Balliol of Scotland refuses King Edward I of England's demands for support in a planned invasion of France. This decision ultimately leads to the negotiation of the Auld Alliance with France and Norway, setting the stage for the Scottish Wars of Independence.
events.name: John Balliol refuses Edward I's demands

events.enhanced_description: In 1294, Strata Florida Abbey, which had been destroyed during King Edward I's conquest of Wales, is rebuilt. This reconstruction symbolizes the resilience of monastic life and the cultural heritage of the region.
events.name: Strata Florida Abbey is rebuilt

events.enhanced_description: In 1294, architect Arnolfo di Cambio begins designing the Florence Cathedral, known as Il Duomo, and starts work on the Basilica of Santa Croce. His contributions significantly influence the architectural landscape of Florence during the Renaissance.
events.name: Arnolfo di Cambio designs Florence Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In 1294, England and Portugal enter into the first iteration of the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance, which becomes the oldest alliance in the world still in force. This alliance lays the groundwork for future diplomatic and military cooperation between the two nations.
events.name: Anglo-Portuguese Alliance established

events.enhanced_description: In 1294, King Edward I of England and King Philip IV of France formally declare war on each other. This conflict leads to increased tensions and military engagements, significantly impacting the political landscape of medieval Europe.
events.name: Edward I and Philip IV declare war

events.enhanced_description: Kublai Khan, the fifth Khagan of the Mongol Empire and the founder of the Yuan Dynasty in China, dies on February 18, 1294. His death marks a significant turning point as the Mongol Empire begins to fracture into separate khanates, including the Chagatai Khanate, the Golden Horde, the Ilkhanate, and the Yuan Dynasty, leading to a decline in centralized power.
events.name: Kublai Khan dies

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1294, a Novgorodian army led by Prince Roman Glebovich attempts to storm the fortified town of Vyborg. The assault ultimately fails, reflecting the ongoing military struggles in the region during this period.
events.name: Novgorodian army attempts storm of Vyborg

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1294, following the arrival of a Swedish fleet, an offensive leads to the capture of Kexholm by Swedish forces. This event is part of the broader conflicts in the Baltic region during the late 13th century.
events.name: Sweden captures Kexholm

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1294, following a contentious papal election, Pope Celestine V is elected as the 192nd pope, succeeding Nicholas IV. His papacy is notably brief, lasting only five months, as he later abdicates in favor of Pope Boniface VIII.
events.name: Pope Celestine V succeeds Nicholas IV

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 1294, Madog ap Llywelyn leads a revolt against English rule in response to the actions of new royal administrators in north and west Wales. This uprising is part of the ongoing resistance to English domination in Wales.
events.name: Madog ap Llywelyn leads revolt

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1294, Pope Boniface VIII ascends to the papacy following the abdication of Pope Celestine V, who had wished to return to a life of asceticism after a brief and tumultuous reign. Boniface VIII's papacy would be marked by significant conflicts with secular rulers.
events.name: Pope Boniface VIII succeeds Pope Celestine V

events.enhanced_description: In 1295, Marco Polo returns to Venice after 24 years of travel in Asia, particularly in China. His experiences and accounts of the East would later inspire European exploration and trade.
events.name: Marco Polo returns to Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1295, construction begins on Beaumaris Castle in Anglesey, directed by architect James of Saint George. This castle is part of Edward I's campaign to consolidate control over Wales and exemplifies medieval military architecture.
events.name: Construction of Beaumaris Castle begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1295, King Jayavarman VIII is overthrown after a 52-year reign in the Khmer Empire. He is succeeded by his son-in-law Indravarman III, marking a significant change in leadership for the region.
events.name: King Jayavarman VIII overthrown

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1295, the Battle of Maes Moydog occurs, where English forces led by William de Beauchamp defeat Welsh rebels near Llanfair Caereinion. This battle is part of the ongoing conflict between the English crown and Welsh resistance.
events.name: Battle of Maes Moydog

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1295, King Sancho IV of Castile dies after an 11-year reign, leading to the ascension of his 9-year-old son Ferdinand IV. This transition of power occurs amidst ongoing political challenges, including hostilities with Portugal.
events.name: King Sancho IV of Castile dies

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1295, Pope Boniface VIII arranges the Treaty of Anagni, aiming to bring peace between King Philip IV of France, Charles II of Naples, and James II of Majorca. This treaty seeks to resolve conflicts stemming from the War of the Sicilian Vespers.
events.name: Treaty of Anagni

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1295, Przemysł II is crowned king of Poland at Gniezno, marking the first coronation of a Polish ruler in 219 years. His reign signifies a crucial moment in Polish history as he seeks to strengthen the monarchy and unify the kingdom.
events.name: Przemysł II crowned king of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1295, the War of Curzola begins as Genoese raids on the Venetian quarter in Constantinople lead to a formal declaration of war between the Republic of Genoa and the Republic of Venice. This conflict reflects the intense rivalry between these maritime powers.
events.name: War of Curzola begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1295, Baydu Khan is executed after a brief seven-month reign in Tabriz. His death leads to the rise of Ghazan, who converts to Islam, marking a significant shift in the leadership of the Ilkhanate.
events.name: Baydu Khan executed

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1295, the first treaty forming the Auld Alliance between Scotland and France is signed in Paris by King John Balliol and King Philip IV of France. This alliance is aimed at countering English aggression and solidifies a long-standing partnership.
events.name: Auld Alliance treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1295, King Edward I of England summons the Model Parliament to Westminster, which sets a precedent for future parliamentary structures. This assembly agrees to raise taxes to fund military campaigns against France and Scotland.
events.name: Model Parliament summoned

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military action, Boniface of Verona successfully expelled the Byzantines from their last strongholds on the island of Euboea. This event marked a crucial moment in the power dynamics of the region during the late medieval period.
events.name: Boniface of Verona expels the Byzantines from Euboea

events.enhanced_description: Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan spent a year at the court of Khmer King Indravarman III in Angkor, documenting his experiences and observations in a journal. His writings provide valuable insights into the culture, society, and politics of the Khmer Empire during this period.
events.name: Zhou Daguan's observations at the court of Khmer King Indravarman III

events.enhanced_description: In a dramatic display of martial prowess, Wareru defeated Tarabya, the self-proclaimed king of Pegu, in single combat on war elephants. This victory was pivotal in establishing Wareru's dominance in the region.
events.name: Tarabya defeated by Wareru

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1296, King Edward I of England captures Berwick-upon-Tweed, resulting in significant bloodshed and the sacking of this Scottish border town. This event escalates tensions leading to the Scottish Wars of Independence.
events.name: Capture of Berwick

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1296, King Mangrai the Great of Ngoenyang establishes a new capital by founding Chiangmai, which becomes the center of the Mangrai Dynasty that rules the Lanna Kingdom for centuries. This foundation is celebrated as a pivotal moment in the region's history.
events.name: King Mangrai the Great establishes Chiangmai

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1296, the Battle of Dunbar takes place, where the Scottish army led by John Balliol is defeated by an English force commanded by John de Warenne, 6th Earl of Surrey. This battle is a significant event in the early stages of the Scottish Wars of Independence.
events.name: Battle of Dunbar

events.enhanced_description: The death of Jalal ud din Firuz Khalji marked a significant transition in the Delhi Sultanate as his nephew and son-in-law, Ala-Ud-Din-Khalji, ascended to the throne. Ala-Ud-Din would go on to become one of the most powerful rulers of the Khalji dynasty, known for his military conquests and administrative reforms.
events.name: Jalal ud din Firuz Khalji dies and Ala-Ud-Din-Khalji comes to the throne

events.enhanced_description: Alauddin Khalji was formally crowned as Sultan of Delhi, adopting the regnal name Muhammad Shah I. This event solidified his power and set the stage for his ambitious rule, characterized by military expansion and economic reforms.
events.name: Formal coronation of Alauddin Khalji as Sultan of Delhi

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Alcañices was signed between King Denis of Portugal and the young Ferdinand IV of Castile, establishing a long-term alliance of friendship and mutual defense. This treaty would ensure peace between the two kingdoms for the next 40 years.
events.name: Treaty of Alcañices signed

events.enhanced_description: In the winter, Edward I of England accepted a truce proposed by King Philip IV of France, marking a temporary halt to hostilities in Flanders. This truce allowed Edward to refocus his efforts on the ongoing conflict in Scotland.
events.name: Edward I accepts truce with King Philip IV

events.enhanced_description: Pope Boniface VIII intervened in the ongoing rivalry between Genoa and Pisa over the Tyrrhenian islands, appointing King James II of Aragon as regent. This move aimed to stabilize the region and reduce conflict over territorial claims.
events.name: Boniface VIII attempts to mediate Genoa-Pisa rivalry

events.enhanced_description: The Portuguese Water Dog was first described in a monk's report, detailing a heroic act where the dog rescued a drowning sailor. This account highlights the breed's historical significance in maritime communities.
events.name: First description of Portuguese Water Dog

events.enhanced_description: Led by François Grimaldi, the Guelph forces stormed and captured the Rock of Monaco, marking the beginning of the Grimaldi family's long rule over the territory. Disguised as a Franciscan friar, Grimaldi gained entry and opened the gates for his troops, a legendary act that is still commemorated in Monaco's heraldry.
events.name: Guelph forces capture the Rock of Monaco

events.enhanced_description: King Edward I of England made a public appeal outside Westminster Hall, seeking support for his war against France. He acknowledged the heavy tax burdens he had imposed and called for loyalty to his son, Prince Edward, amidst growing opposition.
events.name: Edward I appeals for support for war against France

events.enhanced_description: In May, Scottish rebel leader William Wallace initiated an uprising against English rule at Lanark, killing Sheriff William Hesselrig. This act of defiance marked the beginning of a series of coordinated rebellions against Edward I's authority in Scotland.
events.name: William Wallace's uprising at Lanark

events.enhanced_description: Stefano Colonna, an Italian chief magistrate and papal official, captured a treasure intended for Pope Boniface VIII, which had been sent by the rival Caetani family. This event underscored the intense political rivalries within the papal states.
events.name: Stefano Colonna captures treasure near Rome

events.enhanced_description: In the summer, Edward I of England ordered a punitive expedition against the rebellious Scots, assembling a formidable army at Roxburgh. This military response was part of the broader conflict known as the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Edward I orders punitive expedition against Scots

events.enhanced_description: In July, a confederacy of Scottish nobles, organized by Bishop Robert Wishart, faced defeat against English troops at Irvine. This defeat led to a significant agreement of submission to Edward I, involving key figures such as Robert the Bruce.
events.name: Scottish nobles' confederacy defeated at Irvine

events.enhanced_description: King Louis IX of France, who died in 1270, was canonized by Pope Boniface VIII. Renowned for his devout Christian values, Louis IX's reign was marked by efforts to promote morality and justice in his kingdom.
events.name: Canonization of King Louis IX of France

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Furnes, French forces under Robert II achieved a decisive victory against the Flemings at Veurne. The battle had significant repercussions, including the severe wounding of Robert's son, Philip of Artois.
events.name: Battle of Furnes

events.enhanced_description: Edward I of England led an expedition to Flanders, mobilizing an army of approximately 8,000 men. This military campaign aimed to assert English influence in the region and counteract the growing power of France.
events.name: Edward I's expedition to Flanders

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Stirling Bridge saw Scottish forces, led by William Wallace and Andrew Moray, achieve a stunning victory against an English army commanded by John de Warenne. This battle became a symbol of Scottish resistance during the Wars of Independence.
events.name: Battle of Stirling Bridge

events.enhanced_description: In October and November, William Wallace led Scottish forces in raids across Northumberland and Cumberland, further asserting Scottish resistance against English rule. During this period, Wallace was knighted and appointed Guardian of Scotland.
events.name: Scottish raids in Northumberland and Cumberland

events.enhanced_description: After a protracted siege, the commune of Palestrina surrendered to Papal forces and was subsequently razed to the ground by order of Pope Boniface VIII. This act of debellatio was intended to serve as a warning to other rebellious communes.
events.name: Siege and destruction of Palestrina

events.enhanced_description: In 1298, the Sienese Gran Tavola Bank faced a liquidity crisis as foreign creditors began demanding their deposits back. This event highlighted the vulnerabilities in medieval banking systems and the interconnectedness of European economies.
events.name: Liquidity crisis of the Gran Tavola Bank

events.enhanced_description: In 1298, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Pope Gregory I were collectively recognized as the first Doctors of the Church, a title that signifies their significant contributions to Christian theology and doctrine.
events.name: Doctors of the Church named

events.enhanced_description: In 1298, Wang Zhen, a Chinese inventor and politician, developed a wooden movable type printing system, building on earlier innovations in printing technology. This advancement played a crucial role in the dissemination of knowledge in China.
events.name: Wang Zhen invents wooden movable type printing

events.enhanced_description: The Rindfleisch massacres resulted in the mass execution of Jews in several towns, including Rothenburg ob der Tauber and Würzburg. Led by Rudolph the Dominican, these brutal events led to the deaths of approximately 20,000 Jews across multiple communities.
events.name: Rindfleisch massacres of Jews

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Turaida, forces of the Livonian Order faced a decisive defeat at the hands of the residents of Riga, who were allied with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Vytenis. This battle was a significant moment in the struggle for control in the Baltic region.
events.name: Battle of Turaida

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1298, King Edward I of England led a significant military campaign from Newcastle, traversing through various locations including Alnwick and Roxburgh, ultimately encamping at Kirkliston near Edinburgh. This movement was part of his broader strategy to consolidate English control over Scotland amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: King Edward I (Longshanks) marches from Newcastle

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Göllheim saw Duke Albert I's forces decisively defeat King Adolf of Nassau, leading to Adolf's death and the proclamation of Albert as the new ruler of Germany. This battle was pivotal in the power struggles among the German princes.
events.name: Battle of Göllheim

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1298, the Battle of Falkirk saw English forces, approximately 15,000 strong and led by King Edward I, decisively defeat the Scottish army commanded by William Wallace. The battle showcased the effectiveness of English longbowmen against Scottish formations, leading to a critical victory for Edward in the ongoing Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Falkirk

events.enhanced_description: In August 1298, King Philip IV of France, along with his Seneschal Guichard de Marzé, founded the 'ideal city' of Marciac in southern France. This establishment reflected the medieval ideals of urban planning and governance.
events.name: Foundation of Marciac

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1298, Emperor Fushimi of Japan abdicated after an 11-year reign, passing the throne to his young son Go-Fushimi. This transition marked a significant moment in the Kamakura period of Japanese history.
events.name: Emperor Fushimi abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Curzola, the Genoese fleet, commanded by Admiral Lamba Doria, achieved a significant victory over the Venetian fleet. The battle resulted in the destruction of a majority of the Venetian ships and the capture of the famous explorer Marco Polo.
events.name: Battle of Curzola

events.enhanced_description: In 1299, King Edward I of England began borrowing from Italian merchants, securing a loan of 2,000 pollard marks from the Frescobaldi Firm in London, reflecting the financial strategies of medieval monarchs.
events.name: Edward I borrows from Italian merchants

events.enhanced_description: In 1299, William Wallace embarked on a diplomatic mission to France, seeking support for the Scottish kingship of John Balliol amidst ongoing conflicts with England. This mission underscored the international dimensions of the Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: William Wallace's diplomatic mission to France

events.enhanced_description: In 1299, the Southampton Old Bowling Green was established, marking it as the oldest surviving bowling green in England. This reflects the social and recreational activities of the time.
events.name: Establishment of Southampton Old Bowling Green

events.enhanced_description: In 1299, the Battle of Kili saw Sultan Alauddin Khalji launch a massive attack against Mongol forces, resulting in a fierce confrontation that ended with the capture and execution of Zafar Khan, a key commander in Khalji's army.
events.name: Battle of Kili

events.enhanced_description: In 1299, Sang Nila Utama, a prince of Srivijaya, founded the Kingdom of Singapura, adopting the title Sri Tri Buana. This establishment marked the beginning of a significant trading hub in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Foundation of the Kingdom of Singapura

events.enhanced_description: By 1299, the spinning wheel had become widely adopted in England, revolutionizing the production of woolen yarn. This technological advancement played a crucial role in the textile industry, contributing to economic growth and changing social dynamics in medieval England.
events.name: Widespread use of the spinning wheel in England

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1299, Sultan Alauddin Khalji ordered a large army to prepare for a campaign into Gujarat, demonstrating his ambitions to expand the Delhi Sultanate's influence. The campaign faced internal challenges, including a mutiny among his troops.
events.name: Sultan Alauddin Khalji prepares for march to Gujarat

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, Mongol forces invaded the Delhi Sultanate, prompting Sultan Alauddin Khalji to dispatch Malik Kafur with an army to confront the invaders. The ensuing battle along the banks of the Ravi River resulted in a decisive victory for the Sultan's forces, showcasing the resilience of the Delhi Sultanate against external threats.
events.name: Mongol invasion of India

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1299, Kingston upon Hull was granted city status by royal charter from King Edward I, reflecting the growing importance of urban centers in medieval England.
events.name: Kingston upon Hull granted city status

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1299, King Kyawswa of the Pagan Kingdom and his son were executed by the three brothers of the Myinsaing Kingdom for their allegiance to the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Execution of King Kyawswa of Pagan

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1299, Pope Boniface VIII issued the papal bull "Scimus, Fili," which condemned the invasion and occupation of Scotland by Edward I of England. This act was significant as it highlighted the tension between the English crown and the papacy, as well as the ongoing struggle for Scottish independence.
events.name: Pope Boniface VIII issues the papal bull "Scimus, Fili"

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1299, the Battle of Cape Orlando saw an Aragonese-Angevin fleet led by Admiral Roger of Lauria defeat a Sicilian fleet. The battle was marked by strategic maneuvers and resulted in the capture of 18 Sicilian ships.
events.name: Battle of Cape Orlando

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1299, Osman I declared the independence of the Anatolian beylik from the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, marking the foundation of the Ottoman Empire. This declaration set the stage for the rise of one of history's most influential empires.
events.name: Osman I declares independence of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1299, Pisa and Genoa reached a thirty-year truce, effectively ending hostilities between the two maritime powers and stabilizing the region's political landscape.
events.name: Pisa and Genoa agree to a truce

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1299, King Edward I of England married Margaret of France, the half-sister of King Philip IV, strengthening political ties between England and France through this royal union.
events.name: Edward I marries Margaret of France

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1299, John I, Count of Holland, died and was succeeded by his uncle John II, who established a personal union with the County of Hainaut, impacting the political dynamics of the region.
events.name: Death of John I, Count of Holland

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1299, the Battle of Falconaria resulted in a decisive victory for Sicilian forces under King Frederick II against Philip I of Taranto, who was captured during the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Falconaria

events.enhanced_description: In December 1299, Mongol forces led by Ghazan Khan invaded Syria, successfully capturing Aleppo. This campaign was bolstered by the support of King Hethum II of Cilician Armenia, who sought to reclaim lost territories.
events.name: Mongol forces invade Syria

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1299, the Battle of Wadi al-Khaznadar saw Mongol forces under Ghazan Khan defeat a Mamluk army, leading to significant territorial gains for the Mongols in Syria. Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad's retreat marked a turning point in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Wadi al-Khaznadar

events.enhanced_description: The death of King Andrew III, also known as Andrew the Venetian, marks the end of the Árpád Dynasty in Hungary, leading to a power struggle among various claimants including Wenceslaus III of Bohemia and Charles Robert of Naples. This event sets the stage for a turbulent period in Hungarian history characterized by noble factions vying for control.
events.name: Death of King Andrew III of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: The Second Mongol invasion of Burma commences as Temür Khan's forces reach Myinsaing, the capital of the Myinsaing Kingdom. The siege that follows lasts nearly three months, highlighting the Mongols' persistent attempts to expand their influence in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Second Mongol invasion of Burma begins

events.enhanced_description: At just 16 years old, Edward of Caernarfon is granted the title of the first Prince of Wales, marking a significant moment in Welsh history. This title symbolizes the English crown's authority over Wales and sets the stage for future conflicts regarding Welsh independence.
events.name: Edward of Caernarfon becomes the first Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: After weeks of unsuccessful siege tactics, the Mongol forces launch a major assault on Myinsaing, but the determined Burmese defenders hold out for 12 days. This fierce resistance leads to a temporary truce, showcasing the resilience of the local forces against Mongol might.
events.name: Major assault during the Second Mongol invasion of Burma

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Go-Fushimi abdicates after a brief reign of 2½ years, paving the way for his cousin Go-Nijō to ascend the throne as the 94th emperor of Japan. This transition reflects the ongoing complexities of imperial succession during the Kamakura period.
events.name: Emperor Go-Fushimi abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: After weeks of stalemate in the siege of Myinsaing, negotiations for a truce begin between the Mongol invaders and the Burmese defenders. This diplomatic effort highlights the complexities of warfare and the need for resolution amidst prolonged conflict.
events.name: Negotiations for a truce during the Second Mongol invasion of Burma

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Osman I calls for a military campaign into Byzantine Bithynia, resulting in the capture of key towns such as İnegöl and Yenişehir. This campaign marks the beginning of Ottoman expansion into the region, setting the stage for future conquests.
events.name: Sultan Osman I's military campaign into Byzantine Bithynia

events.enhanced_description: The three Bagan brothers, rulers of the Myinsaing Kingdom, reach an agreement with Mongol leader Temür Khan to pay a substantial sum of gold and silver in exchange for ending the invasion. This settlement reflects the economic pressures and strategic negotiations of the time.
events.name: Agreement to end the Second Mongol invasion of Burma

events.enhanced_description: In a significant military engagement, Rainier I, the first ruler of the Grimaldi family, is forced to flee as Genoese troops besiege Monaco. This event marks the beginning of a prolonged period of Genoese control over the region, lasting over three decades.
events.name: Siege of Monaco by Genoese troops

events.enhanced_description: The Diet of Hungary votes to invalidate the coronation of Charles of Anjou, asserting that he was never officially crowned at Székesfehérvár and did not receive the Crown of Saint Stephen. This decision underscores the political turmoil following the death of Andrew III and the struggle for legitimacy among claimants.
events.name: Invalidation of Charles of Anjou's coronation

events.enhanced_description: Nicola Boccasini, who will later become Pope Benedict XI, begins his role as the Roman Catholic apostolic legate to Hungary, representing Pope Boniface VIII. His appointment signifies the Church's involvement in the political affairs of Hungary during a time of instability.
events.name: Nicola Boccasini begins duties as apostolic legate to Hungary

events.enhanced_description: King Edward I of England initiates his sixth campaign into Scotland, crossing the border into Berwickshire from Northumberland. This military action is part of the ongoing First War of Scottish Independence, reflecting the tensions between England and Scotland.
events.name: Edward I launches campaign into Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Alauddin Khalji's forces successfully capture Ranthambore Fortress, a significant stronghold in Rajasthan. The siege is marked by the death of General Nusrat Khan Jalesari, demonstrating the fierce combat and high stakes involved in the conquest.
events.name: Capture of Ranthambore Fortress

events.enhanced_description: The English Army, under the command of King Edward I, reaches Glasgow as part of his campaign during the First War of Scottish Independence. This movement signifies the continued military pressure on Scottish territories.
events.name: English Army reaches Glasgow

events.enhanced_description: Wenceslaus III of Bohemia is crowned King of Hungary, taking the regnal name King Vencel, in a ceremony at Székesfehérvár. This event marks a significant shift in power dynamics within Hungary, as Wenceslaus's reign is largely nominal due to the influence of powerful nobles.

image.caption: Seal of Wenceslaus III.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1896 in the supplied metadata, not to the 1301 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Wenceslaus III crowned King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: During their invasion of Scotland, English troops led by Prince Edward of Caernarfon and Henry de Lacy capture Turnberry Castle, the headquarters of the Bruces. This victory is part of Edward I's broader campaign to assert English dominance over Scotland.
events.name: Capture of Turnberry Castle

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of his father Alberto, Bartolomeo I della Scala ascends as the new Lord of Verona, a prominent city-state in Italy. His rule marks a continuation of the della Scala family's influence in the Veneto region.
events.name: Bartolomeo I della Scala becomes Lord of Verona

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic alliance, the Emirate of Granada, under Muhammad al-Faqih, and the Kingdom of Aragon, ruled by Jaime II the Just, sign a military agreement to combat the Kingdom of Castile. This pact reflects the ongoing conflicts in the Iberian Peninsula during the Reconquista.

image.caption: Map of the Kingdom of Granada.

events.name: Military agreement between Granada and Aragon

events.enhanced_description: Hojo Morotoki is appointed as the 10th regent for the Kamakura shogunate, taking on a significant role in the governance of Japan during a critical period. His leadership will influence the political landscape of the shogunate.

image.caption: Portrait of Hōjō Morotoki, reproduced from 絵本鎌倉北条九代記.
