image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Hojo Morotoki becomes regent for the Kamakura shogunate

events.enhanced_description: Abu Numayy I, the Arabic ruler of the Emirate of Mecca, abdicates in favor of his two sons, Rumaythah and Humaydah. His abdication and subsequent death shortly thereafter mark a significant transition in leadership for the emirate.
events.name: Abdication of Abu Numayy I in Mecca

events.enhanced_description: Charles of Valois is summoned to Italy by Pope Boniface VIII to mediate peace between the Guelphs and Ghibellines. His arrival in Florence leads to significant political changes, including the return of the Neri faction and the exile of poet Dante Alighieri.
events.name: Charles of Valois summoned to Italy by Pope Boniface VIII

events.enhanced_description: Bolko I, known as Bolko the Strict, passes away, leaving his three young sons as his successors. His death creates a power vacuum in the region, with his brother-in-law Herman serving as regent during their minority.
events.name: Death of Bolko I of Poland

events.enhanced_description: Pope Boniface VIII issues the papal bull Ausculta Fili, accusing King Philip IV of France of malfeasance in office. This document escalates tensions between the papacy and the French crown, highlighting the struggles for power between secular and religious authorities.
events.name: Papal bull Ausculta Fili issued by Pope Boniface VIII

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand IV of Castile, having reached the age of 16, is proclaimed of age and prepared for his coronation as King of Castile and León. This moment marks a transition in leadership as he steps into a role that he has held nominally since the age of 9.
events.name: Ferdinand IV of Castile reaches age of majority

events.enhanced_description: In August 1303, King Ferdinand the Summoned, under the supervision of his mother, Queen-Regent María de Molina, signed a three-year peace treaty with Muhammad III of Granada in Córdoba. This treaty aimed to stabilize relations and secure tribute payments, reflecting the complex political landscape of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Peace treaty signed at Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: In September 1303, Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos sought military support from European kingdoms to fend off a potential siege of Constantinople by Ottoman-Turkish forces. He enlisted Roger de Flor and the Catalan Company to bolster the Byzantine defenses.
events.name: Andronikos II seeks support from Europe

events.enhanced_description: A significant earthquake strikes Byzantium and Constantinople, leading to widespread devastation. Emperor Michael IX Palaiologos responds by invoking divine warnings, reflecting the era's intertwining of faith and governance.
events.name: Major earthquake strikes Byzantium and Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: John XII was forced to resign from his position as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople following a devastating earthquake that struck the city on January 17, 1303. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the Eastern Orthodox Church, as it led to a power vacuum and changes in church leadership.
events.name: John XII forced to resign as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Chittorgarh commenced on January 28, 1303, as Sultan Alauddin Khalji of Delhi sought to conquer the Medapata Kingdom, ruled by Emperor Ratnasimha. This marked the beginning of a protracted conflict that would culminate in the fall of one of India's most formidable forts.
events.name: Siege of Chittorgarh begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1303, Scottish forces led by John Comyn III and Simon Fraser launched a surprise attack against an English scouting party at Roslin, resulting in a decisive victory. The battle showcased the tactical prowess of the Scots and significantly impacted the ongoing conflict between Scotland and England.
events.name: Battle of Roslin

events.enhanced_description: Joan II of the Anscarids ascended to the title of Countess of Burgundy on March 17, 1303, following the death of her father, Otto IV. This event marked a significant transition in the governance of Burgundy, a free state within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Joan II becomes Countess of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1589, King Henry IV of France achieved a decisive victory against the forces of the Catholic League at the Battle of Arques, led by Charles of Lorraine, Duke of Mayenne. This battle was pivotal in Henry's efforts to consolidate power during the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Battle of Arques

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1303, Pope Boniface VIII established the University of Rome through the papal bull In Supremae praeminentia Dignitatis. This institution became the first pontifical university, aimed at providing ecclesiastical studies under papal authority.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Rome

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Marj al-Saffar occurred on April 22, 1303, where Mamluk forces under Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad defeated a Mongol army and their Armenian allies. This victory solidified Mamluk control over the region and marked a significant moment in the struggle against Mongol incursions.
events.name: Battle of Marj al-Saffar

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1303, King Edward I of England gathered 7,500 troops at Roxburgh in preparation for a renewed campaign against Scotland. This military buildup signaled the continuation of hostilities between England and Scotland during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Edward I assembles troops at Roxburgh

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1303, Elizabeth Richeza, the daughter of the late King Przemysl II of Poland, married Wenceslaus II of Bohemia at the Prague Cathedral. This marriage united two powerful dynasties and strengthened political ties in Central Europe.
events.name: Marriage of Elizabeth Richeza and Wenceslaus II

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1303, Pope Boniface VIII nullified the election of Wenceslaus as King of Hungary, declaring Károly Róbert as the rightful claimant. This decision intensified the political strife in Hungary and highlighted the Pope's influence over European monarchies.
events.name: Papal nullification of Wenceslaus' election as King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1303, Scottish nobles Edmund Comyn and Simon Fraser led an invasion into England, devastating the area around Carlisle. This incursion was part of the ongoing conflict between Scotland and England, demonstrating the volatility of the border regions.
events.name: Scottish invasion of England

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1303, Athanasius I regained his position as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople after nearly a decade of exile. His return was a significant event for the Eastern Orthodox Church, restoring stability to its leadership.
events.name: Athanasius I returns as Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1303, a powerful earthquake struck Crete, resulting in the destruction of the Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. This event marked a significant loss in architectural history and demonstrated the vulnerability of ancient structures to natural disasters.
events.name: 1303 Crete earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1303, after an eight-month siege, Delhi forces led by Sultan Alauddin Khalji captured Chittor Fort, resulting in a massacre of its inhabitants. This event marked a pivotal moment in the history of the region, showcasing the military might of the Delhi Sultanate.
events.name: Siege of Chittorgarh concludes

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1303, Pope Boniface VIII was imprisoned by Guillaume de Nogaret on behalf of King Philip IV of France at his residence in Anagni. This incident marked a significant low point in papal authority and highlighted the tensions between the papacy and the French crown.
events.name: Boniface VIII imprisoned

events.enhanced_description: The Kagen era commenced on September 16, 1303, during the reign of Emperor Gonijo in Japan. This era is noted for its cultural developments and the continuation of the imperial lineage amidst the political complexities of the time.
events.name: Kagen era begins in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1303, a catastrophic earthquake struck the cities of Taiyuan and Pingyang in China, resulting in the deaths of approximately 200,000 people. This disaster had profound effects on the region's population and infrastructure.
events.name: Hongdong earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Pope Boniface VIII died on October 11, 1303, while imprisoned in Anagni, after an eight-year pontificate marked by significant political strife and conflict with secular powers. His death led to a pivotal moment in the history of the papacy.
events.name: Death of Pope Boniface VIII

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1303, a papal conclave in Rome resulted in the unanimous election of Cardinal Nicolò Boccasini as the new Pope. This election was crucial in restoring stability to the papacy following the tumultuous reign of Boniface VIII.
events.name: Papal conclave elects new Pope

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1303, Cardinal Nicolò Boccasini was crowned as Pope Benedict XI at St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City. His coronation marked the beginning of a new papacy aimed at healing the divisions caused by his predecessor's controversial reign.
events.name: Coronation of Pope Benedict XI

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1303, King Edward I of England spent the winter at Dunfermline Abbey, planning an attack on Stirling Castle. His military strategy included deploying forces to raid and plunder Scottish territories, intensifying the conflict between England and Scotland.
events.name: Edward I plans attack on Stirling Castle

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1303, Pope Benedict XI issued a mandate to protect the rights of Cardinal Jean Lemoine of France regarding income from the dioceses of Bayeux and Amiens while serving as papal legate. This decision highlighted the Pope's role in managing church affairs and protecting the interests of his cardinals.
events.name: Pope Benedict XI issues mandate

events.enhanced_description: In 1304, Sultan Alauddin Khalji ordered a second invasion of Gujarat, which resulted in the annexation of the Kingdom of Vaghela into the Delhi Sultanate. This military campaign was part of Khalji's broader strategy to expand his empire.
events.name: Sultan Alauddin Khalji orders a second invasion of Gujarat

events.enhanced_description: In 1304, the Battle of Skafida took place near Sozopol, where Byzantine Emperor Michael IX Palaiologos sent an expeditionary force to confront the advancing Bulgarians led by Tsar Theodore Svetoslav. The battle resulted in a significant defeat for the Byzantines, who suffered heavy losses and were ultimately routed.
events.name: Battle of Skafida

events.enhanced_description: In 1304, the island of Chios in the Aegean Sea was lost by the Byzantines to the Genoese under Admiral Benedetto I Zaccaria. He established an autonomous lordship on the island, justifying his actions as a necessary measure against Turkish pirates.
events.name: Byzantines lose Chios to Genoese

events.enhanced_description: In 1304, ambassadors from the Mongol rulers of Central Asia and the Yuan Dynasty presented a peace proposal to Toqta Khan, the ruler of the Golden Horde. This led to the reopening of commercial networks across the Mongol khanates and solidified Toqta's rule over the Rus' princes.
events.name: Mongol ambassadors propose peace to Toqta Khan

events.enhanced_description: The Ypres Cloth Hall, a significant medieval structure, was completed in 1304. This hall became a central hub for the cloth trade in Ypres, reflecting the city's economic prosperity during the late Middle Ages.

image.caption: Ypres Cloth Hall and belfry in Belgium.
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the reconstructed Cloth Hall as it appeared in 2018; it documents the site, not the building’s medieval completion.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Completion of Ypres Cloth Hall

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1304, messengers from King Edward I of England arrived at Kinclaven Castle to negotiate peace with Scottish noble John Comyn. This meeting was part of the broader context of the ongoing War of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Messengers from King Edward of England arrive at Kinclaven Castle

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1304, King Philip IV of France issued a mandate in Toulouse aimed at preventing civil war by prohibiting violence against his subjects. This decree followed discussions with Franciscan friar Bernard Délicieux regarding the Dominican Inquisition.
events.name: King Philip the Fair issues a mandate at Toulouse

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1304, Cardinal Nicolò Albertini de Prato was dispatched by Pope Benedict XI as a papal legate to mediate peace negotiations in the regions of Tuscany, Romagna, and the Marca Trevigiana, reflecting the Pope's efforts to stabilize the political landscape in Italy.
events.name: Cardinal Nicolò Albertini de Prato dispatched as papal legate

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1304, Scottish nobles led by Robert the Bruce and John Comyn negotiated a peace treaty with King Edward I of England. The treaty allowed the Scots to retain their lands and laws while submitting to English rule, marking a significant moment in the War of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Scottish nobles negotiate a peace treaty with King Edward I

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1304, the Battle of Happrew took place where Scottish rebels led by William Wallace and Simon Fraser engaged in guerilla warfare against King Edward I's forces. Despite their efforts, the Scots were defeated and forced to retreat, narrowly escaping capture.
events.name: Battle of Happrew

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1304, Cardinal Nicolò Albertini entered Florence, where he was granted special powers by the government to facilitate peace negotiations. His mission was crucial in addressing the conflicts affecting the region during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Cardinal Albertini enters Florence

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1304, John I of Arborea, also known as 'Chiano', passed away. He was the ruler of western Sardinia and was succeeded by his sons Marianus III and Andrew, marking a significant transition in the leadership of the region.
events.name: Death of John I of Arborea

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1304, Count Albert I of Gorizia died, and his son Henry III succeeded him. This transition marked a significant change in the governance of the Gorizia region.
events.name: Death of Count Albert I of Gorizia

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1304, Mahmud Ghazan, the Mongol ruler of the Ilkhanate, died and was succeeded by his brother Öljaitü Qaghan. Ghazan's reign was marked by significant cultural and political developments in the region.
events.name: Death of Mahmud Ghazan

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1304, Abu Said Uthman I, the Zenata Berber ruler of Tlemcen, died and was succeeded by his son Abu Zayyan I. This succession marked a continuation of the Zenata dynasty's influence in the region.
events.name: Death of Abu Said Uthman I

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1304, Pope Benedict XI died after a brief pontificate lasting only eight months. His death initiated a papal conclave to elect his successor, which would be marked by significant political maneuvering.
events.name: Death of Pope Benedict XI

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1304, a papal conclave convened in Perugia with 15 of the 19 living Roman Catholic cardinals to elect a successor to Pope Benedict XI. The conclave would remain deadlocked for nearly a year, highlighting the political complexities of the time.
events.name: Papal conclave assembles at Perugia

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1304, King Edward I of England successfully captured Stirling Castle after a four-month siege involving twelve siege engines, including the massive Warwolf. The surrender of William Oliphant and his garrison marked a pivotal moment in the English campaign against Scottish resistance.
events.name: Siege of Stirling Castle

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1304, Andrey III Aleksandorovich, a Kievan nobleman and Grand Prince of the Principality of Grand Duchy of Vladimir, died. He was succeeded by his uncle Mikhail of Tver, marking a significant shift in the leadership of the region.
events.name: Death of Andrey III Aleksandorovich

events.enhanced_description: In August 1304, Flemish forces under John II, Duke of Brabant, and Guy of Dampierre occupied Zeeland and Holland. This occupation prompted a response from John II, Count of Holland, who managed to recover these territories shortly before his death on August 22.
events.name: Flemish forces occupy Zeeland and Holland

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1304, King Ferdinand IV of Castile signed the Treaty of Torrellas with King James II of Aragon, concluding a long-standing conflict over the Kingdom of Murcia. The treaty restored significant territories to Castile and resolved disputes that had persisted for nearly three decades.
events.name: Treaty of Torrellas

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1304, the Battle of Zierikzee occurred when a French-Hollandic fleet, supported by Genoese ships under Admiral Rainier I, defeated a Flemish fleet. The battle resulted in the capture of Flemish commander Guy of Namur and the annihilation of his fleet.
events.name: Battle of Zierikzee

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1304, the Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle took place, where French forces led by King Philip IV defeated a Flemish army. The battle resulted in the death of Flemish leader William of Jülich and a retreat to Lille, marking a significant victory for France.
events.name: Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1304, Brinolfo Algotsson, the Swedish Catholic Bishop of Skara, was rewarded for his financial assistance in rebuilding Norway's Stavanger Cathedral. He received a holy relic, purported to be a thorn from the crown of thorns worn by Jesus Christ, which was transported to Skara Cathedral.
events.name: Brinolfo Algotsson rewarded for rebuilding Stavanger Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1304, Thomas of Corbridge, the powerful Archbishop of York, died after serving for just over four years. His death led to a vacancy in the archbishopric, prompting the resignation of Lord Chancellor William Greenfield to take up the position.
events.name: Death of Thomas of Corbridge

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1304, the Treaty of Treviso was signed between the Italian commune of Padua and Venice, concluding the Salt War. The treaty established Venice's salt monopoly and regulated salt rights for merchants, significantly impacting the local economy.
events.name: Treaty of Treviso

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1304, Ottoman-Turkish forces led by Sultan Osman I conquered the ancient city of Ephesus from the Byzantine Empire. This conquest involved the massacre and deportation of its native population, marking a significant expansion of Ottoman territory.
events.name: Ottoman forces conquer Ephesus

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1304, King Edward I summoned the English Parliament for the first time in over two years. This gathering was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts with Scotland and the need for royal support.
events.name: King Edward I summons the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In December 1304, Roger de Flor, an Italian nobleman and adventurer, settled with the Catalan Company in Gallipoli and other towns in southern Thrace. He used these locations as bases for his operations, demanding payment for his forces while living off the local population.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Roger de Flor.
image.credit: Biondi — Biografia degli uomini illustri del Regno di Napoli (Napoli, 1818-1821, vol.7)
image.date_qualification: Nineteenth-century engraving. The saved 2012 timestamp does not establish the engraving's creation date; that date is unknown.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Roger de Flor settles with the Catalan Company

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1304, William Greenfield, who served as Lord Chancellor of England, was elected Archbishop of York by church leaders in the diocese. Following his election, he traveled to Rome to receive consecration from Pope Clement V, marking a significant moment in the ecclesiastical hierarchy of England.
events.name: William Greenfield elected Archbishop of York

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1304, William de Hamilton was nominated by King Edward I to serve as Lord Chancellor of England, the highest office for a member of Parliament at that time. His appointment signified the king's trust in de Hamilton's capabilities to manage the affairs of the realm.
events.name: William de Hamilton nominated Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1305, the marriage of Bastam, the 8-year-old son of Oljaitu Khan, to Uljay Qutlugh Khatun, the 7-year-old daughter of the late Ghazan Khan, took place in Tabriz. This union was part of a political alliance between the Mongol rulers.
events.name: Marriage of Bastam and Uljay Qutlugh Khatun

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1305, William de Hamilton was formally invested as Lord Chancellor of England, the highest-ranking elected official at the time. His role was crucial in the governance of the kingdom during a period of political strife.
events.name: William de Hamilton invested as Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1305, Henry II Kőszegi, the Ban of Slavonia, completed his conquest of Croatian territories in Požega and Valkó. He issued a charter of annexation from his encampment, asserting his control over the newly acquired lands.
events.name: Henry II Kőszegi's conquest of Croatian territory

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1305, King James II of Aragon and King Ferdinand IV of Castile convened a summit at the Monastery of Santa María de Huerta. This meeting was attended by various nobles and aimed at addressing territorial and political issues between their kingdoms.

locations.name: Monastery of Santa María de Huerta

events.name: Summit at Monastery of Santa María de Huerta

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1305, the 52nd English Parliament assembled in Westminster. This gathering was significant in the ongoing political developments of England during the reign of King Edward I.
events.name: 52nd English Parliament assembles

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1305, Amir Chupan, the Duke of Yi, was betrothed to Dowlandi Khatun, the daughter of Öljaitü. This marriage was part of the intricate alliances within the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Amir Chupan betrothed to Dowlandi Khatun

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1305, King Edward I dissolved the 52nd Parliament in Westminster. This action was part of the ongoing political maneuvering during his reign.
events.name: King Edward dissolves the 52nd Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1305, Juan Manuel of Castile was made Lord of Alarcón. This title was significant in the feudal hierarchy of Castile and reflected his influence in the region.
events.name: Juan Manuel made Lord of Alarcón

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1305, Byzantine Emperor Michael IX Palaiologos invited Roger de Flor to Edirne, where he was assassinated along with many of his followers. This act led to increased hostilities from the Catalan Company against Byzantine territories, marking a period known as the 'Catalan Revenge.'
events.name: Assassination of Roger de Flor

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1305, the Treaty of Elche was signed between King James II of Aragon and King Ferdinand IV of Castile. This treaty revised the territorial borders established in the earlier Treaty of Torrellas, reflecting the ongoing negotiations between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Treaty of Elche signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1305, Pope Clement V, previously the Archbishop of Bordeaux, was elected as the 195th pontiff of the Catholic Church, succeeding Pope Benedict XI. His papacy would later be marked by significant events, including the relocation of the papal court to Avignon.
events.name: Pope Clement V succeeds Pope Benedict XI

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1305, Öljaitü, the new Mongol Ikhanate, married Qutlughshah Khatun, the daughter of the Kerait Emir Irinjin. This marriage was part of the political alliances that characterized the Mongol Empire during this period.
events.name: Öljaitü marries Qutlughshah Khatun

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1305, Wenceslaus III ascended to the thrones of Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland at the young age of 14, following the death of his father, King Wenceslaus II. His reign was marked by challenges as he navigated the complexities of ruling multiple kingdoms.
events.name: Wenceslaus III becomes ruler

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1305, Irinjin, in recognition of his daughter's marriage to Öljaitü, was appointed Viceroy of Anatolia. This appointment highlighted the importance of familial alliances in the political landscape of the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Irinjin appointed Viceroy of Anatolia

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1305, the Battle of Apros occurred, where Byzantine forces under Michael IX Palaiologos engaged the Catalan Company. Despite a strong initial charge, the Byzantines faced desertion from their allies and ultimately suffered defeat.
events.name: Battle of Apros

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1305, King Edward I summoned a new Parliament to assemble on September 15. This action was part of his ongoing efforts to manage the political landscape of England.
events.name: King Edward summons new Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1305, William Wallace, the Scottish rebel leader, was captured near Glasgow at Robroyston by English troops led by John de Menteith. His capture marked a significant turning point in the Scottish struggle for independence.
events.name: William Wallace captured

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1305, after a three-week trial at Westminster, William Wallace was convicted of treason and executed in Smithfield, London. His brutal execution was intended to serve as a warning to other rebels and solidified his status as a martyr for Scottish independence.
events.name: William Wallace executed

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1305, King Edward I of England issued ordinances aimed at establishing control over Scotland, following the tumultuous period of the Wars of Scottish Independence. This included the first commission of Trailbaston, which empowered judicial commissions to punish various crimes, reflecting Edward's attempts to impose English law and order in the region.
events.name: King Edward I of England issues ordinances for the government of the Kingdom of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1305, Öljaitü, the Mongol Ilkhan of Persia, received an ambassador from the Yuan dynasty of China in Tabriz. This event underscored the diplomatic relations between the Mongol states and highlighted the interconnectedness of the Mongol Empire during this period.
events.name: Öljaitü receives the Mongol ambassador from Yuan dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1305, King Wenceslaus III of Bohemia married Viola Elizabeth of Teschen, a strategic alliance that aimed to strengthen his claim to the Hungarian throne. This marriage occurred amidst political turmoil, as Wladyslaw II the Elbow-High began to assert his own claims over Polish territories.
events.name: King Wenceslaus III marries Viola Elizabeth of Teschen

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1305, Mahalakadeva, the King of Malwa, was killed while attempting to flee from the invading forces of the Delhi Sultanate. Following his death, Ayn al-Mulk Multani was appointed as the Sultanate's Governor of Malwa, marking a significant shift in power in the region.
events.name: Mahalakadeva, King of Malwa, is killed

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1305, Öljaitü, the Mongol Ilkhan, received an ambassador sent by Toqta, the Khan of the Golden Horde, in Tabriz. This meeting highlighted the ongoing diplomatic interactions within the fragmented Mongol Empire and the importance of alliances among the khanates.
events.name: Öljaitü receives the ambassador from Toqta, Khan of the Golden Horde

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1305, the Battle of Amroha took place, where Mongol forces invaded the Delhi Sultanate. Sultan Alauddin Khalji dispatched a cavalry force led by Vizier Ghazi Malik to repel the invasion, resulting in a decisive victory for the Delhi forces, who captured many Mongol soldiers.
events.name: Battle of Amroha

events.enhanced_description: During the winter of 1306, Robert the Bruce retreated to the Isle of Rathlin with a small band of followers, including his brothers and notable allies. This strategic withdrawal allowed him to regroup and plan for his future campaigns to reclaim Scotland from English control.
events.name: Robert the Bruce retreats to the Isle of Rathlin

events.enhanced_description: In an effort to regulate air quality and public health, a city ordinance in London prohibited the use of coal for heating during parliamentary sessions. Despite its intentions, the ordinance proved largely ineffective, reflecting the challenges of governance in urban environments.
events.name: London coal heating ordinance

events.enhanced_description: Storkyrkan, the current cathedral of Stockholm, was consecrated by Birger Jarl Magnusson, marking a significant moment in the religious and cultural history of Sweden. This event underscored the importance of the church in medieval society and its role in the governance of the realm.
events.name: Consecration of Storkyrkan Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1306, Deshou Khan, the only son of Chinese Emperor Chengzong of the Yuan dynasty, died unexpectedly, leaving the Mongol Empire without a clear heir. This event raised concerns about succession and stability within the Yuan dynasty.
events.name: Deshou Khan dies

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1306, Pope Clement V issued a papal bull that established the University of Orléans in France, granting it the title and privileges of a university. This event marked a significant development in higher education during the medieval period.
events.name: Creation of the University of Orléans

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1306, Sunni Muslim theologian Ibn Taymiyyah was found innocent of heresy after hearings conducted by the Indian Qur'an scholar Safi al-Din al-Hindi. However, he would later be convicted by a panel of judges in the Mamluk state, leading to his imprisonment.
events.name: Ibn Taymiyyah found innocent of heresy

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1306, Robert the Bruce murdered his political rival John Comyn III in a fit of rage at Greyfriars Church in Dumfries. This act of violence led to Bruce's excommunication by Pope Clement V and intensified the conflict between the Scots and the English.
events.name: Robert the Bruce murders John Comyn III

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1306, at the young age of 11, Hugh V ascended to the title of Duke of Burgundy following the death of his father, Robert II. His ascension marked a significant moment in the history of the Burgundian state, which would play a crucial role in European politics.
events.name: Hugh V becomes Duke of Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1306, Robert the Bruce was crowned king of Scotland at Scone by Bishop William de Lamberton. This coronation was a defiant act against English claims of sovereignty, occurring in the absence of traditional regalia that had been taken to London.
events.name: Robert the Bruce crowned king of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1306, Amalric, Lord of Tyre, orchestrated a coup d'état against his brother, Henry II of Cyprus, with the support of the Knights Templar. Although Henry remained the nominal king, Amalric effectively seized control, marking a significant power struggle within the kingdom.
events.name: Amalric stages a coup against Henry II of Cyprus

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1306, Charles the Lame, King of Naples, accused Philip I of Piedmont and Isabella of Villehardouin of disloyalty, stripping them of their rights to rule the Principality of Achaea. This decision reflected the ongoing political tensions in the region and Charles's attempts to consolidate power.
events.name: Charles the Lame deprives Philip I of Piedmont of rule in Achaea

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1306, a fleet from the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, commanded by Sultan Muhammad III, launched a surprise attack on Ceuta, capturing the city. This military action was part of a broader conflict involving the Marinid Sultanate and marked a significant moment in the struggle for control over North African territories.
events.name: Moorish Nasrid fleet captures Ceuta

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1306, during the Feast of the Swans at Westminster Abbey, King Edward I of England proclaimed that all squires willing to join the invasion of Scotland would be knighted. This event was marked by Edward's vows to avenge the murder of John III Comyn and to wage war against the Scots.
events.name: Feast of the Swans

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1306, the English Parliament convened at Westminster for a one-day session, where they passed a five percent tax on citizens and communities across the realm. This decision was part of Edward I's efforts to fund his military campaigns and maintain control over his territories.
events.name: English Parliament passes a tax

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1306, after concluding the Flemish War, King Philip IV of France ordered a reform of the livre coins, raising their silver content back to the level of 1285. This economic decree aimed to stabilize the currency but led to public unrest and rioting.
events.name: Philip IV of France orders coinage reform

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1306, the Battle of Methven occurred, where Robert the Bruce's Scottish forces faced defeat against the English army. The Scots were caught off guard by a surprise attack, leading to significant losses and forcing Bruce to retreat.
events.name: Battle of Methven

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1306, the Knights Hospitaller, led by Grand Master Foulques de Villaret, landed on the island of Rhodes, initiating a four-year siege to capture the fortified city. This marked the beginning of a significant military campaign in the region.
events.name: Knights Hospitaller land on Rhodes

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1306, King Philip IV of France ordered the expulsion of Jews from France, seizing their properties to alleviate his debts. This event, known as the Great Exile, reflected the growing anti-Semitic sentiments and economic pressures of the time.
events.name: The Great Exile of 1306

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1306, King Wenceslaus III of Bohemia was assassinated at the age of 16 in Olomouc, marking the end of the Přemyslid dynasty. His death led to a power vacuum, with his sister Anne administering the kingdom until a new ruler was elected.
events.name: Assassination of Wenceslaus III of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1306, the Battle of Dalrigh took place, where Robert the Bruce was defeated by rival Scottish forces led by John the Lame of Argyll. This battle was a significant setback for Bruce, who narrowly escaped capture.
events.name: Battle of Dalrigh

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1306, English forces under Edward of Caernarfon captured and sacked Kildrummy Castle in Aberdeenshire. This event was part of the broader conflict between England and Scotland, leading to the capture of several members of the Bruce family.
events.name: Capture of Kildrummy Castle

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1306, the Knights Hospitaller besieging the island of Rhodes captured Feraklos Castle. This victory was part of their campaign to establish control over Rhodes and the surrounding islands.
events.name: Knights Hospitaller capture Feraklos Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Hatuna Games, a significant event in Swedish history, culminated in the capture of King Birger Magnusson and his wife, Martha of Denmark, by his brothers Eric and Valdemar Magnusson. This act of betrayal led to a power struggle for the Swedish throne, marking a pivotal moment in the political landscape of medieval Sweden.
events.name: The Hatuna Games are played in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In recognition of his military service against the Scots, Robert FitzWalter, 1st Baron FitzWalter, received a pardon for all debts owed to King Edward I of England. This act underscored the intertwining of loyalty and financial obligations in the feudal system of medieval England.
events.name: Robert FitzWalter, 1st Baron FitzWalter is pardoned

events.enhanced_description: In a politically significant ceremony, King Rudolf I of Bohemia married Elizabeth Richeza, the widow of his predecessor, King Wenceslaus II. This union not only solidified Rudolf's claim to the throne but also reinforced alliances within the region.
events.name: King Rudolf I of Bohemia marries Elizabeth Richeza

events.enhanced_description: After suffering defeat at the hands of King Edward of England, James Stewart, the 5th High Steward of Scotland, reaffirmed his loyalty by swearing fealty at Lanercost Priory. His oath, taken upon sacred relics, highlighted the complex loyalties and religious undertones of feudal allegiances during this tumultuous period.
events.name: James Stewart swears fealty to King Edward

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move to address the ongoing conflict in Scotland, King Edward I of England summoned Parliament to meet in Carlisle. This gathering aimed to discuss the governance and stabilization of Scotland following the recent upheavals.
events.name: King Edward summons Parliament to Carlisle

events.enhanced_description: The monetary policies implemented by King Philip IV of France sparked a revolt in Paris, leading to significant unrest among the populace. The provost's house was set ablaze, forcing the king to seek refuge in the fortress of the Temple, illustrating the volatile relationship between the monarchy and its subjects.
events.name: Monetary policy revolt in Paris

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Glen Trool, Scottish forces led by Robert the Bruce achieved a significant victory against the English army. Utilizing the terrain to their advantage, the Scots executed a surprise attack that decimated the English forces, marking a turning point in the Scottish struggle for independence.
events.name: Battle of Glen Trool

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1307, Januli I da Corogna seized the Aegean Island of Sifnos, declaring himself an autonomous lord after renouncing his allegiance to the Knights Hospitaller. This act marked a significant shift in control over the island.
events.name: Januli I da Corogna seizes Sifnos

events.enhanced_description: In 1307, Duwa Khan, the Mongol ruler of the Chagatai Khanate, passed away after a 25-year reign. He was succeeded by his son Könchek, marking a transition in leadership within the Mongol Empire.
events.name: Duwa Khan dies

events.enhanced_description: In 1307, the village of Heerle in North Brabant was officially proclaimed an independent parish. This development reflected the growing autonomy of local communities in the region.
events.name: Heerle proclaimed an independent parish

events.enhanced_description: King Wareru, the founder of the Martaban Kingdom in southern Myanmar, was assassinated by his grandsons, Shin Gyi and Shin Nge, in a violent act of vengeance for their father's execution. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the kingdom and led to the ascension of Hkun Law as the new king.
events.name: Assassination of King Wareru

events.enhanced_description: The Tokuji era commenced in Japan, marking a new period in the historical timeline. This era would be characterized by significant political and cultural developments as Japan navigated its feudal structure.
events.name: Beginning of the Tokuji era in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Loch Ryan, Thomas de Brus and Alexander de Brus led an invasion force but faced defeat at the hands of rival Scots under Dungal MacDouall. The battle resulted in the capture of the leaders and marked a setback for the Scottish resistance against English rule.
events.name: Battle of Loch Ryan

events.enhanced_description: Temür Khan, the sixth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, passed away at the age of 41 after a 12-year reign. His death marked a significant transition in Mongol leadership as he was succeeded by his nephew, Külüg Khan.
events.name: Death of Temür Khan

events.enhanced_description: Following their capture at Loch Ryan, Thomas de Brus, Alexander de Brus, and Reginald Crawford were executed in Carlisle. Their deaths underscored the harsh realities of the conflict between Scotland and England during this period.
events.name: Execution of Thomas de Brus and others

events.enhanced_description: Fra Dolcino, along with Margaret of Trent and Longino da Bergamo, leaders of the New Apostles movement, were captured in Val Sesia and subsequently tried for heresy on the orders of Pope Clement V. Their trial highlighted the tensions between emerging religious movements and established church authority.
events.name: Capture of Fra Dolcino and others

events.enhanced_description: In spring 1307, King Robert the Bruce of Scotland crossed from the Isle of Arran to his earldom of Carrick with a small force. He attacked the English garrison at Turnberry Castle, while The Black Douglas led a brutal assault on the English garrison at Douglas Castle during a church mass, known as the 'Douglas Larder'.
events.name: King Robert the Bruce crosses to Carrick

events.enhanced_description: King Edward I of England dismissed the Parliaments of Ireland, a significant political maneuver that would leave the governance of Ireland in a state of uncertainty until a new Parliament was convened in 1310.
events.name: Dismissal of the Parliaments of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: Persian historian Rashid al-Din Hamadani completed his monumental work, the Jami' al-tawarikh, which chronicled the history of Persia. This comprehensive account became a vital source for understanding Persian history and culture.
events.name: Completion of Jami' al-tawarikh

events.enhanced_description: Ralph Baldock, Bishop of London, ascended to the position of Lord Chancellor of England following the death of William Hamilton. His tenure, however, was brief, lasting less than four months, reflecting the instability of political appointments during this period.
events.name: Ralph Baldock becomes Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Loudoun Hill saw Scottish forces under Robert the Bruce decisively defeat an English army led by Aymer de Valence. The Scots' strategic use of the marshy terrain thwarted the English cavalry, marking a crucial victory in the ongoing Wars of Scottish Independence.
events.name: Battle of Loudoun Hill

events.enhanced_description: Abu Yaqub Yusuf an-Nasr, the Marinid ruler of Morocco, was assassinated, leading to a power vacuum and potential instability within the Marinid dynasty. His death marked a significant event in the political landscape of North Africa.
events.name: Assassination of Abu Yaqub Yusuf an-Nasr

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Külüg Khan as Khan of the Mongol Empire and Emperor Wuzong of the Yuan dynasty took place in Khanbaliq, present-day Beijing. This event marked the continuation of Mongol rule in China and the consolidation of power under Külüg Khan.
events.name: Coronation of Külüg Khan

events.enhanced_description: Rudolf I, the king of Bohemia, passed away, marking the end of his reign. His death had significant implications for the political landscape of Bohemia and the surrounding regions.
events.name: Death of Rudolf I of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: King Edward I of England, known as Edward Longshanks, died at Burgh by Sands after a 34-year reign. His death marked a significant transition in English history, leading to the ascension of his son, Edward II, and a shift in the political dynamics of the kingdom.
events.name: Death of King Edward I of England

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1307, King Edward II of England, shortly after his proclamation as king, journeyed from London to Scotland. In Dumfries, he received homage from his Scottish supporters, marking a significant moment in his early reign as he sought to consolidate power in the turbulent Scottish territories.
events.name: King Edward II travels from London to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1307, King Edward II of England made significant changes to his government by appointing Gilbert Segrave as Lord Chancellor, replacing Ralph Baldock. This marked the beginning of Edward's efforts to establish his authority and reshape the English administration.
events.name: Gilbert Segrave replaces Ralph Baldock as Lord Chancellor

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1307, King Edward II of England decided to abandon his military campaign against Scotland, opting instead to recall his favorite, Piers Gaveston, from exile. This decision was pivotal as it reflected Edward's prioritization of personal alliances over military endeavors.
events.name: King Edward II abandons the campaign against Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1307, William Cragh testified before a papal commission in Hereford regarding the alleged miracle of his resurrection, attributed to Bishop Thomas de Cantilupe. This event was part of the process leading to Cantilupe's eventual canonization.
events.name: William Cragh testifies before a papal commission

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1307, John de Benstede was dismissed from his position as Chancellor of the Exchequer by King Edward II, who appointed John Sandale in his place. This change was part of Edward's broader strategy to consolidate power and reshape his administration.
events.name: John de Benstede dismissed as Chancellor of the Exchequer

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1307, Walter Reynolds was appointed as the new Lord High Treasurer of England, succeeding Walter Langton. This appointment was part of King Edward II's efforts to establish a loyal and effective government.
events.name: Walter Reynolds becomes Lord High Treasurer

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1307, King Edward II summoned his first Parliament, instructing members to be elected and convene in Northampton on October 13. This event marked a significant step in Edward's governance as he sought to involve the nobility in the political process.
events.name: King Edward II summons his first Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1307, Pope Clement V issued a papal bull confirming that the island of Rhodes would be the property of the Knights Hospitaller. This decision solidified the Knights' influence in the region during a time of significant political and military activity.
events.name: Papal bull confirming Rhodes as property of the Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1307, a marriage contract was finalized between Otto IV, Count of Burgundy, and King Philip IV of France for the marriage of Otto's daughter Blanche to Philip's son Charles. This alliance was significant in strengthening ties between the two noble houses.
events.name: Marriage contract between Otto IV and Philip IV's son

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of all members of the Knights Templar in France, including their Grand Master Jacques de Molay. This event marked the beginning of a brutal crackdown on the Templars, leading to widespread torture and confessions of heresy.
events.name: King Philip IV orders the arrest of the Knights Templar

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1307, the Mongol General Bilarghu hosted Armenian Kings Hethum II and Leo III at a banquet in his castle at Anazarbus. Tragically, after the banquet, Bilarghu ordered the massacre of the Armenian royalty and nobles, showcasing the brutal political dynamics of the time.
events.name: Mongol General Bilarghu hosts Armenian Kings

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1307, the legendary Swiss hero William Tell is said to have shot an apple off his son's head with a crossbow in Altdorf, Switzerland. This act of defiance against tyranny has become a symbol of Swiss independence and resistance.
events.name: William Tell shoots the apple off his son's head

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1307, following King Philip IV's lead, Pope Clement V issued a decree instructing all Christian monarchs to arrest the Knights Templar and confiscate their lands. This papal bull significantly impacted the Templars' fate across Europe.
events.name: Pope Clement V issues decree against the Knights Templar

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1307, Theodoric IV, the ruler of the semi-independent states of Lusatia, Osterland, and Thuringia, was murdered in Leipzig by Philip of Nassau. This assassination led to a power shift in the region, with Frederick the Brave and Otto IV of Brandenburg succeeding him.
events.name: Theodoric IV is murdered at Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1307, the three-day Battle of Slioch commenced in Scotland, where King Robert the Bruce and his forces successfully repelled the troops of John Comyn. This battle was part of the larger struggle for Scottish independence.
events.name: Battle of Slioch begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1308, Hungarian nobles formally elected the 20-year-old Charles Robert of Salerno as King of Hungary and Croatia in Pest, now part of Budapest. Although crowned as Charles I, his rule faced challenges, remaining nominal in many parts of the realm.
events.name: Election of Charles Robert of Salerno as King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Mesud II, a Seljuk vassal of the Mongol Ilkhanate, was murdered on January 1, 1308, after a five-year reign characterized by a lack of real authority. His death marked the end of the Sultanate of Rum, which had lasted for 230 years.
events.name: Murder of Sultan Mesud II

events.enhanced_description: In 1308, King Philip IV of France purchased the Hôtel de Nesle in Paris, where he constructed one of the earliest indoor tennis courts. This development reflects the growing popularity of tennis in medieval France.
events.name: King Philip IV purchases Hôtel de Nesle

events.enhanced_description: Following the victory at Inverurie, Scottish forces under Edward Bruce conducted the harrying of Buchan in 1308, devastating the lands of John Comyn and his supporters. This campaign furthered Robert the Bruce's efforts to consolidate power in Scotland.
events.name: Harrying of Buchan

events.enhanced_description: In 1308, Dante Alighieri began composing his monumental work, the Divine Comedy, which includes the sections Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. This epic poem is considered one of the most significant works of medieval literature.
events.name: Dante Alighieri begins work on Divine Comedy

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1308, King Edward II of England married Isabella of France, the 13-year-old daughter of King Philip IV. The marriage, held in Boulogne, was politically motivated, but Edward's favoritism towards Piers Gaveston soon caused tensions with the nobility.

image.caption: Monument to Edward II at Gloucester Cathedral.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2023-08-19; this is a later monument, not a contemporary image of the marriage.

events.name: King Edward II marries Isabella of France

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1308, Herman I the Tall, Margrave of Brandenburg-Salzwedel, died and was succeeded by his son John V. This transition marked a significant moment in the governance of Brandenburg during a period of political complexity.
events.name: Herman I the Tall dies

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1308, Edward II was crowned at Westminster Abbey, with Bishop Henry Woodlock officiating. The ceremony was notable for Piers Gaveston's prominent role, which later fueled discontent among the nobility regarding Edward's favoritism.
events.name: Edward II crowned at Westminster Abbey

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1308, King Denis of Portugal, known as 'the Poet King', granted a charter to Póvoa de Varzim, allowing 54 families to establish a municipality around Praça Velha. This act was significant in the development of local governance in Portugal.
events.name: King Denis grants charter to Póvoa de Varzim

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1308, brothers Andrei Rurik and Lev II Rurik ascended as co-monarchs of Ruthenia following the death of their father, King Yuri I of Galicia. Their reign would last until their deaths in 1323, during a battle against Mongol invaders.
events.name: Andrei Rurik and Lev II Rurik become co-monarchs of Ruthenia

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1308, Abu Hammu I ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Tlemcen following the death of his brother, Sultan Abu Zayyan I. This transition marked a continuation of the ruling dynasty in the region.
events.name: Abu Hammu I becomes ruler of Tlemcen

events.enhanced_description: King Albrecht I of Germany, a prominent ruler within the Holy Roman Empire, was assassinated by his nephew John of Swabia in Windisch, Switzerland, following a heated argument at a banquet in Winterthur. This act of familial betrayal marked a significant turning point in the power dynamics of the region.
events.name: Assassination of King Albrecht I of Germany

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Inverurie, Scottish forces led by King Robert the Bruce achieved a decisive victory over the rival Scots under John Comyn. This battle not only solidified Bruce's power but also marked a significant decline for Clan Comyn in Scotland.
events.name: Battle of Inverurie

events.enhanced_description: Piers Gaveston was exiled for the second time by the English Parliament due to allegations of corruption. Despite this, he was granted land in Gascony and appointed Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, showcasing the complex interplay of power and favoritism in Edward II's reign.
events.name: Exile of Piers Gaveston

events.enhanced_description: Following the conviction of 138 members of the Knights Templar for heresy, a trial was held for 54 Templars who testified before Pope Clement V. Most confessed to at least one charge, leading to significant repercussions for the order.
events.name: Trial of the Knights Templar

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1308, Scottish forces led by King Robert the Bruce defeated the Clan MacDougall at the Battle of the Pass of Brander. Utilizing strategic positioning, Bruce's forces overcame their rivals, solidifying his control over the region.
events.name: Battle of the Pass of Brander

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 1308, Malik Kafur led forces from Delhi to invade the Yadava Kingdom, which was ruled by King Ramachandra. The invasion resulted in Ramachandra acknowledging Delhi's overlordship after seeking peace.
events.name: Invasion of the Yadava Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: Alauddin Khalji, the Sultan of Delhi, initiated the siege of Siwana Fort, which he successfully captured in September 1308. This military campaign was part of his broader strategy to expand his empire in northern India.
events.name: Siege of Siwana

events.enhanced_description: The death of Abu Thabit 'Amir marked a significant transition in the Marinid Sultanate, as he was succeeded by his brother Abu al-Rabi Sulayman. This change in leadership would influence the political landscape of Morocco.
events.name: Death of Abu Thabit 'Amir

events.enhanced_description: Chungseon of Goryeo ascended to the throne of Korea for the second time following the death of his father, King Chungnyeol. His return to power was significant in the context of Goryeo's turbulent political landscape.
events.name: Chungseon of Goryeo becomes King of Korea

events.enhanced_description: Pope Clement V authorized the Knights Hospitaller to commence the Crusade of the Poor, reflecting the ongoing religious fervor and the complex dynamics of power within the Church during this period.
events.name: Pope Clement V grants permission for the Crusade of the Poor

events.enhanced_description: Pope Clement V published the papal bull Faciens Misericordiam, which absolved the Knights Templar from heresy charges and established that the Roman Catholic Church would oversee future accusations against the order.
events.name: Papal Bull Faciens Misericordiam

events.enhanced_description: The death of King Ananta Malla after a 34-year reign left the kingdom of Nepal without a monarch for five years, leading to a power vacuum and potential instability in the region.
events.name: Death of King Ananta Malla of Nepal

events.enhanced_description: The Knights Hospitaller completed their conquest of the Greek island of Rhodes after four years of military campaigns, establishing a significant stronghold in the Eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: Conquest of Rhodes by the Knights Hospitaller

events.enhanced_description: The Chinon Parchment, authored by Cardinal Berengar Fredol the Elder, summarized the findings of investigations into the Knights Templar. This document remained hidden in the Vatican Apostolic Archive for nearly seven centuries before its rediscovery.
events.name: Chinon Parchment written

events.enhanced_description: Prince Morikuni ascended to the position of the ninth and last shogun of the Kamakura bakufu, marking the end of an era in Japanese feudal history.
events.name: Prince Morikuni becomes Shogun

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 11, Hanazono ascended to the throne as the 95th Emperor of Japan following the death of his cousin, Emperor Go-Nijō. His reign would last until 1348, during a tumultuous period in Japanese history.
events.name: Hanazono becomes Emperor of Japan

events.enhanced_description: The death of Guy II de la Roche at the young age of 28 marked the end of the de la Roche dynasty in the Duchy of Athens. His cousin, Walter V, Count of Brienne, succeeded him, leading to a shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Death of Guy II de la Roche

events.enhanced_description: The English Parliament convened for its fourth session during the reign of King Edward II at Westminster, reflecting the ongoing political developments and challenges of the time.
events.name: Fourth session of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: Following the fall of Siwana, Prince Sital Deva was ambushed while attempting to escape to Jalor. His subsequent decapitation and presentation of his head to Sultan Alauddin Khalji underscored the brutal nature of the conflict.
events.name: Ambush of Prince Sital Deva

events.enhanced_description: The Teutonic Knights captured Gdańsk through treachery while a Brandenburger force laid siege to the city. This brutal act resulted in widespread destruction and marked a significant expansion of Teutonic power in the region.
events.name: Capture of Gdańsk by the Teutonic Knights

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Emperor Hanazono took place in Edo, marking the beginning of his reign during a critical period in Japanese history. His rule would last until 1348, influencing the course of the Kamakura period.
events.name: Coronation of Emperor Hanazono of Japan

events.enhanced_description: Henry VII of Luxembourg was elected the new Holy Roman Emperor in Frankfurt, with the backing of his brother Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier. This election was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Election of Henry VII as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: King Władysław I Łokietek of Poland imprisoned Jan Muskata, the Bishop of Kraków, leading to widespread revolts among Polish and German citizens. The king's harsh response to the uprising highlighted the tensions within his rule.
events.name: Imprisonment of Jan Muskata

events.enhanced_description: Tran Anh Tong ascended to the throne of Dai Viet following the death of his father, Tran Nhan Tong. His reign would continue the legacy of the Tran dynasty in northern Vietnam.
events.name: Tran Anh Tong becomes Emperor of Dai Viet

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Alcalá de Henares was signed by King Ferdinand IV of Castile and King James II of Aragon, establishing an alliance against Granada. This treaty was significant in the context of the Reconquista in Spain.

locations.name: Alcalá de Henares, Community of Madrid, Spain

events.name: Treaty of Alcalá de Henares

events.enhanced_description: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi completed writing Tanqih al-Manazir in Ramadan 708 H.E. The work revised Ibn al-Haytham’s optics treatise.

image.caption: Photograph of Kamal al-Din al-Farisi’s autograph manuscript, *Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir*.

events.name: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi completes the Tanqih al-Manazir

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1309, Henry of Luxemburg was crowned as 'King of the Romans' in Aachen, a title that positioned him as the heir to the Holy Roman Emperor. He would later ascend to the imperial throne in 1312.
events.name: Coronation of Henry of Luxemburg

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1309, Pope Clement V initiated an investigation and posthumous trial of his predecessor, Pope Boniface VIII, in Avignon. Boniface had been accused of heresy and sodomy, a controversial move that reflected the political tensions of the time.
events.name: Investigation of Pope Boniface VIII
